title: After Christendom & the Captive Church
subtitle: Faith after the flag, the tribe, and the empire
blurb: Essays on the church's captivity to nation, tribe, and culture — Christian nationalism, the end of cultural Christianity, and what a faithful, exiled church looks like on the other side.

chapters.title: Christendom Is Ending. Christianity Is Not.
chapters.summary: The arrangement that made Christianity the default religion of the West is dying, and many believers are grieving the wrong thing.
chapters.body:
A pastor I respect told me the country is losing its faith, and he meant it as a funeral. The polls back him up. Church attendance falls. The category of no religion grows fastest. Prayer leaves the schools, the chaplain leaves the statehouse by degrees, and the cultural assumption that a decent person is probably some kind of Christian has thinned to almost nothing. He called it the end of Christianity in America. He grieved. So did I, for a while.

Then I noticed we were grieving two different things and using one word for both. There is Christianity, the body of people who confess that Jesus is Lord and order their lives around a crucified man who walked out of a tomb. And there is Christendom, the social arrangement in which that confession is the default setting of a civilization, baked into its laws and its calendar and its manners, so that belonging to the culture and belonging to the church feel like the same act. These are not the same thing. One is dying. The other has survived the death of empires before, and will survive this one.

The text I want to carry through this is older than the problem. The kingdom of God is like a grain of mustard seed, the smallest of seeds, which becomes a tree where the birds nest (Matthew 13:31-32 ESV). Notice what the parable does not promise. It does not promise that the tree will own the field, or pass the laws, or seat the king. It promises growth from smallness, life from something you could lose in the dirt. Jesus described his movement in terms of the smallest thing in the garden, not the largest thing in the empire. We spent sixteen centuries assuming he meant the empire anyway.

The steel man is strong, and I will not pretend otherwise. The defenders of Christendom are not power-drunk theocrats in a cartoon. They are people who have looked at what replaces a Christian cultural frame and found it wanting. They point out, correctly, that the institutions a skeptic loves, the hospital, the university, the very idea that the weak have worth the strong must honor, grew in soil that Christendom tilled. They point out that a culture does not float free of its founding convictions, and that when you pull the root you should not be surprised when the fruit rots. Oliver O'Donovan has made the serious case that political authority itself was reshaped by the gospel, that the West did not merely tolerate Christianity but was bent by it into new shapes of mercy and law (O'Donovan 1996). When such people grieve the end of Christendom, they are grieving something real. A scaffolding is coming down, and scaffolding holds things up.

So here is the answer to the strong version, not the weak one. Yes, Christendom built hospitals and universities and a moral grammar the secular world still borrows without paying. But the same arrangement that built those things also built something the gospel never asked for, a Christianity you could inherit without ever meeting Christ. When faith is the default, faith is cheap. When the whole culture calls itself Christian, the word stops meaning anyone in particular. Soren Kierkegaard saw this in the nineteenth century and called it the great illusion of Christendom, a nation of Christians none of whom had been confronted by the offense of the cross, because everyone was already a Christian the way everyone was already Danish (Kierkegaard 1850). The thing dying now is partly the thing he was trying to kill from the inside.

Trace the root. The arrangement begins with a date, 312, the night before the Milvian Bridge, when Constantine reportedly saw a sign and won an empire and gave the church the keys to the city it had been dying outside of. By 380 the Edict of Thessalonica made Nicene Christianity the official religion of the Roman state. In three generations the faith went from a persecuted minority that buried its martyrs in secret to the establishment that could persecute in turn. That is the founding of Christendom, and it was a genuine mercy after the slaughter, and it was also the moment the mustard seed got mistaken for the cedar of Lebanon. The faith stopped looking like Jesus describing the smallest seed and started looking like the thing the seed was supposed to replace.

Here is the reversal the grieving pastor could not see. The end of Christendom is not the defeat of the church. It is the return of the church to the only conditions under which it has ever known how to grow. The faith was born under a hostile empire, with no laws on its side, no calendar in its favor, no social reward for belonging. It grew anyway, faster in those three centuries before Constantine than in many of the centuries after. Stanley Hauerwas and William Willimon wrote that the church does not have a social strategy, the church is a social strategy, a colony of resident aliens whose very existence is its witness, and they called the demise of the Constantinian arrangement not a death to lament but an opportunity to celebrate, the freeing of the church to be faithful again (Hauerwas and Willimon 1989). Not because loss is good. Because clarity is.

Lesslie Newbigin came home to England in 1974 after decades as a missionary in India and found his own country a stranger, a place that had been Christian and was now something harder to name, a pagan culture with Christian memories. He did not try to rebuild the establishment. He asked the more useful question, how does the gospel address a culture that thinks it already knows what the gospel is and has moved on (Newbigin 1986). That is the question on the table now, and you cannot ask it while you are busy defending a throne.

There is a second mercy hidden in the loss, and it has to do with witness. When the culture and the church wore the same clothes, the watching world could not see anything distinct to be drawn toward, because the Christians looked exactly like everyone else, voted the same fears, chased the same security, divorced at the same rate, and the only visible difference was an hour on Sunday. A faith that cannot be distinguished from its surroundings cannot bear witness to anything beyond them. The end of Christendom strips the camouflage. It forces the question the early church answered with their bodies, what does this community do that the surrounding world cannot explain, and a church that has no answer to that question was never the seed at all. It was the dirt the seed got lost in.

I feel the loss honestly. I have five sons, and the world that will hand them their assumptions is not the world that handed me mine, where a closed store on Sunday still meant something. Part of me wants the old scaffolding back, the cultural Christianity that made my job easier, that filled pews with people who came because that is what people did. But I have to be honest about what filled those pews. Habit filled them. Respectability filled them. The fear of being the odd family on the street filled them. Those are not the gospel. Those are the things the gospel has to compete with, and Christendom hid the competition by making them wear the same clothes.

The cross does the work here, where it always does. A crucified Lord cannot be the mascot of a comfortable culture, because the culture that crucified him was the comfortable, established, respectable one, the one that had its religion and its empire arranged just so. When the church holds power, it forgets this. It starts to imagine that the gospel needs a throne to be true. But the gospel was truest when it had nothing, when it was a man on a Roman cross and a handful of terrified followers who had bet everything on a story that ended in execution. That faith did not need Christendom to be born. It will not need Christendom to survive its death.

So grieve the right thing. Grieve the hospitals if they close and the mercy if it curdles, and fight for those, because they are good. But do not grieve the death of cultural Christianity as if the church were in the coffin. The seed is still in the ground. It was always smaller than the tree we mistook it for.

What dies is the empire's religion. What remains is the crucified man's church.

### Works Cited

Hauerwas, Stanley, and William H. Willimon. Resident Aliens: Life in the Christian Colony. Nashville: Abingdon Press, 1989.

Kierkegaard, Soren. Practice in Christianity. 1850. Translated by Howard V. Hong and Edna H. Hong. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1991.

Newbigin, Lesslie. Foolishness to the Greeks: The Gospel and Western Culture. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 1986.

O'Donovan, Oliver. The Desire of the Nations: Rediscovering the Roots of Political Theology. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1996.

chapters.title: Consumerism Is a Spiritual Formation
chapters.summary: The mall is not neutral, it is a cathedral, and we have been worshiping in it longer than we have been worshiping anywhere else.
chapters.body:
My sons can tell the difference between two phones I cannot see a difference between. They were not taught this in any class. No one sat them down. They absorbed it the way I absorbed my father's absence, which is to say through the body, through repetition, through a thousand small mornings that added up to a shape before anyone named the shape. They have been formed. The question that should keep a pastor awake is not whether they have been formed but by what, and toward what end.

We assume that what makes us who we are is what we believe. State the doctrine, win the mind, and the life follows. This is the great quiet error of the modern church, and I held it for years. We built ministries on the premise that the human being is fundamentally a thinker, a brain on a stick, and that if we could only get the right information into the head the body would fall in line. So we lectured. We informed. And we watched people who could pass a theology exam live indistinguishably from their unbelieving neighbors, and we blamed their willpower, when the problem was never the head.

Here is the strongest case for the way we have done it, and it deserves respect. Truth matters. Doctrine is not optional. The mind is not nothing, and a faith that cannot say what it believes is a feeling waiting to evaporate. The long Christian tradition of catechism, of teaching the faith as content, saved generations from sentimentality and heresy alike. A church that stops caring whether things are true has already begun to die. I will not give an inch on that. The skeptic who prizes evidence and clear thinking is closer to the kingdom than the believer who prizes a warm vague glow.

But here is where that case runs out. You are not primarily what you think. You are what you love, and you do not choose your loves the way you choose your beliefs. James K. A. Smith put it as sharply as anyone has in a generation. He argues that human beings are desiring creatures before we are thinking creatures, that we are shaped most deeply not by ideas we consider but by practices we repeat, by what he calls cultural liturgies, the rituals that aim our love at something before our mind ever weighs in (Smith 2009). And the most powerful liturgy in the modern world is not held in a church. It is held in a mall, and now it is held in your hand.

Walk through what the mall does, because Smith is right that it is a temple and we should say so plainly. It has a clean and beautiful interior set apart from the street. It has icons in the windows, images of the redeemed life, bodies made perfect, the promise of belonging. It has an order of service. You enter, you wander, you are met by ministers who help you find your size, you make your sacrifice at the register, and you leave carrying a small sacrament in a bag, briefly fuller, soon empty, certain to return. No one believes a doctrine here. Everyone is being formed here. The mall does not care what you think about the mall. It only needs you to keep coming, and you do.

Carry one text. Jesus does not say where your treasure is, there your thinking will be correct. He says, For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also (Matthew 6:21 ESV). Notice the order. He does not say fix your heart and your spending will follow. He says follow the money and you will find the heart, because the heart goes where the treasure has already gone. Spending is not the symptom. Spending is the formation. Every purchase is a small act of worship that trains the desires a little more, and after ten thousand of them you are a certain kind of person, and you never decided to be.

Trace the history, because this captivity has a date. The American economy of the early twentieth century faced a crisis the founders of advertising named openly. Production had outrun need. The factories could make more than people wanted. The solution, pioneered by men like Edward Bernays in the 1920s, was to manufacture wants, to attach products to desires that had nothing to do with the product. Bernays famously staged a group of women lighting cigarettes in a public parade, an image his circle framed as torches of freedom, and the method he helped pioneer taught a generation of admakers to bind a product to status or identity rather than to mere use. The point, in his hands and theirs, was to sell the cigarette as emancipation and, later, the car as a self, to graft the product onto a hunger it could never actually satisfy. Jacques Ellul saw the deeper machinery. He argued that modern technique and the propaganda that serves it do not merely persuade us of things, they integrate us into a system, forming the individual to fit the apparatus, so that the person comes to want exactly what the system needs him to want and calls it his own free choice (Ellul 1964). The genius of consumer formation is that it never feels like formation. It feels like me being myself. That is what makes it a liturgy and not an argument.

Now the reversal. We think the danger of consumerism is that it makes us want bad things. The deeper danger is what it does to wanting itself. It trains us to be people who are constituted by acquisition, who resolve every ache by purchasing, who cannot sit in an unsatisfied moment for ninety seconds without reaching for the phone to buy our way out of it. It does not corrupt our desires so much as it corrupts our capacity to desire God, who cannot be acquired, who will not fit in the bag, who asks not to be consumed but to be loved. A people trained for sixty years to fill every emptiness will not know what to do with a God who sometimes leaves the emptiness in order to fill it himself.

Law before grace, and the law is heavy. I am formed by this. I do not stand above it as a diagnostician. I reach for my phone in the silence. I have measured my worth by what I could afford and felt the lift of a purchase and called that lift joy. I have preached against the mall on Sunday and shopped my way through Monday's anxiety, and the gap between those two days is the size of my actual discipleship. The honest word is that the liturgies of the market have catechized me more hours than the church ever has, and it is not close.

The grace is that formation answers formation. If we are shaped by repeated practice and not by single decisions, then the worn old disciplines of the church are not quaint, they are counter formation, deliberate liturgies aimed at retraining a heart the market has trained against itself. The Lord's table is the anti mall, a meal you cannot buy, a sacrifice already made, a belonging you did not shop for. The Sabbath is a refusal to produce or to purchase for one day in seven, a weekly act of treason against an economy that needs you restless. These are not tips. They are the slow reconstruction of a person, and like all formation they work only by repetition, only by years, only by coming to the table on the mornings you would rather be at the store.

We became what we bought while we were busy guarding what we believed.

The heart went where the treasure went. It always does.

### Works Cited

Smith, James K. A. Desiring the Kingdom: Worship, Worldview, and Cultural Formation. Grand Rapids: Baker Academic, 2009.

Ellul, Jacques. The Technological Society. Translated by John Wilkinson. New York: Vintage Books, 1964.

The Holy Bible. English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

chapters.title: Deconstruction Is Not Destruction
chapters.summary: Deconstruction is not a trend, a phase, or a gateway to atheism. It is the ancient, necessary work of distinguishing the living God from the idols we have built in God's name. The church's failure to understand this is accelerating the very losses it fears.
chapters.body:
The word "deconstruction" has become, in certain Christian circles, a term of opprobrium, a diagnosis that means the patient has been infected by the culture and is now spiritually terminal. Pastors warn against it from pulpits. Podcasters devote entire series to refuting it. Denominational leaders treat it as a contagion to be quarantined. The anxiety is palpable, and it is almost entirely misdirected.

What most of these critics are reacting to is not deconstruction itself but a caricature of it: a social media phenomenon in which photogenic former evangelicals announce their departure from the faith in a series of Instagram posts, accumulate followers, and monetize their disenchantment. This phenomenon is real, and some of it is indeed shallow. But to confuse it with the actual process of deconstruction is like confusing a fast-food advertisement with the agricultural science that produces the food. The surface presentation tells you almost nothing about what is actually happening underneath.

Deconstruction, properly understood, is not a TikTok trend. It is a philosophical and theological process with deep roots in Western intellectual history, and it describes something that the church's own scriptures commend, demand, and model.

What Deconstruction Actually Means

The term "deconstruction" entered the philosophical lexicon through Jacques Derrida, the French-Algerian philosopher who developed it in the late 1960s. Derrida's project was epistemological: he was interested in how meaning is constructed through language, and he argued that all systems of meaning contain internal contradictions, assumptions, and hierarchies that, upon examination, reveal the instability of what had appeared stable. Deconstruction, for Derrida, was not demolition. It was analysis. It was the patient work of examining the foundations of a structure to understand what they were actually made of.

The theologian John Caputo, who has done more than anyone to bring Derrida's thought into conversation with Christian theology, argues that deconstruction is not the enemy of faith but its ally. "Deconstruction is the hermeneutics of the kingdom of God," Caputo writes in What Would Jesus Deconstruct? (2007). By this he means that the prophetic tradition, the tradition of Jesus himself, is a tradition of questioning established structures, exposing pretense, and refusing to allow human institutions to claim divine authority uncritically.

When applied to faith, deconstruction does not mean tearing everything down. It means examining the layers: distinguishing between the bedrock of genuine encounter with God and the cultural, political, and psychological material that has accumulated on top of it. It means asking which of your beliefs are actually rooted in scripture, reason, and experience, and which are inherited assumptions that you have never questioned because questioning was not permitted.

This is, by any honest account, a necessary process. Every thoughtful person of faith does it to some degree. The question is whether the church will accompany people through it or punish them for undertaking it.

Deconstruction vs. Deconversion

One of the most critical distinctions the church consistently fails to make is between deconstruction and deconversion. They are not the same thing. They may overlap in some cases, but they describe fundamentally different processes.

Deconstruction is the critical examination of one's faith framework: the beliefs, practices, assumptions, and authorities that have shaped one's understanding of God, the Bible, the church, and the moral life. It is interrogation, not abandonment. A person who is deconstructing is asking, "Is what I was taught actually true? Is it faithful to the tradition it claims to represent? Does it produce the kind of life it promises?" These are not the questions of an enemy. They are the questions of someone who cares deeply enough to demand honesty.

Deconversion is the departure from faith altogether. It is the conclusion, reached after examination or exhaustion or both, that the entire framework is untenable, that there is no God, no transcendence, no story worth believing. Deconversion is a real phenomenon, and it deserves to be taken seriously rather than dismissed. But it is not the inevitable outcome of deconstruction. It is one possible outcome among many.

The church's tragic error has been to treat deconstruction as if it were always the first step toward deconversion, and therefore to resist it at all costs. This resistance has the perverse effect of making deconversion more likely. When a person begins to question their inherited faith and is met with fear, hostility, and threats of damnation, the message they receive is clear: this tradition cannot withstand scrutiny. A faith that punishes questions is a faith that has already conceded it does not have answers. And a person who has been told that questioning is the same as leaving will eventually take the church at its word and leave.

What Gets Deconstructed

It is essential to be specific about what people are actually deconstructing, because the objects of deconstruction are rarely the things the church assumes.

Most people who describe themselves as deconstructing are not questioning whether God exists. They are questioning whether the God they were taught about exists, the God who sends billions of people to eternal conscious torment for failing to recite the correct prayer, the God who ordained male headship as a cosmic principle, the God who blesses America specifically, the God who requires young-earth creationism as a condition of salvation, the God who hates the same people the congregation hates. They are not deconstructing the divine. They are deconstructing a particular construction of the divine, and they are discovering, often with great relief, that the construction is not the same as the reality.

Others are deconstructing toxic theology: the prosperity gospel's equation of faithfulness with financial success, purity culture's reduction of human sexuality to a set of prohibitions and shame, the nationalist theology that equates Christianity with Western civilization, the authoritarian ecclesiology that demands unquestioning obedience to pastoral authority. These are not peripheral issues. They are, for millions of people, the only version of Christianity they have ever known. When someone says, "I am deconstructing my faith," they may well mean, "I am dismantling the only theology I was ever given, because it made me hate myself and fear God and distrust my own conscience."

Still others are deconstructing power structures: the patriarchal systems that exclude women from leadership, the racial hierarchies that have been baptized as divine order, the class assumptions that make middle-class American culture the unmarked norm of Christian life, the celebrity pastor culture that concentrates spiritual authority in charismatic individuals with no meaningful accountability. These structures are not the faith. They are barnacles on the hull, and scraping them off is not an act of vandalism but of maintenance.

Biblical Precedent: The Tradition of Holy Disruption

The irony of the church's resistance to deconstruction is that the Bible itself is, in significant measure, a record of deconstruction. The prophetic tradition, which stands at the heart of Israel's self-understanding, is a tradition of relentless institutional critique.

The book of Job is a sustained deconstruction of retributive theology, the belief that suffering is always a punishment for sin and prosperity is always a reward for righteousness. Job's friends, who are stand-ins for conventional religious wisdom, insist that Job's suffering must be deserved. Job refuses to accept this. He demands an audience with God, not to reject God but to insist that God is more than the theology his friends have constructed. When God finally speaks from the whirlwind, the answer is not a defense of conventional theology but a demolition of it: "Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth?" The message is clear. Your theology is too small. The reality of God exceeds your categories.

Ecclesiastes is perhaps the most radical act of deconstruction in the entire biblical canon. Its author, traditionally identified as Solomon, systematically dismantles every source of meaning that conventional wisdom offers: wealth, pleasure, achievement, even wisdom itself. "Vanity of vanities," the Preacher declares, "all is vanity." This is not nihilism. It is the necessary clearing away of false foundations so that something more durable can be built. The book ends not with despair but with a chastened, honest faith: "Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of humanity."

The Psalms of lament, which constitute roughly one-third of the Psalter, are acts of deconstruction addressed directly to God. Psalm 88 ends in darkness, with no resolution, no upward turn, no reassuring conclusion. Psalm 22 begins with the cry that Jesus himself would quote from the cross: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" These are not psalms of doubt. They are psalms of faith so honest that they refuse to pretend things are fine when they are not. They deconstruct the pious fiction that faith means perpetual contentment, and they insist that honest anguish is more faithful than dishonest praise.

And then there is Jesus, who overturned the tables in the temple, a physical act of deconstruction so violent and deliberate that it cannot be spiritualized away. The temple was the center of Israel's religious life, the dwelling place of God, the institution that mediated between the human and the divine. Jesus did not critique it from a safe distance. He walked in and disrupted it. He accused its managers of turning a house of prayer into a den of robbers. He did not destroy the temple, though the Gospels record him prophesying its destruction. He deconstructed its pretensions, its economic exploitation, its claim to be the exclusive point of access to God.

If deconstruction is faithless, then Job is faithless. Ecclesiastes is faithless. The Psalmists are faithless. Jesus is faithless. The tradition that condemns deconstruction must reckon with the fact that its own scriptures are full of it.

How to Deconstruct Without Losing Everything

The danger of deconstruction, real and not to be dismissed, is that it can become an end in itself. There are people for whom the critical posture becomes habitual, who find in perpetual questioning a way to avoid the vulnerability of commitment. Deconstruction without reconstruction is demolition. Tearing down a building may be necessary, but if you never build anything in its place, you are left standing in a vacant lot.

The key to healthy deconstruction, the kind that leads to deeper faith rather than to nihilism, lies in several practices that the church could facilitate if it chose to.

First, honesty about what is actually being questioned. Not every doubt is the same. Questioning whether God exists is different from questioning whether the particular God described by your youth pastor exists. Questioning whether the Bible is worth reading is different from questioning whether a literalist hermeneutic is the only faithful way to read it. Specificity matters. The person who says, "I am losing my faith," often means, "I am losing a particular version of my faith," and the distinction is everything.

Second, historical perspective. Most of what feels unprecedented about contemporary deconstruction has happened before, many times. The early church fathers debated the meaning of scripture with the same intensity that modern deconstructors bring to the task. The Reformation was a massive act of deconstruction directed at medieval Catholic theology and practice. The liberal theology of the nineteenth century was a response to the intellectual challenges posed by Enlightenment thought. Every generation of Christians has had to distinguish between the faith once delivered to the saints and the cultural packaging in which it arrived. You are not the first person to have these questions. You are participating in a tradition.

Third, intellectual seriousness. Many people who deconstruct do so armed with the theology they absorbed in childhood, which is to say, a theology designed for children. They reject a young-earth creationism they were taught in Sunday school without ever encountering the sophisticated theology of creation developed by Aquinas, Barth, or Moltmann. They reject a penal substitutionary atonement presented as the only theory of the cross without ever learning about Christus Victor, moral influence, or participatory atonement. The remedy for bad theology is not no theology. It is better theology.

The Role of Community

Deconstruction in isolation is almost always destructive. The process requires companions: people who have walked the path before, people who can hold space for doubt without panicking, people who can affirm that the questions are valid without pretending they have easy answers.

The church, at its best, has always been this kind of community. The monastic tradition created spaces for contemplation, questioning, and spiritual struggle within a framework of communal support. The Quaker tradition built its entire practice around corporate discernment, the conviction that truth emerges not from individual certainty but from patient, communal listening. The Black church tradition developed what the theologian James Cone called a "theology of survival," a faith forged in the crucible of suffering that did not pretend away the horror of oppression but insisted, against all evidence, that God was present in the struggle.

These traditions demonstrate that honest questioning and deep community are not opposites. They are partners. The community that cannot tolerate questions is not strong. It is brittle. And brittle things break.

What those in deconstruction need from community is not a set of correct answers delivered with confidence. They need accompaniment: people who will sit in the uncertainty with them, who will not rush to resolve the tension, who will affirm that the God who created the human mind is not threatened by its honest use. They need what the Benedictine tradition calls stabilitas, stability, the commitment to stay in relationship even when it is difficult, even when the questions are uncomfortable, even when the process takes longer than anyone wants.

What Reconstruction Looks Like

The testimony of those who have come through deconstruction to a renewed faith is remarkably consistent. The faith on the other side is almost always smaller, humbler, and more honest than the one that preceded it. The grandiose systems, the absolute certainties, the comprehensive worldview that had an answer for everything, these are gone. What remains is sparser and, paradoxically, stronger.

The theologian Richard Rohr describes this as the movement from "first-half-of-life faith" to "second-half-of-life faith." The first half is characterized by boundary-setting, identity formation, and the need for certainty. The second half is characterized by mystery, paradox, and the willingness to hold tension without resolving it. Both are necessary. You cannot skip the first to get to the second. But you also cannot remain in the first without eventually suffocating.

Reconstruction often involves a return to the ancient practices that predate the modern accretions: the liturgical calendar, the daily office, the Eucharist, the lectio divina, the practices of contemplative prayer. People who have deconstructed a megachurch evangelicalism often find themselves drawn to traditions that are older, slower, and less dependent on the personality of a single leader. They discover that the church has resources they were never told about, a two-thousand-year treasury of wisdom, prayer, art, and practice that their particular tradition had walled off.

Reconstruction also involves a more honest relationship with scripture. The Bible, read not as a flat text of equally weighted propositions but as a diverse library of genres, perspectives, and voices in conversation across centuries, becomes richer, not poorer, when the wooden literalism is abandoned. The scholar Walter Brueggemann speaks of the Bible as "a text in travail," a document that wrestles with God rather than simply describing God. This is a Bible that can survive scrutiny, because it was never designed to be read uncritically in the first place.

Deconstruction, rightly understood, is not the enemy of faith. It is faith's immune system, the mechanism by which the body identifies and expels what does not belong so that what does belong can function properly. A faith that cannot survive examination was never worth having. And a faith that emerges from honest examination, scarred and simplified and stripped of pretense, is a faith that can actually bear the weight of a human life.

The church has a choice. It can continue to treat deconstruction as a threat, circling the wagons, demanding loyalty, and excommunicating questioners. This approach will produce exactly the outcome it fears: a steady exodus of the most thoughtful, most committed, most spiritually serious members of the community. Or it can recognize deconstruction for what it is, a painful but necessary process of refinement, and learn to walk with people through it. The latter requires courage, humility, and a willingness to admit that some of what the church has built deserves to come down.

The prophet Jeremiah, commissioned by God, was told his vocation involved two movements: "to pluck up and to pull down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant." The sequence is not accidental. The tearing down comes first. You cannot plant in ground that has not been cleared. You cannot build on a foundation that has not been tested. Deconstruction is the tearing down. It is not the end of the story. But it is, for many, the only honest place to begin.

chapters.title: Exvangelical: When Leaving Isn't Losing Faith
chapters.summary: The exvangelical movement is not a rejection of Jesus. It is a rejection of what certain institutions have done with his name, and the distinction matters more than most churches are willing to admit.
chapters.body:
The word arrived with the force of a confession. Exvangelical. It surfaced on social media around 2016, coined by Blake Chastain as a podcast title, but the reality it named had been gathering for at least a decade before that. People were leaving evangelical churches in numbers that could no longer be dismissed as backsliding or cultural drift. They were leaving deliberately, articulately, and often in tremendous pain. They were not becoming atheists, most of them. They were becoming something the evangelical framework had no category for: Christians who could no longer remain in the tradition that had formed them.

The distinction is essential and almost always collapsed. To leave evangelicalism is not to leave Christianity. It is to leave a particular institutional and theological expression of Christianity — one that, for many who have departed, had become so identified with political power, cultural rigidity, and institutional self-protection that it no longer resembled the faith it claimed to represent. The conflation of leaving a tradition with leaving the faith is itself one of evangelicalism's most damaging habits of thought. It assumes that evangelicalism is Christianity's final and most faithful form, and that departure from it is departure from God. That assumption is historically illiterate and theologically unsustainable, but it remains the operating framework for millions of American Christians.

To understand the exvangelical movement, you must first understand what they are leaving and why the leaving carries such weight.

What Evangelicalism Became

American evangelicalism, as a coherent movement, is younger than most of its adherents realize. The National Association of Evangelicals was founded in 1942. The movement coalesced in the postwar period as a deliberate alternative to both mainline Protestantism, which was seen as theologically compromised, and fundamentalism, which was seen as culturally disengaged. Figures like Billy Graham, Carl F.H. Henry, and Harold Ockenga sought a third way: theologically conservative but intellectually engaged, culturally present but not combative.

That project held for roughly two generations. By the late 1970s, the movement had begun its fateful merger with political conservatism. Jerry Falwell's Moral Majority, founded in 1979, was the visible expression of a deeper shift: evangelicalism was no longer merely a theological identity. It was becoming a political one. The Reagan coalition welded together evangelical piety, free-market economics, and Cold War nationalism into a package that was presented as Christian faithfulness but was, in historical terms, a contingent political alliance with no necessary theological basis.

By the time the children of that alliance reached adulthood, many of them could not tell where the theology ended and the politics began. That was not an accident. It was the point.

The exvangelical movement is composed largely of people who grew up inside this synthesis and eventually found it impossible to maintain. They are the homeschooled children of the culture wars, the youth group alumni who were told that voting Republican was a Christian obligation, the worship leaders who watched their churches become arms of a political movement and were told that objecting to that development was a sign of weak faith.

The Catalysts

No single event produced the exvangelical exodus, but several converging crises accelerated it beyond what the movement's institutions could absorb.

The first was the abuse crisis. Beginning in the early 2010s and accelerating through the rest of the decade, a cascade of revelations exposed systematic patterns of sexual abuse, institutional cover-up, and leadership failure across evangelical organizations. The Southern Baptist Convention's abuse scandal, documented in devastating detail by the Houston Chronicle's 2019 investigation and the subsequent Guidepost Solutions report, revealed that denominational leaders had maintained a list of credibly accused abusers for years while publicly insisting they had no mechanism to track such cases. Ravi Zacharias, one of evangelicalism's most celebrated apologists, was posthumously revealed to have been a serial sexual predator. Bill Hybels, founder of Willow Creek and architect of the seeker-sensitive movement, resigned amid multiple allegations of harassment and abuse. Mark Driscoll, Mars Hill Church. James MacDonald, Harvest Bible Chapel. The list grew so long that it ceased to function as a list of exceptions and began to function as an indictment of the system itself.

For many exvangelicals, the abuse revelations were not merely about individual failures. They were about a theology of authority that made those failures predictable. Complementarian gender theology, pastoral authoritarianism, the absence of meaningful accountability structures, the prioritization of institutional reputation over victim safety — these were not bugs in the evangelical system. They were features. And the people who named them as such were the ones who were shown the door.

The second catalyst was the LGBTQ+ question. As American culture moved rapidly toward acceptance of same-sex relationships, evangelical churches doubled down on exclusion with a ferocity that many younger members found incompatible with the Jesus they had been taught to follow. The issue was not merely theological disagreement about sexual ethics. It was the pastoral cruelty that accompanied the disagreement: conversion therapy, family rejection, the casual dehumanization of queer people from the pulpit, the refusal to engage with the growing body of affirming biblical scholarship, and the willingness to make opposition to LGBTQ+ rights a defining marker of Christian identity.

For parents of queer children, for closeted members sitting in pews, for allies who had watched their friends be wounded, the cost of staying became higher than the cost of leaving. Many report that the moment they could no longer remain was not an intellectual moment but a moral one: they could not, in conscience, participate in an institution that treated people they loved as inherently disordered.

The third catalyst was racial reckoning. The killings of Michael Brown, Eric Garner, Breonna Taylor, and George Floyd forced a national conversation about race that evangelical churches were catastrophically unprepared for. The movement's history on race is damning: the Southern Baptist Convention was founded in 1845 explicitly to defend the right of slaveholders to serve as missionaries. Bob Jones University maintained its ban on interracial dating until 2000. The overwhelming whiteness of evangelical leadership, the persistent segregation of Sunday morning, the movement's deep roots in the theology of the Lost Cause — all of this was suddenly, unavoidably visible.

Black and brown evangelicals who raised these issues were met with a response that was revealing: they were told they were being divisive. Critical race theory became the new enemy, a label applied so broadly and indiscriminately that it functioned less as a description of an academic framework and more as a mechanism for silencing any conversation about structural racism. For many Christians of color and their white allies, the message was clear: this movement values its racial comfort more than its commitment to justice. And so they left.

The fourth catalyst was the Trump era. The 2016 election and its aftermath did not create the contradictions within evangelicalism, but it made them impossible to ignore. When eighty-one percent of white evangelicals voted for a thrice-married casino magnate who bragged about sexual assault, many younger evangelicals experienced a dissonance so severe that it fractured their relationship with the movement permanently. It was not merely that evangelical leaders endorsed Trump. It was that they did so enthusiastically, that they provided theological justification for it, that they compared him to Cyrus and Nehemiah, that they treated criticism of him as persecution, and that they did all of this while claiming to represent the moral center of American life.

The hypocrisy was not new. But its scale was.

Where They Go

The assumption that exvangelicals become secularists is widespread and wrong. Research by the Public Religion Research Institute and other organizations consistently shows that the majority of people who leave evangelicalism do not abandon faith entirely. They migrate.

Some move to mainline Protestant traditions — Episcopal, ELCA Lutheran, Presbyterian (PCUSA), United Methodist — drawn by liturgical richness, intellectual freedom, and a theology that does not demand the subordination of conscience to institutional authority. They find in these traditions a Christianity that can hold ambiguity, that has a longer memory than the evangelical movement, that does not treat doubt as disloyalty.

Some move to Roman Catholicism or Eastern Orthodoxy, seeking rootedness in a tradition older than the Reformation, a sacramental theology that locates God's presence in material reality rather than in emotional experience alone, and a theological depth that evangelicalism's pragmatic orientation often sacrificed for accessibility.

Some construct what the sociologist Nancy Ammerman calls "a la carte" spirituality — drawing from contemplative traditions, Celtic Christianity, liberation theology, and other sources that evangelicalism had dismissed or never engaged. They read Richard Rohr and Howard Thurman. They practice lectio divina and the Examen. They attend Quaker meetings or sit in centering prayer groups. They are not less Christian. They are differently Christian, and the difference is one their former communities cannot process.

And some, it must be said, leave religion entirely. The wounds are too deep, the associations too painful, the word "God" too contaminated by the uses to which it has been put. For these, the departure is not a theological conclusion but a survival mechanism. They are not rejecting the divine. They are protecting themselves from the human institutions that claimed to represent it. Whether they return is a question only grace and time can answer.

What is striking across all of these trajectories is how few exvangelicals describe their departure as a loss of faith. The language they use is more precise than that: deconstruction, reconstruction, untangling, sifting. They are not throwing away the faith. They are separating what they actually believe from what they were told they had to believe — separating Jesus from the Jesus Industrial Complex, the scriptures from the hermeneutic that was imposed upon them, the genuine encounter with God they experienced in prayer or worship from the institutional machinery that surrounded and claimed ownership of that encounter. This is not apostasy. It is curation under duress, performed without a guide, often at great personal cost.

The data supports this reading. Ryan Burge's research on the "nones" — those who claim no religious affiliation — reveals that a significant subset of this population maintains private spiritual practices, believes in God or a higher power, and would return to organized religion if they could find a community that did not replicate the patterns they left. They are, in a meaningful sense, believers without belonging, and their existence is an indictment not of belief itself but of the institutions that made belonging unbearable.

The Grief of Departure

What outsiders rarely grasp is the cost. Leaving evangelicalism is not like switching political parties or changing gyms. For people raised in the tradition, evangelicalism was not one part of their identity. It was the organizing principle of their entire world. Their friendships were formed there. Their marriages were blessed there. Their children were dedicated there. Their moral framework, their understanding of history, their conception of what happens after death — all of it was sourced from a community they are now leaving.

The grief is compound. There is the loss of community, which for many was the only genuine community they had ever known. There is the loss of certainty, which for people raised in a tradition that prizes doctrinal confidence feels like vertigo. There is the loss of family relationships, because in many evangelical families, leaving the church is treated as a betrayal equivalent to moral failure, and the response — shunning, conditional love, relentless attempts at re-conversion — can be devastating.

There is also a specific grief that is harder to name: the grief of realizing that the story you were told about yourself and the world was, in significant ways, wrong. That the church you trusted protected abusers. That the theology you internalized was designed to control you. That the God you were given was too small, too angry, too American, too white, too male, too invested in your compliance and not enough in your flourishing. Reconstructing a faith after that realization is not a weekend project. It is the work of years, and it is done largely without institutional support, because the institution you left was the only one you knew.

And there is the grief of language itself. The words that once carried transcendence — worship, fellowship, salvation, blessing — now arrive pre-contaminated, triggering associations with manipulation, performance, and control. The exvangelical does not merely lose a community. They lose a vocabulary. They must learn to speak about God, about meaning, about hope, in a language that has not been weaponized against them. Some find that language in the contemplative tradition, in the mystics, in poets. Some find it in therapy. Some simply go silent for a season, unable to pray in the old words and not yet fluent in new ones. That silence is not the absence of faith. It is faith in transit, between the language it was given and the language it has not yet found.

The psychologist Marlene Winell coined the term "Religious Trauma Syndrome" to describe the cluster of symptoms common among people leaving authoritarian religious environments: anxiety, depression, difficulty making decisions, a pervasive sense of being watched or judged, the inability to trust one's own perceptions. Winell's work, and the growing body of clinical literature on religious trauma, confirms what exvangelicals have been saying for years: leaving is not merely an intellectual adjustment. It is a psychological upheaval comparable in its effects to leaving any high-control environment. The church that produced the trauma rarely acknowledges it, which means the healing must happen entirely outside the system that inflicted the wound.

What the Church Must Learn

The evangelical church's dominant response to the exvangelical movement has been dismissal. They were never really saved. They loved the world more than God. They wanted to sin without guilt. This response is pastorally catastrophic and historically oblivious. It is the response of an institution that cannot distinguish between loyalty to itself and faithfulness to God.

The prophetic question is not "why are they leaving" but "what are they telling us by leaving." The exvangelical exodus is a prophetic indictment delivered not in words but in feet — people walking out the door because the institution no longer embodies the gospel it preaches. The church that cannot hear that indictment is the church that will keep producing it.

What would it mean to listen? It would mean taking the abuse crisis seriously — not as a public relations problem but as a theological failure that reveals something rotten in the movement's understanding of authority and power. It would mean engaging the LGBTQ+ conversation with genuine theological humility rather than treating the traditional position as self-evident and every other position as capitulation. It would mean reckoning with the movement's racial history honestly, without the defensive posture that treats acknowledging complicity as attacking the faith. It would mean disentangling the gospel from partisan politics with enough conviction that a visitor could attend an evangelical church for a year and never know how the pastor voted.

It would mean, in short, repentance. Not the performative kind that issues statements. The structural kind that changes how power works.

The church that treats its critics as enemies will eventually have no one left but sycophants. The church that treats its departures as data — painful, prophetic data about its own failures — has a chance of becoming something worth staying in.

The exvangelicals are not the church's enemies. They are its mirror. And the reflection, for anyone willing to look, is a call not to defensiveness but to the kind of reform that the church has always needed and has always resisted — until the cost of resistance became higher than the cost of change.

That cost is now being counted in empty pews, in broken families, in a generation that learned the word "Christian" as a synonym for hypocrisy and is not wrong about why. The question is whether the evangelical church can hear that without hearing it as an attack. The answer to that question will determine whether what is happening is a death or a reformation.

The difference between the two has always depended on whether the institution loves its own survival more than it loves the truth. And the truth, as always, is not comfortable. It is not affirming. It is not what the institution wants to hear. But it is, if received, the only thing that can set it free.

chapters.title: Flags in the Sanctuary: A Theology of the Nation
chapters.summary: The flag stands on most American platforms because nobody put it there on purpose, and that is precisely the problem.
chapters.body:
There are two flags on the platform of the church where I learned to preach. I did not put them there. Neither did the pastor before me, or the one before him. They have stood beside the pulpit longer than anyone alive in the congregation can remember, which means no one ever decided to place them there. They simply appeared, sometime in the middle of the last century, and they have been guarding the Word ever since with a quiet authority that no business meeting ever granted them.

That is the strange thing about the flag in the sanctuary. Almost nobody chose it. It arrived the way the air in a room arrives, without a vote, and now to move it would feel like an act of aggression, while to have placed it would have felt like nothing at all. The asymmetry is the whole subject of this essay. We will defend to the point of fury an arrangement that we never once chose to make. And a thing you will fight to keep but would never have thought to install is worth examining, because it has more power over you than the things you actually decided.

Let me make the honest case for the flag before I question it, because the case is real and the people who make it are not fools. They say the flag in the sanctuary is simple gratitude, a way of honoring the country that protects the freedom to gather and worship at all. They say it honors the men and women of the congregation who served, some of whom did not come home, and that to remove it would wound the families of the dead for the sake of a theological abstraction. They say the church does not live in heaven yet but in a particular country, under particular laws, and that pretending otherwise is its own dishonesty. Every one of those points has weight. The freedom to gather is a real gift. The dead are owed real honor. The church is in a real place. I will not wave any of that away.

The strongest version of the case goes further, and I want to state it at full strength. It says that removing the flag is not neutrality but a statement of its own, a signal that the church is ashamed of its country, that it has joined the cultured despisers who look down on ordinary patriotic believers. And that is sometimes exactly what removal means and exactly how it is meant. I have seen the flag taken down as a sneer, not a confession, by people more eager to perform their sophistication than to worship. So the question is not settled by simply removing the cloth. A bare platform can serve pride as easily as a draped one can serve idolatry. The object is not the disease. The disease is in what the object is permitted to mean.

Now I will answer the strongest case, and I will answer it with a question about geography. Where does the flag stand. Not in the lobby, where we might thank God for the gift of a free country and the service of its soldiers. On the platform. Beside the pulpit. Inside the space the architecture reserves for the most sacred things, the Word and the table and the waters of baptism. The placement is a sermon, and it preaches every week whether or not anyone notices, because the eye learns from arrangement faster than the ear learns from speech. A symbol that stands beside the cross will eventually be read as the cross's equal, and a child raised in that room will absorb the equality long before he could put words to it. My own children have.

Robert Bellah taught us to see this as liturgy and not decoration. Civil religion, he wrote in 1967, is a real religion with its own sacred objects, its own holy days, its own scriptures in the founding documents, and its own saints among the founders and the war dead (Bellah 1967). The flag is not a neutral piece of fabric. It is a sacred object in a functioning religion, and when you carry a sacred object from one religion into the holy space of another, you do not get nothing. You get fusion. You get a worshiper who can no longer feel the seam between the two faiths, who experiences his patriotism and his Christianity as one undivided devotion, which is the precise definition of the thing the careful scholars call Christian nationalism (Whitehead and Perry 2020).

Carry the governing text. When Solomon finished the temple, the glory of the Lord filled the house so that the priests could not stand to minister, because the glory filled it (1 Kings 8:11 ESV). The sanctuary in Scripture is the place where one glory dwells, and it tolerates no rival in its space. The whole architecture of Israel's worship was a long lesson in the danger of bringing the symbols of the nations into the holy place. When the kings of Judah set up the altars of other gods beside the altar of the Lord, the prophets did not call it diversity. They called it the thing that brought the house down. The sanctuary is jealous space. It was built to be jealous. To bring a second glory into it is not addition. It is competition, and the second glory always wins eventually, because it asks for less and flatters more.

I cannot write this from a safe distance. The flags on my platform have outlasted my objections to them. I have stood beside them Sunday after Sunday and preached the kingdom that is not of this world while the kingdom of this world stood at my right hand, and I have not moved it, because I know what moving it would cost and I have not been willing to pay it. That is the confession underneath this essay. I am not the prophet clearing the temple. I am the priest who has grown used to the second altar and tells himself it is only cloth. The law lands on me first. I have let the symbol stand because the symbol is easier to keep than to explain.

Here is where the cross does its work in the room itself. The cross is the one symbol in that sanctuary that refuses to share. It is not a symbol of strength but of a state execution, the empire's own instrument turned into the throne of God. When you stand the flag of any nation beside the cross, you have placed the sword of empire beside the thing the empire used to kill God, and you have asked them to mean the same devotion. They cannot. The cross is the permanent judgment on every nation, including the one whose colors stand beside it, because every nation would have done to Christ exactly what Rome did, and most of them have done it to his people since. The cross does not bless the flag. The cross indicts the flag, gently, and waits to see whether the church will hear.

So what is the theology of the nation that the sanctuary should teach. Not contempt for the country. Honor it, in its place, in the lobby of gratitude, in the prayers of the people, in the genuine thanks we owe for freedom and for the dead. But not on the platform, not beside the Word, not in the jealous space where one glory dwells. The nation is a real thing that God uses and judges, owed honor and owed truth, and the church serves it best by refusing to worship it. A church that cannot tell its country the truth has already handed the country the throne, and the arrangement of its furniture confessed the surrender before the preacher said a word.

I have not moved the flags yet. Writing this is the beginning of moving them, or it is one more way of not. The reader will know which when he visits, and so will my sons, who are watching where their father puts the second glory. The sanctuary teaches whether or not we mean it to. The only question is what we are willing to let it teach.

### Works Cited

Bellah, Robert N. Civil Religion in America. Daedalus, 1967.

Whitehead, Andrew L., and Samuel L. Perry. Taking America Back for God: Christian Nationalism in the United States. Oxford University Press, 2020.

chapters.title: Formed by Screens: Technology and the Soul
chapters.summary: The screen does not only fill our time, it slowly remakes the kind of soul we have time for.
chapters.body:
My youngest can find a video faster than I can find my keys. He is not corrupt. He is a boy with a boy's open face, and he loves his mother and asks me hard questions about God at bedtime. But I have watched something happen to his attention over a season, a fraying, a difficulty in staying with one slow thing, and I cannot honestly blame him, because I have watched the same fraying happen to me. I sit down to read Scripture and my hand reaches for the phone before my mind has settled, and the reaching is so automatic that it has stopped feeling like a choice. Something is forming us both, and it is not the Word.

The question is not whether technology is good or evil. That question is too small and too old, and it always ends in a shrug about how anything can be used well or badly. The real question is sharper. What kind of person does a given technology make of you simply by being used as it was designed to be used. Not abused. Used. Because every tool carries inside it a hidden curriculum, a way of forming the one who holds it, and the screen has a curriculum, and we have all enrolled, and most of us never read the syllabus.

Give the strongest case for the screen, and give it honestly. These devices are astonishing gifts. I can carry the whole of Scripture, the Fathers, the Reformers, and a thousand sermons in one hand. A grandmother sees her grandchild's face across an ocean. A man in a remote village hears the gospel he could never have reached in print. The pandemic years would have been unbearable without the screen that kept the lonely connected to the living. To call all of this captivity would be ungrateful and untrue, the grumbling of a man who wishes for a past that was never as holy as he remembers. Technology is a good gift of a creative God to creative creatures. I use it to write the words you are reading. I will not pretend otherwise.

But here is what the grateful case keeps stepping around. A tool is not only what it does for you. It is what it does to you while you use it, and these two are often opposites. Charles Taylor described the modern self as buffered, sealed off from a world that once pressed in on it from every side, and the screen is the final architecture of that buffering, the wall made portable and pleasant (Taylor 2007). It promises to connect us and it insulates us. It puts a pane of glass between me and the man across the table, between me and the slow boredom out of which prayer is born, between me and my own unmanaged thoughts, which are exactly the thoughts in which God has always done his quietest work. The screen does not merely occupy the silence. It abolishes the capacity for silence, and silence is where the soul learns to hear.

Carry one text, and let it be strange enough to wake us. After the wind and the earthquake and the fire, none of which held the Lord, there came a low whisper. And when Elijah heard it, he wrapped his face in his cloak and went out (1 Kings 19:12 ESV). God was not in the spectacle. He was in the whisper, the sound that requires a quiet so deep that a man would have to have built his whole life around the practice of listening to hear it at all. Now ask the honest question. Could the version of me that checks the phone in the silence of his own prayers hear a whisper. The screen is a technology of the wind and the earthquake and the fire, endless spectacle, endless noise, and a God who speaks in a whisper is a God we have engineered ourselves to miss.

Trace the history, because formation by tools is not new, only newly total. Jacques Ellul argued in the middle of the last century that the deepest danger of modern life is not any single machine but technique itself, the relentless drive toward efficiency that subordinates every human end to the question of what works, until the person is reshaped to serve the apparatus rather than the apparatus the person (Ellul 1964). The screen is technique made intimate. Neil Postman, building on this, warned that the move from the printed word to the image does not just change our entertainment, it changes the structure of our thought, training us for fragments and against arguments, for stimulation and against contemplation, until a whole civilization loses the patience that sustained things like reading a long book or sitting with a hard truth or praying without a phone in reach (Postman 1985). They saw the river's direction before most of us felt the current. We are now far downstream.

Here is the reversal, and it is the one that matters most. We believe we are using these devices to save time, and we are, and then we have no idea what the saved time was for, so we give it back to the same devices, and we are formed not by the content we consume but by the ten thousand small acts of consuming, the reach, the scroll, the flick, the refresh, repeated until they are no longer things we do but the shape of who we are. The danger was never that the screen would make us believe something false. The danger is that it would make us into a certain kind of soul, restless, distractible, incapable of the long slow attention that love and prayer and presence require, and that it would do this so gently we would mistake the new self for the only self we ever had.

Law before grace, and the law has my name on it. I have prayed with one ear on the notification. I have been bodily present with my sons and mentally somewhere in a feed, and they know the difference even when I pretend they do not, because children read presence the way the rest of us read words. I have told my congregation that God speaks in the whisper and then lived a life arranged so that no whisper could ever reach me. I am not the doctor here. I am the patient, and the diagnosis is the same one I would write for the man in my office who cannot sit still long enough to be loved by God.

The grace is that we are formed creatures, which means we can be re formed, and the church has known the medicine for two thousand years. The old disciplines of silence and solitude and fasting are not nostalgia. They are deliberate counter formation, structured acts of refusing the wind and the earthquake and the fire so that the whisper has a chance to land. To put the phone in another room and sit in the unbearable quiet until it stops being unbearable is not a productivity hack. It is repentance with a body, the slow undoing of a formation we did not choose, the clearing of enough silence that a God who has been whispering the whole time can finally be heard saying what he said to Elijah, which was not condemnation but a question, gentle and terrible. What are you doing here.

The screen did not steal our time. It quietly stole the kind of soul that has time for God.

Not a tool we are using. A liturgy that is using us. We can still walk out into the silence, wrap our faces, and listen.

### Works Cited

Taylor, Charles. A Secular Age. Cambridge, MA: Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, 2007.

Ellul, Jacques. The Technological Society. Translated by John Wilkinson. New York: Vintage Books, 1964.

Postman, Neil. Amusing Ourselves to Death: Public Discourse in the Age of Show Business. New York: Viking, 1985.

The Holy Bible. English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

chapters.title: How Individualism Changed the Way We Read the Bible
chapters.summary: We did not stop believing the Bible, we quietly rewrote who it was talking to, and the someone it now addresses is me alone.
chapters.body:
A man stands in my office and tells me God has a plan for his life. He means his life. Singular. The job, the move, the woman he is unsure about. I believe God is at work in all of it. But I notice what he does not notice, which is that the sentence he reached for to describe the will of God landed entirely inside the borders of one person, and that person is himself. He did not learn that sentence from Scripture. He learned it from the air he breathes.

The question is not whether God cares about individuals. He does, down to the hairs of the head. The question is whether the individual has become the only unit we can see, the lens so close to the eye that we no longer recognize it as a lens. We think we are reading the Bible. We are often reading ourselves into it, and calling the echo revelation.

Let me give the strongest version of the other side, because it is strong. The defender of the personal Bible will say that the gospel really is personal, that Jesus left the ninety nine for the one, that Paul writes I have been crucified with Christ, that conversion is not a committee vote, that every believer stands before God without a mediator but Christ, and that the Reformation itself fought and bled for the conscience of the single soul against the machinery of the institution. All of that is true. I would die on that ground. The recovery of the individual conscience before God is one of the great gifts of the church to the world, and the skeptic who values his own freedom of conscience is living, whether he knows it or not, on borrowed Christian capital.

But here is what that argument gets right and then takes too far. It is true that I am saved as a person. It is not true that I am saved as an isolate. The same Paul who says I have been crucified with Christ spends most of his ink writing to churches, in the plural, about a body with many members, and almost every you that English readers hear as singular is in the Greek a you that means all of you together. We read a letter written to a congregation as if it were a note left on my pillow.

Carry one text through this. When Jeremiah delivers the most quoted promise in the American devotional, For I know the plans I have for you, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope (Jeremiah 29:11 ESV), he is not whispering to a discouraged individual about a career change. He is writing a letter to a nation in exile in Babylon, a deported people, telling them to build houses, plant gardens, marry, and seek the welfare of the very city that conquered them, because their God has not abandoned the community even in captivity. The you is a people. The plan is corporate, generational, costly, and seventy years long. We took a word spoken over a traumatized nation and shrank it to fit a coffee mug.

How did this happen. Trace it. Robert Bellah and his colleagues, studying American life in the early 1980s, named the thing precisely. They called it expressive individualism, the conviction that each person has a unique core of feeling and intuition that must be unfolded if individuality is to be realized, and they showed how even the most religious Americans had absorbed it so deeply that they described their faith in the language of personal preference (Bellah 1985). One woman in their study named her own religion after herself. Sheilaism. Charles Taylor traced the longer arc, the slow construction across five centuries of what he calls the buffered self, the modern interior shielded from the world, sealed off, the meaning of a life generated from inside rather than received from outside (Taylor 2007). The porous self of the ancient world, open to God and neighbor and the dead, became the buffered self of the mall, open mainly to its own desires.

The church did not resist this. The church baptized it. By the time American revivalism had run its course through the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, the altar call had made the decision of the individual the hinge of everything, which is half a glory and half a wound. The glory is that no one is saved by belonging to a crowd. The wound is that we began to imagine the crowd did not matter at all, that a Christian is a sovereign consumer of religious goods who attends a church the way he subscribes to a service, retaining at all times the right to cancel.

Now watch the reversal, because Scripture refuses our flattery. The most individual moment in the Bible, a man alone in a garden at night, sweating blood, is the moment Jesus is least alone in purpose, because he is there for a body he is about to gather out of the whole earth. He prays not for himself but for them, and not only for these, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that they may all be one (John 17:20 ESV). The cross is the most personal act in history and the least private. He died, one man, for a people. The pronoun is singular at the nail and plural at the empty tomb.

This is where law has to come before grace, and the law is this. If I read the Bible as a private message to me, I will use it. I will mine it for the verses that serve my plans and skip the ones that bind me to people I did not choose. I will treat the church as a vendor and my neighbor as scenery. And I will do all of this with a Bible open on my lap, sincerely, never once suspecting that I have made the living God into an accessory to a life I was going to live anyway. That is not a small sin. That is the slow theft of the whole counsel of God, one comforting verse at a time. I have done it. I do it on the mornings I am tired and want the text to console me rather than command me.

The grace is that the God of the letter to Babylon does not abandon the captives, even the captives of our own age, even the ones whose captivity is so comfortable they call it freedom. He still writes to a people. He is still building a house with many rooms and many members, and he means to put me in it next to someone I would not have picked, and call that salvation.

So read the next verse you love and ask the question first. Who is the you. If the answer turns out to be all of you together, and it almost always does, then the verse was never the private property you thought it was. It was a word to a people, and you were being invited to stop being an audience of one.

We made the Bible smaller to make ourselves larger. The book will not stay that size.

### Works Cited

Bellah, Robert N., Richard Madsen, William M. Sullivan, Ann Swidler, and Steven M. Tipton. Habits of the Heart: Individualism and Commitment in American Life. Berkeley: University of California Press, 1985.

Taylor, Charles. A Secular Age. Cambridge, MA: Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, 2007.

The Holy Bible. English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

chapters.title: How the Religious Right Was Built
chapters.summary: The political movement that taught a generation of Christians to read faithfulness as voting was assembled by particular people in particular years, and the assembly is documented.
chapters.body:
The young pastor who shadowed me for a summer assumed the religious right had always existed. He could not imagine a time when American Christians were not sorted into political camps, when faithfulness did not come with a voter guide attached. To him it was simply the weather, the climate faith had always lived in. I had to tell him that the movement he took for the air itself was younger than my parents, that it was built, on purpose, by people whose names we know, in years we can count. The thing that feels eternal was assembled inside living memory.

That is the first thing to understand about the religious right, and it is the thing most of its members do not know. It is not the ancient form of Christian political engagement. It is a specific coalition, constructed in the 1970s, around specific grievances, by specific organizers, for specific ends. To say this is not to call it evil. Coalitions get built for good reasons too. It is to refuse the story the movement tells about itself, the story that it is simply what serious Christians have always been, the story that erases its own construction so it cannot be questioned. A thing that hides the date it was built does not want you to know it could have been built differently.

Let me grant the strongest defense first, the one that has truth in it. The defender says that Christians were not wrong to enter politics in the 1970s, that the culture was changing fast and faith has every right to a public voice, that to organize believers to vote their conscience is democracy working as designed. He says the movement formed around real concerns, the protection of the unborn chief among them, and that to sneer at the religious right is often to sneer at people who simply refused to be silent while their convictions were legislated against. There is weight here. Political organizing is not a sin. The unborn are owed protection. A faith with no public voice has surrendered something it had no right to surrender. I hold all of that.

But the honest history complicates the founding story, and the complication is documented, not invented. The popular account says the religious right rose up spontaneously in response to the 1973 Roe decision, that abortion lit the fire and the movement formed to fight it. The historian Randall Balmer, who was inside evangelicalism and reported what its own architects told him, has argued that this is largely a later rationalization (Balmer 2014). His is one influential reading of the founding, and an argued case rather than a closed one. In the years right after Roe, white evangelical leaders were notably quiet about abortion, some even cautiously approving of the decision. The Southern Baptist Convention passed resolutions in 1971 and again after 1973 that affirmed abortion in certain cases. The fire that actually organized the movement was lit elsewhere.

It was lit, Balmer argues, over the question of segregation. The federal government moved in the early 1970s to strip tax-exempt status from private religious schools that practiced racial discrimination, and the flashpoint was Bob Jones University, whose exemption was challenged for its racial policies. The organizer Paul Weyrich, who spent years trying to mobilize evangelicals politically and failing, is reported to have said that abortion was not the issue that finally moved them. It was the defense of the segregated schools against federal interference (Balmer 2014). On Balmer's reading, abortion became the unifying banner afterward, once it was clear that segregation could not be defended in public.

I should be honest that this is a contested thesis and not a settled verdict. Other historians push back, dating the movement's real galvanizing more to the 1973 Roe v. Wade decision and the slow awakening of evangelicals to abortion, and pointing out that the 1978 grassroots fury over the schools and the rise of the pro-life cause were braided together rather than sequential. The cleanest segregation not abortion story is too tidy for the evidence. What is fair to say is narrower and still uncomfortable.
