Race and the defense of segregated institutions were woven into the movement's origins far more deeply than its own founding myth admits, whether or not they were the single spark. A movement that tells itself it was born purely defending the unborn has edited out a harder part of its own genealogy.

The pieces came together quickly once the organizers found their footing. Jerry Falwell founded the Moral Majority in 1979, and the historian Daniel Williams has traced how he gathered conservative Protestants, Catholics, and Mormons into a single voting bloc around a shared sense that Christian America was under siege (Williams 2010). Weyrich supplied the political machinery. The 1980 election delivered the proof of concept when the coalition helped carry Ronald Reagan, a divorced Hollywood actor who was not notably devout, over Jimmy Carter, a Southern Baptist Sunday school teacher who spoke openly of being born again. The choice told the truth about the movement. It was not about personal piety. It was about political power, and it would prefer the powerful sinner to the pious opponent every time. That preference has only hardened since.

Carry the governing text, because Scripture saw this exchange long before Falwell. In the wilderness the tempter offered Jesus all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, on one condition, that he bow (Matthew 4:9 ESV). The condition is always the same. The kingdoms are real and available, and the only price is a redirected worship, a single bow toward power instead of God. The religious right was offered the kingdoms of American politics, real access, real influence, real seats at real tables, and the price was a bow, the slow reorientation of a faith around the winning of elections. Many bowed without ever feeling the descent, because the tempter never announces the transaction. He only shows the kingdoms and names the modest-seeming price.

Mark Noll, surveying the intellectual cost, wrote the sentence that named the wound. The scandal of the evangelical mind, he said, is that there is not much of an evangelical mind (Noll 1994). He meant that the movement had traded the hard work of thinking Christianly about the world for the easier work of fighting culture wars, that it had become reactive, politicized, and intellectually thin precisely because it had let political combat replace theological labor. A faith organized for winning stops doing the slow work of understanding, because understanding might complicate the fight, and the fight has become the point. The mind atrophies in the muscle of the campaign.

I cannot tell this history as an outsider, because the movement made me before I could examine it. The first Christianity I received, coming up out of atheism with no church background to sort it against, was already this fused thing, faith and party welded so tightly that I assumed the weld was the gospel. Nobody lied to me on purpose. They handed me what they had been handed. But I voted my way into what I thought was discipleship for years, mistaking a political reflex for the obedience of Christ, and I did not know there was a difference, because the people who discipled me did not know either. We were all carrying a hundred-year-old construction and calling it the ancient faith. The law lands on the whole house, and I am inside it.

The cross does the work the history cannot. Because the cross is what exposes the bargain for what it is. Jesus was offered the kingdoms and refused them, and then he was killed by the very political power the religious right has spent fifty years trying to capture. Rome put him to death as an enemy of the state, and he let it, and he rose anyway, which means the entire premise of the movement is broken at the root. The premise is that the kingdom of God needs political victory to arrive. The cross says the kingdom of God arrived through political defeat, through the state's machinery turned against the Son of God and failing to keep him buried. A movement built on the necessity of winning was founded on a misreading of the one event where God won by losing.

So the religious right was built. That is the verdict the history forces. Not eternal, not the ancient shape of faithful Christianity, but a coalition assembled in the 1970s by named men around grievances more tangled, and more entangled with race, than its own founding myth admits, sold to a generation as the gospel itself. Knowing this does not require anyone to abandon their convictions about justice or the unborn. It requires them to hold those convictions as Christians rather than as soldiers, to refuse the bow that comes with the kingdoms, to remember that they were handed a construction and not a revelation.

The young pastor thought it was the weather. I had to tell him it was a building, and that anything built by men in years we can count can also, by the grace of God, be examined, repented, and rebuilt. We start by learning the date it went up.

### Works Cited

Balmer, Randall. The Real Origins of the Religious Right. Politico Magazine, 2014.

Noll, Mark A. The Scandal of the Evangelical Mind. Eerdmans, 1994.

Williams, Daniel K. God's Own Party: The Making of the Christian Right. Oxford University Press, 2010.

chapters.title: Outrage Is Not a Spiritual Gift
chapters.summary: We mistook the heat of our anger for the fire of the Spirit, and the machine that sells our attention was happy to let us believe it.
chapters.body:
I caught myself last week reaching for my phone before I had finished the prayer. Not after. During. There was a thing happening online, an outrage cycling through the people I follow, and my body wanted to be in it the way a younger man wants to be in a fight. I noticed the hunger and it frightened me, because it was not a hunger for righteousness. It was a hunger for the feeling of righteousness, which is a different and more dangerous thing, and I had been trained to crave it by an instrument I carry in my pocket and call a tool.

The question underneath the noise is whether our public anger is the holy thing we tell ourselves it is. We call it standing for truth. We quote the prophets. We remember that Jesus made a whip and cleared the temple, and we use that one afternoon to justify a permanent disposition of fury at strangers. The question is whether the anger forming us is the anger of God or the anger of the algorithm, and whether we have lost the ability to tell them apart.

Give the strongest case for the anger, because there is one. Some things ought to make us furious. A world without holy anger is a world that has made peace with cruelty. The prophets burned. Jesus wept over a city and overturned tables in a temple. The abolitionist who was not enraged by the slave market had a defective conscience, not a mature one. Anger at genuine evil is not a sin, it is a sign of life, the proof that you still love something enough to be wounded when it is violated. A faith that produces only mild men who are upset by nothing is not Christianity, it is sedation. I will defend righteous anger. Scripture commands it.

But here is where the case collapses under its own weight. The Bible never treats anger as a reliable indicator of righteousness. It treats it as a fire that must be watched every moment it burns. Be angry and do not sin, Paul writes, and then immediately, do not let the sun go down on your anger, and give no opportunity to the devil (Ephesians 4:26 ESV). Read what that assumes. It assumes anger, even permitted anger, even righteous anger, is precisely the doorway through which the enemy enters, that it has a shelf life of hours, that it spoils by nightfall and becomes something the devil can use. The text does not celebrate the anger. It puts a clock on it. It treats holy anger the way you treat a controlled burn, useful, necessary, and one gust of wind from destroying the whole field.

Now here is the part we will not want to hear. The machine that delivers our anger to us was engineered, deliberately, to make sure the sun never goes down on it. Trace the history. In 2009 the major platforms gave us the instruments of measurement, the Facebook like button in February and the Twitter retweet button that November, with the frictionless share spreading across the web in the years on either side, small buttons that turned communication into a tally. Engineers learned quickly what kept people on the screen, and it was not joy and it was not peace. It was moral emotion, and the most engaging moral emotion is outrage at an outgroup. The systems were then tuned, by optimization more than by malice, to surface exactly the content that made us angriest at people not like us, because angry people scroll, angry people share, and angry people return. Jonathan Haidt has assembled the data with care, showing that the years following this redesign tracked with a sharp rise in adolescent anxiety, depression, and self harm beginning around 2012, especially among girls, a generation rewired by the very engines of moral outrage and social comparison they were handed before they could drive (Haidt 2024). We did not stumble into a culture of rage. We were farmed for it.

Marshall McLuhan said the thing decades before the engineers proved him right. The medium is the message. The form of a technology shapes us more than any content we pour through it, and we are constitutionally blind to the form because we are mesmerized by the content (McLuhan 1964). We argue about what to post. The medium has already decided what we are becoming by posting, and what we are becoming is people for whom the resting state of the soul is a low grade fury looking for an object.

Carry the reversal here. We believe we are using the outrage to fight evil. The outrage is using us to feed the machine, and the machine does not care which side we are on. It profits identically from the rage of the right and the rage of the left. It will hand the progressive his daily villain and the conservative hers, and bill them both, and call it engagement. The most sobering fact about Christian outrage online is that it is indistinguishable in form from every other outrage, runs on the same fuel, serves the same masters, and produces the same fruit, which Paul lists plainly as enmity, strife, fits of anger, rivalries, dissensions, divisions, the works of the flesh wearing the costume of conviction.

Law before grace, and I am the chief defendant. I have felt the rush of the righteous post and refreshed the screen to count who agreed. I have been angrier at a stranger on the internet than at my own sin, which is the exact inversion of the gospel order. I have let the sun go down on it, and the next sun, and called the residue zeal. I have modeled this for my five sons, who watch their father reach for the glowing rectangle in the silence, and learn from the reaching what their father actually treasures. The outrage was never a spiritual gift. It was a work of the flesh I had dressed in Scripture so I would not have to repent of it.

The grace is that the Spirit produces something the algorithm cannot manufacture and cannot sell. Against the works of the flesh Paul sets the fruit of the Spirit, and it begins with love and ends with self control, and in the middle, impossibly, it lists peace and patience and gentleness, the precise traits the machine is built to burn out of us (Galatians 5:22 ESV). The Spirit grows slowly and the algorithm rewards instantly, and a person can tell which one is forming him by asking what he is becoming. More peaceful or more reactive. More patient or more triggered. Gentler with his children or quicker to the phone. The fruit does not lie, and it does not trend.

We thought our anger proved we still cared. It proved we had been captured.

Let the sun go down on it. That is not weakness. That is the first free act in a long captivity.

### Works Cited

Haidt, Jonathan. The Anxious Generation: How the Great Rewiring of Childhood Is Causing an Epidemic of Mental Illness. New York: Penguin Press, 2024.

McLuhan, Marshall. Understanding Media: The Extensions of Man. New York: McGraw-Hill, 1964.

The Holy Bible. English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

chapters.title: Purity Culture and Its Wreckage
chapters.summary: Purity culture did not produce purity. It produced shame, silence, and a generation of Christians who were taught that their bodies were the enemy of their souls.
chapters.body:
In 1993, the Southern Baptist Convention launched True Love Waits, a campaign that would eventually collect over 2.5 million pledge cards from teenagers who promised to abstain from sexual activity until marriage. The cards were stacked in displays at denominational events — visual monuments to youthful sexual resolve. In 1994, they covered the National Mall in Washington, D.C. The image was arresting: hundreds of thousands of pledge cards laid out in the shadow of the Capitol, a silent army of committed virgins.

It was also, as a public health strategy and a theological framework, a catastrophe whose wreckage we are still excavating.

True Love Waits was neither the beginning nor the end. It was the most visible expression of a movement that had been building since the early 1990s and would reach its cultural peak in the early 2000s. Joshua Harris published "I Kissed Dating Goodbye" in 1997, when he was twenty-one years old, and it sold over a million copies. The Silver Ring Thing, founded in 1995, toured the country staging elaborate multimedia events where teenagers received purity rings after pledging abstinence. Denny Pattyn, its founder, described the ring as "an outward sign of an inward commitment." The language was sacramental. The theology was not.

What came to be known as purity culture was not, strictly speaking, a theology. It was a set of behavioral prescriptions dressed in theological language, a system of shame management that presented itself as sexual ethics. It taught a generation of young Christians — particularly young women — that their virginity was their most valuable spiritual asset, that sexual desire was evidence of spiritual failure, that their bodies were objects of temptation to be managed rather than dimensions of personhood to be integrated, and that any departure from the prescribed path would result in damage so permanent that even God's grace could not fully repair it.

The movement is now widely discredited. Harris himself renounced his book in 2018, requested that it be taken out of print, and issued a public apology. But the people who were shaped by it — who internalized its categories, performed its rituals, and carry its shame — did not receive an apology from the system that produced it. They received, at best, an acknowledgment that a particular book was flawed. The theological infrastructure that made the book possible remains largely unexamined.

What Purity Culture Actually Taught

The explicit curriculum of purity culture was abstinence before marriage. The implicit curriculum was far more extensive and far more damaging.

It taught that virginity was the supreme moral achievement of adolescence, the marker that distinguished faithful Christians from the world. This was communicated not only through direct instruction but through analogy — and the analogies were devastating. A piece of tape pressed to multiple arms that loses its adhesive. A cup of water passed from mouth to mouth. A rose with its petals plucked off. A piece of chewing gum already chewed. Every analogy communicated the same lesson: sexual experience diminishes you. Each partner takes something from you that cannot be returned. By the time you arrive at marriage — if you arrive at all — you will be a degraded version of what you were supposed to be.

These analogies were not peripheral. They were central. And they were almost exclusively directed at girls. The theological anthropology embedded in purity culture was deeply gendered: women were the gatekeepers of male desire, responsible not only for their own sexual choices but for the sexual imaginations of every man who encountered them. Modesty was framed not as a personal discipline but as a moral obligation owed to men who could not be expected to control their own thoughts. The language of "stumbling blocks" from Romans 14 — which Paul deployed in the context of dietary disputes — was repurposed to place the burden of male lust on female bodies.

Boys received a different curriculum, though its damage was no less real. They were taught that their sexual desire was essentially predatory — a wolf that must be caged, a fire that must be contained, a force that was always one unguarded moment away from destroying everything. The concept of "bouncing your eyes," popularized by Stephen Arterburn and Fred Stoeker's "Every Man's Battle," reduced male sexuality to a stimulus-response mechanism and male sanctification to a program of visual management. The theological vision of transformed desire — the idea that the Holy Spirit does not merely suppress but redirects and integrates human longing — was entirely absent. What was offered instead was behavioral management strategies dressed in devotional language.

The result was a generation of young men who were taught to fear their own desire and a generation of young women who were taught that their worth was located in their sexual history. Both lessons are theological lies. Neither has been adequately corrected by the institutions that taught them.

What It Got Wrong

Purity culture's failures were not incidental. They were structural, arising from foundational theological errors that infected everything the movement produced.

The first error was reductionism. Purity culture reduced the Bible's complex, multi-layered sexual ethic to a single binary: virgin or not. The Hebrew Bible's engagement with sexuality is far richer and stranger than this. The Song of Solomon celebrates erotic desire with an explicitness that has made commentators uncomfortable for millennia. Ruth's encounter with Boaz on the threshing floor operates in territory that purity culture's categories cannot map. The story of Tamar in Genesis 38 — a woman who poses as a prostitute to secure justice from her father-in-law — is not a morality tale about sexual sin. It is a story about power, obligation, and the subversion of patriarchal systems. The Bible's sexual ethic is an ethic, not a checklist. It requires wisdom, discernment, and the capacity to hold complexity. Purity culture offered none of these. It offered a rule and a threat.

The second error was transactional theology. Purity culture operated on an implied bargain: maintain your virginity and God will reward you with a godly spouse, a satisfying sex life, and a marriage free from the damage that sexual sin produces. This bargain was stated explicitly in countless youth group talks, Christian dating books, and purity conferences. It was also a lie. Not because sexual choices have no consequences — they do — but because the bargain framed God's gifts as payments for good behavior, framed sexual difficulty in marriage as punishment for pre-marital failure, and left no room for the thousands of faithful Christians whose marriages were sexually difficult for reasons that had nothing to do with their pre-marital history.

The transactional framework also meant that people who had been sexually active before marriage — whether by choice or, crucially, by coercion — were categorized as damaged goods. The system could not distinguish between sexual agency and sexual violence. A teenager who had been raped occupied the same category as a teenager who had been sexually active by choice: both were no longer virgins, and in purity culture's framework, virginity was the only metric that mattered. The pastoral cruelty of this cannot be overstated. Abuse survivors sat in purity seminars and heard themselves described as chewed gum, used tape, plucked roses. They learned that what had been done to them had also, in the eyes of God and the church, diminished them permanently.

The third error was the erasure of consent. Because purity culture was built on a prohibition rather than an ethic, it had no framework for consent. The question it asked was not "was this mutual, was this honoring, was this characterized by genuine care for the other person?" The question it asked was "did this happen before marriage?" A coerced sexual encounter within marriage was, by purity culture's logic, acceptable. A consensual, loving relationship outside of marriage was not. The system's inability to distinguish between these — its fundamental disinterest in the quality and character of sexual encounter as opposed to its timing — reveals that what it was protecting was not people. It was a rule.

The Psychological Wreckage

The clinical literature on purity culture's effects is now substantial and consistent. Researchers including Linda Kay Klein, whose book "Pure" documented extensive interviews with purity culture survivors, and Jamie Lee Finch, whose "You Are Your Own" examined the somatic effects of religious sexual shame, have documented patterns that are remarkably uniform across demographic and denominational lines.

Sexual dysfunction in marriage is the most commonly reported consequence. People who spent their formative years being told that sexual desire was dangerous, that their bodies were sources of temptation, that sexual pleasure was suspect — these people did not experience a seamless transition to healthy sexuality on their wedding night. The switch that purity culture promised — from "sex is dangerous and dirty" to "sex is a beautiful gift from God" — did not flip. Bodies that had been trained to associate arousal with shame did not unlearn that association because a ceremony had occurred. The shame was not theological. It was neurological, wired into the body through years of reinforcement, and no amount of "you're married now, it's okay" could undo it.

Anxiety and depression related to sexual shame are pervasive among purity culture survivors, including those who "did everything right." Even people who maintained their virginity until marriage report chronic shame about their sexuality, difficulty experiencing pleasure without guilt, and a persistent sense that their sexual selves are fundamentally at odds with their spiritual selves. This is not the effect of disobedience. It is the effect of the teaching itself.

The shame also extends beyond sexuality into a broader pattern of self-distrust. People who were taught not to trust their own desires — who were told that the heart is deceitful above all things, that their feelings are unreliable, that their bodies are not to be listened to — often struggle to trust themselves in any domain. The epistemological damage of purity culture is underexamined: it trained people to distrust their own experience, to override their own instincts, to defer to external authority on questions that are fundamentally internal. This training does not stay in the sexual domain. It generalizes.

The Theological Correction

The Bible's actual sexual ethic is not the absence of an ethic. The overcorrection — the move from purity culture's rigid rule to a framework with no sexual ethics at all — is understandable but inadequate. What is needed is not the abandonment of Christian sexual ethics but their recovery from the distortion that purity culture imposed.

The biblical vision of sexuality is grounded not in prohibition but in anthropology — in an understanding of what human beings are and what their bodies are for. Genesis 2 presents the creation of sexual difference and sexual union as a response to aloneness, a remedy for the incompleteness that characterizes human existence prior to relationship. The "one flesh" of Genesis 2:24 is not merely a description of physical union. It is a description of a new social reality, a kinship bond created through sexual and covenantal union that reorganizes the identities of both persons involved.

Paul's engagement with sexuality in 1 Corinthians 6-7 is far more nuanced than purity culture's use of it suggests. His statement that the body is a temple of the Holy Spirit (6:19) is not a prohibition against sex. It is a claim about the dignity and significance of embodied life. The body matters. What you do with it matters. But it matters not because the body is dangerous, but because it is sacred. The direction of Paul's argument is not toward shame but toward honor — toward treating the body with the seriousness that its status as God's dwelling-place demands.

The Song of Solomon, which purity culture either ignored or allegorized into irrelevance, presents sexual desire as a good — not a domesticated good, not a safe good, but a real good that participates in the goodness of creation. The woman of the Song is not ashamed of her desire. She pursues it. She articulates it. She is not a gatekeeper. She is a subject, not an object, of erotic longing. The theology of the Song is not "desire is dangerous." It is "desire is powerful, and powerful things require wisdom, not fear."

What Healthy Sexual Theology Looks Like

A Christian sexual ethic adequate to the wreckage purity culture has left behind must be built on different foundations. Not the absence of foundations — the sexual nihilism that treats all choices as equally valid is not an improvement on the sexual legalism that treated one choice as the only valid one. What is needed is an ethic built on theological convictions rather than behavioral rules.

The first conviction is embodiment. Christianity is, at its core, a religion of incarnation — a faith that claims God took on a body, lived in a body, died in a body, and was raised in a body. Any theology that treats the body as the enemy of the soul is not Christian theology. It is Gnosticism with a worship band. A healthy sexual theology begins with the affirmation that bodies are good, that they are not obstacles to spiritual life but dimensions of it, and that the integration of body and spirit is not a problem to be solved but a gift to be received.

The second conviction is mutuality. The Bible's vision of sexual relationship, properly read, is not one of hierarchy but of reciprocity. Paul's instruction in 1 Corinthians 7:3-5 — that the husband's body belongs to the wife and the wife's body belongs to the husband, and that neither should deprive the other except by mutual consent — is radical in its symmetry. In a first-century context where a wife's body was legally her husband's property, Paul's insistence on mutual authority over each other's bodies was not a conservative statement. It was a revolutionary one. Healthy sexual theology takes mutuality seriously: both persons are subjects, both are agents, both have desires that matter and boundaries that must be honored.

The third conviction is consent. This word does not appear in the Bible in its modern form, but the principle it names is deeply biblical. The Song of Solomon's refrain — "do not arouse or awaken love until it so desires" — is a consent framework. The biblical prohibitions against sexual violence are consent frameworks. The insistence throughout scripture that love is patient and does not insist on its own way (1 Corinthians 13:4-5) is a consent framework. A sexual ethic that does not center consent is not a biblical ethic, regardless of what other biblical language it employs.

The fourth conviction is grace. This is where purity culture failed most catastrophically. The Christian gospel is a message about grace — about a God who meets people in their failure, their shame, their damage, and offers not condemnation but restoration. Purity culture preached a gospel in which grace was the fine print: technically available but practically irrelevant, because the damage of sexual sin was presented as permanent and the consequences as inescapable. A chewed piece of gum cannot be unchewed. A plucked rose cannot be unplucked. These metaphors are not merely bad analogies. They are anti-gospel. They claim, implicitly but unmistakably, that there are categories of human experience beyond the reach of redemption. That claim is heresy. It should be named as such.

The Road to Healing

Healing from purity culture is not accomplished by rejecting sexual ethics altogether. That overcorrection, while understandable, trades one set of problems for another. The person who moves from rigid sexual legalism to the abandonment of any sexual ethic has not been liberated. They have merely changed cages.

Healing requires, first, the honest naming of damage. This is not self-pity. It is diagnosis. What did purity culture teach you about your body? About your desire? About your worth? What messages did you internalize that you now recognize as false? The naming is itself therapeutic, because shame operates in silence and loses power when spoken.

Healing requires, second, a reconstruction of theology. Not the abandonment of theology but its renovation — the slow, difficult work of separating what the Bible actually says about sex and the body from what purity culture claimed it said. This work is best done in community and with competent guides: therapists who understand religious trauma, pastors who have done their own theological work, and fellow travelers who are navigating the same terrain.

Healing requires, third, the reintegration of body and spirit. For many purity culture survivors, the body has been an enemy for so long that learning to inhabit it — to trust its signals, to welcome its desires, to treat it as an ally rather than an adversary — is genuinely difficult. Somatic therapies, body-based spiritual practices, and the patient work of learning to be present in one's own skin are not luxuries. For people whose bodies were weaponized against them by a system that claimed to speak for God, they are necessities.

The God who made bodies is not embarrassed by them. The God who invented sexual desire is not threatened by it. The God who became flesh did not do so reluctantly. Any theology that produces shame about the body God made and called good is a theology that has lost its way, however sincerely it was intended.

Purity culture was sincere. Its architects genuinely believed they were protecting young people from harm. That sincerity does not mitigate the damage, but it does complicate the story. The movement was not born of malice. It was born of fear — fear of a sexually permissive culture, fear of teenage pregnancy, fear of disease, fear of the consequences that sexual freedom might bring. Fear is a poor foundation for theology. It produces systems that protect institutions rather than people, that prioritize control over formation, that mistake compliance for holiness.

The generation that was shaped by purity culture deserves more than an apology. They deserve a theology robust enough to hold the complexity of human sexuality without reducing it to a rule, generous enough to extend grace without conditions, honest enough to name the body as good without pretending that goodness is simple, and courageous enough to trust that the Holy Spirit is a better guide than shame has ever been.

That theology exists. It has always existed, in the deeper currents of the Christian tradition that purity culture ignored. Recovering it is not a departure from faithfulness. It is a return to it.

chapters.title: Religious Trauma Is Real
chapters.summary: The psychological damage inflicted by authoritarian religion is not a failure of individual faith. It is a predictable consequence of theological systems designed to control through fear, shame, and the systematic dismantling of personal agency.
chapters.body:
She sat in my office and told me she could not pray without having a panic attack. Not because she had lost her faith — she had not, or at least she was not sure she had — but because every time she closed her eyes and tried to address God, her body flooded with the same terror she had felt at fourteen, kneeling at an altar while a pastor told her that her doubts were evidence of demonic influence. She was thirty-seven. She had a graduate degree, a stable career, a therapist she trusted. And she could not bow her head without her hands shaking.

This is not an unusual story. It is, in fact, so common that researchers have given it a name. What she was experiencing has characteristics consistent with what psychologist Marlene Winell has termed Religious Trauma Syndrome — a condition that, while not yet included in the DSM-5, has been documented with increasing rigor by clinicians working at the intersection of psychology and religion. The church has been slow to acknowledge this reality, and the reasons for that slowness are themselves part of the problem. To admit that religion can traumatize is to admit that the institution charged with healing souls has, in some cases, been the instrument of their wounding.

What Religious Trauma Is

Marlene Winell, a human development consultant who has worked with survivors of authoritarian religion for over three decades, first described Religious Trauma Syndrome (RTS) in a 2011 paper in the British journal Cognitive Behaviour Therapy Today. Winell defined RTS as the condition experienced by those who are struggling with leaving an authoritarian, dogmatic religion and coping with the resulting damage to their normal development. She identified it as a complex of symptoms — cognitive, affective, functional, and social — resulting from immersion in a controlling religious environment and the struggle to leave it.

Winell's framework drew on existing research into the psychological effects of high-demand groups. Robert Jay Lifton's work on thought reform and Steven Hassan's BITE model (Behavior, Information, Thought, and Emotional control) identified mechanisms of psychological manipulation that find particularly fertile ground in religious contexts — precisely because religion claims ultimate authority. A political party can demand your vote. An employer can demand your labor. But a religion that claims to speak for God can demand your soul, and the psychological leverage this creates is qualitatively different from any secular form of coercion.

It is important to be precise about what religious trauma is and what it is not. It is not the ordinary difficulty of living within a moral framework that makes demands on one's behavior. Every serious ethical commitment involves tension, sacrifice, and the occasional experience of guilt. A teaching that challenges you is not the same as a teaching that damages you. Religious trauma occurs when the religious environment systematically undermines a person's sense of self, their capacity for autonomous thought, their ability to trust their own perceptions, and their fundamental sense of safety in the world. It is the difference between a coach who pushes you hard and a coach who breaks your bones.

The Sources: How Trauma Gets Produced

Religious trauma does not emerge from nowhere. It is produced by identifiable structures, practices, and theological frameworks. Understanding these sources is essential because it moves the conversation from individual pathology — "something is wrong with you for being hurt by church" — to systemic analysis: "something is wrong with systems that predictably produce this kind of damage."

Authoritarian leadership is the most commonly cited source. In congregations where a single leader exercises unchecked authority — where questioning is equated with rebellion, where dissent is treated as sin, where the leader claims a direct line to God that ordinary members lack — the conditions for psychological harm are structurally present. This is not about personality types. It is about systems that lack accountability. When a church board serves at the pastor's pleasure rather than as an independent governing body, when the congregation is told that to criticize the leader is to "touch God's anointed," the system is designed to produce abuse regardless of the leader's intentions.

Fear-based theology is a second major source. There is a difference between a theology that takes seriously divine judgment and a theology that weaponizes fear as a tool of behavioral control. When children are told in graphic detail about the torments of hell, when teenagers are warned that a single moment of doubt could consign them to eternal damnation, when adults are taught that God is perpetually angry and surveilling them for infractions, the result is not reverence but terror. Jonathan Edwards's "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God" (1741) is a masterpiece of homiletical rhetoric, but the theology it represents — a God whose primary posture toward humanity is wrath, held in check only by a fragile thread of grace — has left a long trail of psychological casualties.

Purity culture, particularly as it developed in American evangelicalism in the 1990s and 2000s, has been a significant source of sexual and relational trauma. The movement, popularized by Joshua Harris's I Kissed Dating Goodbye (1997) and reinforced by programs like True Love Waits, taught that sexual purity was the defining characteristic of a person's spiritual worth. Young women were told their virginity was a gift to be presented to their future husband — a framework that reduced female personhood to sexual status and produced devastating shame in those who "failed." Harris himself eventually recanted the book and apologized publicly. But the damage had been done to a generation.

The practice of shunning — cutting off contact with those who leave the faith or violate community norms — represents one of the most psychologically destructive tools in the religious arsenal. While most commonly associated with Jehovah's Witnesses and the Amish practice of Meidung, informal shunning occurs across traditions. The college student who comes out as gay and is told not to come home for Christmas. The seminary graduate who expresses doubts and finds old friends no longer return calls. The message is consistent: belonging is conditional, and the condition is conformity. For social animals like humans, the threat of exile from the community is, at a neurological level, experienced as a threat to survival.

Conversion therapy — the attempt to change a person's sexual orientation or gender identity through religious or psychological means — deserves particular mention. Condemned by every major medical and psychological organization, the practice has produced well-documented harm: depression, anxiety, self-hatred, and suicide. The Trevor Project's 2022 National Survey found that LGBTQ young people who underwent conversion therapy were more than twice as likely to attempt suicide. The theological conviction that homosexuality is sinful is one thing. The attempt to psychologically coerce a person into changing their orientation — under the guise of spiritual care — is another. The former is a theological position. The latter is abuse.

The Symptoms: What Trauma Looks Like

Religious trauma manifests across cognitive, emotional, physical, and social domains. Clinicians working with survivors report a consistent cluster of symptoms that, while overlapping with other forms of complex trauma, carry distinctive features rooted in the religious context.

Cognitively, survivors often experience difficulty with independent decision-making. Years of being told that their own judgment was unreliable — that the heart is "deceitful above all things" (Jeremiah 17:9), that human wisdom is foolishness before God — can produce a profound distrust of one's own perceptions. Black-and-white thinking, instilled by binary moral frameworks, persists long after the person has left. The world was divided into saved and lost, righteous and wicked, God's people and the world. Learning to inhabit the gray space between these categories is slow, difficult work.

Emotionally, anxiety and depression are the most commonly reported symptoms. The hypervigilance that served as a survival strategy within the religious environment — constantly monitoring one's thoughts for doubt, one's body for lust, one's speech for insufficient faith — does not switch off when the person leaves. It persists as a free-floating watchfulness, a sense that one is perpetually being observed and evaluated. Guilt metastasizes into a chronic condition unattached to any specific behavior.

The body, as Bessel van der Kolk demonstrated in The Body Keeps the Score (2014), does not forget trauma simply because the conscious mind has moved on. Van der Kolk established that traumatic experiences are stored not only in explicit memory but in the body's nervous system — in patterns of muscular tension, in the hyperactivation of the amygdala, in the dysregulation of the autonomic nervous system. Religious trauma follows the same neurological pathways. The person who was struck during a prayer meeting may flinch at the sound of prayer decades later. The child locked in a room for "spiritual discipline" may experience claustrophobia in churches. The body remembers what the mind tries to forget.

Socially, survivors face a double bind. Leaving the religious community means losing one's entire social network. But remaining means continuing to exist within the system causing harm. Many describe a period of profound isolation after leaving — too wounded to return to church, too shaped by religion to feel at home in secular spaces.

The Difference Between a Hard Teaching and an Abusive One

The church's instinctive response to claims of religious trauma is often defensive: "The gospel is supposed to be challenging. Jesus said to take up your cross. If the truth hurts, that does not make it abuse." This response contains a legitimate concern — the fear that any difficult teaching will be labeled traumatic, that the gospel will be softened into therapeutic pablum — but it fundamentally misunderstands the nature of trauma.

A hard teaching is one that challenges your behavior or your assumptions while respecting your dignity and your agency. "Love your enemies" is a hard teaching. "Sell everything you have and give to the poor" is a hard teaching. "Forgive seventy times seven" is a hard teaching. These teachings confront the self without dismantling it. They call for transformation without requiring annihilation.

An abusive teaching is one that systematically undermines your capacity to function as a whole person. "You are worthless apart from God" — stated not as a theological claim about dependence on grace but as a psychological assault on self-worth — is abusive. "Your feelings are not trustworthy" — stated not as a caution against unchecked emotivism but as a blanket dismissal of the person's inner life — is abusive. "If you leave this church, you will lose your salvation" — used not as a pastoral expression of concern but as a threat to prevent departure — is abusive. The distinction is not between comfortable and uncomfortable teachings. It is between teachings that empower growth and teachings that enforce control.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer drew a related distinction between what he called "cheap grace" and "costly grace." Cheap grace was grace without discipleship, forgiveness without repentance, baptism without the cross. Costly grace was the real thing — demanding, transformative, and life-giving precisely because it cost something. But there is a third category that Bonhoeffer did not name because he did not need to: weaponized grace, in which the language of grace is used to maintain power. "God has forgiven the pastor, so you must too" — said to a victim of the pastor's abuse. "Grace means not holding grudges" — said to someone who has been deeply wronged by the institution. This is neither cheap grace nor costly grace. It is the use of theological language to silence legitimate pain.

The Church's Responsibility

The church bears a twofold responsibility regarding religious trauma: it must stop causing it, and it must help heal it. Neither task is simple, and both require structural change, not merely attitudinal adjustment.

Stopping the harm requires accountability structures that actually function. This means independent governance boards with the authority to investigate and discipline leaders. It means transparent financial reporting. It means mandatory training in recognizing and preventing abuse. It means ending the culture of pastoral celebrity that insulates charismatic leaders from scrutiny. It means listening to survivors rather than managing their stories.

It also requires theological reform. Fear-based theology must be confronted not merely as pastorally unwise but as theologically deficient. A God whose primary tool is terror is not the God revealed in Jesus Christ. The Johannine assertion that "perfect love casts out fear" (1 John 4:18) is not a sentimental platitude. It is a theological claim about the nature of God — a claim that stands in direct contradiction to preaching traditions built on the manipulation of fear. This does not mean eliminating all talk of judgment from Christian theology. It means ensuring that judgment is always situated within the larger narrative of a God whose fundamental disposition toward creation is love.

Healing the harm requires the church to develop what might be called a trauma-informed theology — a way of thinking about God, Scripture, community, and spiritual formation that takes seriously the reality of psychological damage and the conditions necessary for recovery. This is not a capitulation to secular psychology. It is a recognition that the same God who created the soul also created the psyche, and that attending to the latter is not a betrayal of the former.

Trauma-Informed Theology in Practice

What does trauma-informed theology look like in practice? Several principles are emerging from the work of theologians, clinicians, and communities that are taking this question seriously.

First, it prioritizes safety. Before any spiritual formation can occur, people must feel physically, emotionally, and psychologically safe. This means creating worship environments where people are free to participate or not, where emotional expression is neither coerced nor suppressed, where consent is honored in every interaction — from the handshake line to the altar call. For survivors of authoritarian religion, the simple act of being told "you are free to leave at any time" can be profoundly healing.

Second, it restores agency. Authoritarian religion systematically strips people of their capacity for autonomous decision-making. Trauma-informed theology reverses this by treating people as competent moral agents capable of discerning truth, making choices, and bearing responsibility. This does not mean abandoning spiritual authority. It means exercising authority in ways that empower rather than diminish.

Third, it holds complexity. Traumatized people have been taught that the world divides neatly into categories: right and wrong, saved and lost, us and them. Recovery involves learning to hold ambiguity, to sit with unanswered questions. A theology that insists on certainty about everything is not strong. It is brittle. A theology that can hold doubt, lament, and unanswered prayer within its framework — as the Psalms do, as Job does, as Ecclesiastes does — is far more resilient and far more honest.

Fourth, it takes the body seriously. If van der Kolk is right that the body keeps the score, then a theology that treats embodiment as incidental to spiritual life is inadequate. Practices that attend to the body — contemplative prayer, liturgical movement, the physical elements of communion, the laying on of hands (with consent), the simple act of breathing together in silence — can reach parts of the person that words alone cannot touch. The incarnation is, among other things, God's declaration that the body matters.

"The wound that is not acknowledged cannot be healed. And the church that refuses to acknowledge the wounds it has inflicted will continue to inflict them — not out of malice, in most cases, but out of the willful ignorance that is malice's most respectable cousin."

Resources for Recovery

For those who are navigating religious trauma, the path forward typically involves several elements, and it is worth naming them plainly because many survivors do not know where to begin.

Professional therapy with a clinician trained in religious trauma is the single most important resource. Not every therapist understands the specific dynamics of religious harm. Organizations such as the Religious Trauma Institute, founded by Brian Peck, provide directories of trained clinicians and educational resources. The Secular Therapy Project maintains a database of therapists who are specifically equipped to work with clients recovering from religious harm without dismissing the significance of their former faith.

Peer support communities offer what individual therapy cannot: the experience of being understood by people who have walked the same path. Groups like Recovering from Religion provide online and in-person support. The Clergy Project serves as a confidential network for religious leaders who no longer hold supernatural beliefs but remain in ministry — a situation more common than most churchgoers would imagine.

Literature can serve as companionship on the journey. Winell's Leaving the Fold remains one of the most practical guides for those leaving authoritarian religion. Judith Herman's Trauma and Recovery (1992) offers a clinical model for the stages of healing. For those who wish to reconstruct rather than abandon faith, Brian McLaren's Faith After Doubt and Peter Enns's The Sin of Certainty offer frameworks for a faith honest about its own fragility.

It must also be said that some people who leave harmful religious environments will not return to any form of faith, and the church must respect this without treating it as a failure. If a person's experience of God has been so thoroughly mediated by an abusive system that they cannot separate the two, their departure from religion may be an act of psychological self-preservation. The church that drove them away does not get to dictate the terms of their recovery.

Religious trauma is real. It is documented. It is widespread. And it is, in a great many cases, preventable. The church that refuses to reckon with this reality will continue to produce it. The church that takes it seriously — that listens to survivors, reforms its structures, revises its theology where revision is warranted, and commits to the slow work of healing — has a chance of becoming what it has always claimed to be: a place where broken people encounter not judgment but grace, not control but freedom, not fear but the love that casts it out.

chapters.title: Spiritual Abuse: How Good Theology Gets Weaponized
chapters.summary: Spiritual abuse is not a failure of theology but its perversion — the deliberate use of scriptural authority to control, isolate, and silence. Understanding how it works is the first step toward ensuring your church is not complicit.
chapters.body:
There is a particular kind of harm that can only be inflicted by someone you trust with your soul. A boss can exploit you, a partner can betray you, a government can oppress you — and in each case, the wound is real but the categories are clear. You know what was taken from you. But when a pastor uses the language of God to manipulate your conscience, when scripture becomes the instrument of control, when the very framework you use to understand reality is turned against you — the damage is of a different order entirely. You do not merely lose trust in a person. You lose trust in the architecture of meaning itself.

This is spiritual abuse, and it is far more prevalent than most churchgoers imagine. It is not confined to fringe cults or aberrant sects. It thrives in mainstream denominations, in megachurches with sophisticated branding, in Reformed congregations with impeccable doctrinal statements, in charismatic fellowships with genuine spiritual gifts. It flourishes precisely where theology is taken seriously, because serious theology provides the most powerful tools — and the most powerful tools, in the wrong hands, inflict the most devastating wounds.

To understand spiritual abuse, we must first name it with precision. We must then trace its patterns, examine its most prominent case studies, and — most critically — identify the theological distortions that enable it and the theological corrections that prevent it. This is not an abstract exercise. There are people in your city, possibly in your congregation, who are living under spiritual abuse right now and lack the vocabulary to describe what is happening to them.

Defining the Problem

The term "spiritual abuse" was first given sustained academic treatment by David Johnson and Jeff VanVonderen in their 1991 book The Subtle Power of Spiritual Abuse, though the phenomenon they described is as old as organized religion itself. Jesus himself identified it when he condemned the Pharisees for tying up heavy burdens and laying them on people's shoulders while refusing to lift a finger to help (Matthew 23:4). The prophet Ezekiel thundered against the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves instead of the flock, who ruled with "force and harshness" (Ezekiel 34:4). The pattern is ancient. Only the terminology is new.

Spiritual abuse can be defined as the use of spiritual authority — whether derived from ordained office, scriptural knowledge, charismatic gifting, or institutional position — to coerce, control, manipulate, or shame individuals in ways that undermine their autonomy, dignity, and relationship with God. It differs from mere bad leadership or theological disagreement in a critical respect: it instrumentalizes the sacred. It takes the things a person holds most dear — their faith, their desire to please God, their trust in spiritual authority — and converts them into levers of control.

This definition excludes legitimate exercises of pastoral authority. A pastor who preaches an unpopular biblical truth is not committing spiritual abuse. A church that practices discipline according to Matthew 18 — with transparency, due process, and the goal of restoration — is not committing spiritual abuse. The line between legitimate authority and abuse is not the exercise of power itself, but whether that power is exercised for the flourishing of the person or for the benefit of the leader.

The Patterns: A Taxonomy of Control

Spiritual abuse is not random. It follows identifiable patterns, and these patterns recur across traditions, denominations, and centuries with a consistency that should alarm anyone who cares about the health of the church. Researchers including Ronald Enroth, Wade Mullen, and Diane Langberg have documented these patterns extensively, and they cluster into several recognizable categories.

Isolation is typically the first move. The abusive leader or system gradually separates congregants from outside relationships and alternative spiritual communities. This may be explicit — "Other churches are compromised; we are the faithful remnant" — or subtle, achieved through an all-consuming schedule of church activities that leaves no time for outside friendships. The theological justification often draws on separation passages like 2 Corinthians 6:17 stripped from context and applied to anyone outside the leader's control. The result is a closed ecosystem in which the leader's interpretation of reality faces no external challenge.

Information control follows naturally from isolation. Questions are reframed as rebellion. Doubt is diagnosed as spiritual deficiency. Access to outside teaching or perspectives is discouraged or forbidden. Bill Gothard's IBLP explicitly warned families against secular education, music, and friendships. Mars Hill maintained an internal culture where questioning the senior pastor was treated as questioning God's anointed. In both cases, the leader became the sole authorized interpreter of truth, and any competing source of information was delegitimized before it could be consulted.

Demands for unquestioning obedience represent the theological core of most spiritually abusive systems. The logic runs: God has placed this leader in authority; to question the leader is to question God; therefore, resistance to the leader is resistance to God. Each premise contains a grain of truth — God does establish authority structures — but the conclusion is a monstrous distortion. It eliminates the possibility of prophetic challenge, congregational accountability, or the simple recognition that leaders are fallen human beings capable of error and sin.

Public shaming serves as the enforcement mechanism. In spiritually abusive churches, those who dissent, question, or attempt to leave are subjected to public rebuke, often from the pulpit. Their character is attacked. Their motives are impugned. Their spiritual condition is questioned in front of the community. This serves a dual purpose: it punishes the dissenter and terrorizes everyone else into silence. The message is unmistakable: this is what happens to those who challenge the leader.

Spiritual gaslighting is perhaps the most insidious pattern because it attacks the victim's capacity to perceive reality. When a congregant raises a concern and is told they have "a spirit of rebellion," when a woman reports abuse and is told to "submit more," when a family questions financial irregularities and is told they "lack faith" — spiritual authority is being weaponized to override the victim's own conscience and judgment. The person is not merely told they are wrong. They are told that their very capacity to evaluate right and wrong is compromised by spiritual deficiency. This is not pastoral care. It is psychological warfare conducted in the name of God.

Case Studies: The Wreckage

The abstract patterns become concrete — and horrifying — in specific cases that have come to public attention in recent years. Each case illustrates a different facet of spiritual abuse, and together they demonstrate that this is not a problem confined to any single tradition or theological camp.

Mars Hill Church and Mark Driscoll. Mars Hill, founded in Seattle in 1996, grew into one of the most influential megachurches in America, with fifteen campuses and roughly 14,000 weekly attendees at its peak. Driscoll attracted a devoted following through his aggressive, hyper-masculine presentation of Reformed theology. Behind the public persona, former elders documented a culture of intimidation and retaliatory shunning. When two elders filed formal charges under the church's own bylaws in 2007, Driscoll responded by rewriting the bylaws to consolidate power. Questioning the senior pastor was equated with opposing God's vision. In 2014, the church collapsed under accumulated scandals — plagiarism, financial irregularities, and a pattern of bullying documented by Christianity Today. Driscoll resigned without formal accountability and launched a new church in Arizona.

IBLP and Bill Gothard. The Institute in Basic Life Principles, founded by Gothard in 1961, influenced millions of American evangelicals through its seminars, homeschool curricula, and network of training centers. Gothard taught a rigid hierarchical system in which wives were subordinate to husbands, children to parents, and all to God-ordained "authorities." His "umbrella of authority" teaching held that those who stepped outside their authority's "covering" were exposed to spiritual attack. This theology was used to silence victims of abuse within IBLP-affiliated families: women who reported domestic violence were told to submit more completely to their husbands; children who reported parental abuse were told to honor their parents regardless of conduct. In 2014, more than thirty women came forward with allegations of sexual harassment against Gothard himself. A lawsuit filed in 2016 alleged that Gothard had used his authority to groom underage girls. IBLP's theology of absolute authority had created the perfect environment for a predator: a system in which questioning the leader was sin and victims had no legitimate pathway for complaint.

Ravi Zacharias. Zacharias was widely regarded as one of the most brilliant Christian apologists of his generation, heading a global organization (RZIM) built on his personal credibility. After his death in May 2020, an independent investigation by the law firm Miller and Martin found that Zacharias had engaged in sexual misconduct with multiple women over many years. The investigation documented patterns of grooming, coercion, and spiritual manipulation. His organization actively suppressed allegations during his lifetime. The case exposed a systemic failure: an organization built entirely around one leader's credibility had no mechanism for holding that leader accountable.

The Southern Baptist Convention. In 2019, the Houston Chronicle revealed that roughly 380 Southern Baptist church leaders and volunteers had been credibly accused of sexual misconduct over the preceding two decades, with more than 700 identified victims. The SBC's congregational polity was used to justify inaction: the convention claimed no authority to maintain a database of abusers or prevent them from moving between churches. In 2022, an independent investigation by Guidepost Solutions found that SBC leaders had maintained a secret list of accused pastors but taken no action to prevent them from continuing in ministry. The executive committee had actively resisted calls for reform and treated survivors as adversaries rather than as victims deserving justice.

Why Churches Are Uniquely Vulnerable

These cases are not anomalies. They are expressions of structural vulnerabilities inherent in religious organizations — vulnerabilities that are unique to the church and that secular institutions, for all their failures, do not share to the same degree.

The first vulnerability is the nature of spiritual authority itself. A corporate manager has authority over your work. A political leader has authority over certain civic obligations. But a pastor claims authority — or is granted authority — over your relationship with God, your eternal destiny, your moral conscience, your understanding of reality. The scope of spiritual authority is, at least in principle, total. It touches everything. And because the stakes are framed as eternal rather than temporal, the pressure to comply is incomparably greater. You might leave a bad job. You are far less likely to leave a church when you have been told that doing so will endanger your soul.

The second vulnerability is the culture of shame. Churches traffic in moral categories — sin, repentance, holiness, purity — and these categories, while theologically legitimate, create an environment in which shame can be weaponized with devastating efficiency. A person who has been taught to see themselves as fundamentally sinful is primed to accept blame for any harm done to them. "If you were more spiritually mature, this would not have happened to you" is a sentence that only has force in a context where spiritual maturity is the supreme value. Abusers in churches exploit this dynamic with precision.

The third vulnerability is the "touch not God's anointed" doctrine. This phrase, drawn from 1 Chronicles 16:22 and Psalm 105:15, is routinely invoked to shield leaders from criticism. In its original context, it referred to the nation of Israel as a whole, not to individual leaders. Its application to pastors has no exegetical warrant whatsoever. Yet it functions as a powerful silencing mechanism: to criticize the pastor is to touch God's anointed, and to touch God's anointed is to invite divine judgment. The doctrine is theologically indefensible but practically devastating, because it transforms accountability into blasphemy.

The fourth vulnerability is the absence of external accountability structures. Many Protestant churches — particularly in the Baptist, nondenominational, and charismatic traditions — operate with complete autonomy. There is no bishop, no presbytery, no denominational body with the authority to investigate complaints, remove abusive leaders, or mandate reforms. The pastor answers only to a board that he often personally selected and that may share his financial interests. This is not a polity designed for accountability. It is a polity designed for independence, and independence without accountability is an invitation to abuse.

The Theology That Enables Abuse

Spiritual abuse is not merely a leadership failure. It is a theological failure — or, more precisely, it is the fruit of specific theological distortions that have become embedded in certain strands of American evangelicalism.

The first distortion is a doctrine of authority divorced from accountability. Scripture teaches that God establishes authority structures (Romans 13), but it never teaches that those structures are exempt from critique or correction. David was God's anointed king, and Nathan the prophet confronted him to his face. Paul withstood Peter to his face at Antioch because Peter was in the wrong (Galatians 2:11). The biblical model is authority exercised within a web of mutual accountability, not authority exercised in a vacuum. When churches teach submission to leaders without simultaneously teaching leaders' accountability to the congregation, they are teaching half a doctrine — and a half-truth in theology is worse than a lie, because it comes dressed in the garments of orthodoxy.

The second distortion is a doctrine of submission without limits. Ephesians 5:21 — "Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ" — is the verse that governs the entire subsequent passage about relationships. The submission Paul describes is mutual, voluntary, and bounded by the character of Christ. When this teaching is distorted into one-directional, compulsory submission — wives to husbands, congregants to pastors, children to parents, regardless of the authority figure's conduct — the result is a theology that sanctifies domination. Gothard's "umbrella of authority" is the clearest example, but the pattern is widespread. Wherever submission is taught as absolute and unidirectional, abuse will follow as surely as night follows day.

The third distortion is the "covering" doctrine. This teaching, prevalent in charismatic and Pentecostal circles, holds that every believer must be "under the covering" of a spiritual authority — typically a pastor — who serves as a mediator between the individual and God. To leave this covering is to be spiritually unprotected, vulnerable to demonic attack and divine displeasure. The doctrine has no clear biblical basis. It contradicts the Reformation principle of the priesthood of all believers. And it creates a relationship of spiritual dependency that mirrors the dynamics of an abusive personal relationship: the person cannot leave because they have been told that leaving itself is the danger.

The Theology That Prevents Abuse

If distorted theology enables abuse, then recovered theology — theology read carefully, in context, with attention to the full witness of scripture — is the church's most powerful tool for preventing it.

The first corrective is mutual submission. Ephesians 5:21 is not a prelude to hierarchy. It is the governing principle. In the body of Christ, authority flows in every direction. Leaders serve the congregation (Mark 10:42-45). The congregation holds leaders accountable (Matthew 18:15-17). Elders are subject to the judgment of the community (1 Timothy 5:19-20). No one in the New Testament operates with unchecked authority. Not the apostles. Not the elders. Not even Paul, who repeatedly submitted his teaching to the judgment of his communities and invited correction.

The second corrective is servant leadership as defined by Jesus, not by the culture of celebrity. When James and John asked for positions of power in the kingdom, Jesus responded with words that should be engraved on the door of every seminary and every pastor's study: "You know that those who are regarded as rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their high officials exercise authority over them. Not so with you. Instead, whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant, and whoever wants to be first must be slave of all" (Mark 10:42-44). This is not metaphor. It is a structural principle. Leadership in the church is defined by service, not by authority. A pastor who demands obedience has already disqualified himself from the office he claims.

The third corrective is congregational transparency. Secrecy is the oxygen of abuse. Every major case of spiritual abuse in recent memory was enabled by secrecy — secret finances, secret personnel decisions, secret disciplinary actions, secret arrangements to protect the leader. The antidote is radical transparency: open financial books, publicly accountable governance, independent grievance procedures, mandatory reporting policies, and a culture in which questions are welcomed rather than punished. A church that cannot withstand scrutiny is a church that should not be trusted with people's souls.

The fourth corrective is a robust theology of human fallenness applied to leaders. The Reformation insisted that all human beings — including pastors, bishops, and popes — are simultaneously justified and sinful (simul justus et peccator). If we truly believe this, then we must build institutions that account for the reality that leaders will sometimes sin, will sometimes abuse their power, and will sometimes need to be removed. The question is not whether leaders will fail. The question is whether the structures around them will catch the failure before it becomes catastrophic.

How to Recognize Spiritual Abuse in Your Church

Discernment in this area is not about suspicion but about clarity. There are concrete indicators that distinguish healthy, if imperfect, church leadership from spiritually abusive systems. Consider the following diagnostic questions with honest eyes.

First, examine how your church handles dissent. In a healthy church, disagreement is treated as a normal feature of community life. People can question a sermon, challenge a policy, or express concern about a leader's behavior without fear of retaliation. In an abusive system, dissent is pathologized. Questioners are labeled as divisive, rebellious, or spiritually immature. If your church treats every question as a threat, something is wrong.

Second, examine the financial transparency. Can any member access a detailed accounting of the church's finances, including the senior pastor's compensation? If not, ask why. Legitimate confidentiality concerns can be addressed without concealing pastoral compensation or discretionary spending. Financial secrecy in a church is a red flag of the most serious kind.

Third, examine how departures are handled. In a healthy church, when people leave, they leave with blessing. Leaders may express sadness, but they do not malign the departing member's character, warn the congregation against them, or cut off their relationships within the community. In an abusive system, departure is treated as betrayal. Those who leave are shunned, slandered, or spiritually condemned. If leaving your church would cost you every friendship within it, you are not in a church. You are in a closed system.

Fourth, examine the leader's response to accountability. Does the pastor have genuine peers who can confront him or her with uncomfortable truths? Is there a board with the authority and the will to discipline or remove the senior leader? Has the church ever exercised this authority, or does it exist only on paper? If the senior leader is functionally unaccountable, the structure is inherently dangerous regardless of the leader's current character.

Fifth, examine the role of guilt and fear in the church's culture. Healthy churches produce gratitude, joy, and a growing sense of freedom in Christ. Abusive churches produce anxiety, guilt, fear of divine punishment, and an exhausting sense that one can never do enough, give enough, or submit enough. Paul writes that "where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom" (2 Corinthians 3:17). If your experience of church is defined by bondage rather than freedom, that is not a failure of your faith. It is a failure of your church.

"The shepherds have fed themselves and have not fed my flock. Therefore, thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against the shepherds, and I will require my flock at their hand and put a stop to their feeding the flock." — Ezekiel 34:8-10

Spiritual abuse is not an inevitable feature of organized religion. It is a corruption — a parasitic distortion that feeds on genuine faith and sincere devotion. The church's task is not to abandon authority but to exercise it rightly: with transparency, accountability, humility, and an unwavering commitment to the flourishing of every person entrusted to its care. Where these qualities are absent, the church is not the church. It is something else entirely.

The victims of spiritual abuse deserve more than sympathy. They deserve structural change — churches that take their own theology seriously enough to apply it to their own leaders, communities where power is exercised in the pattern of Christ, who emptied himself, who washed feet, who submitted to death rather than coerce a single human conscience. The alternative — a church that tolerates the weaponization of the gospel — is not merely unacceptable. It is, in the deepest theological sense of the word, blasphemous.

chapters.title: The Church After Cultural Power
chapters.summary: Now that the church no longer sets the terms of the culture, it has to decide whether it ever knew how to be the church without them.
chapters.body:
The store stayed closed on Sunday because the whole town agreed the day belonged to God, and now it does not, and a certain kind of Christian experiences that as the world ending. I understand the feeling. I grew up at the tail end of an arrangement where the culture did half the church's work for free, where the calendar and the schools and the social pressure all leaned the same direction the sermon did. That arrangement is gone. The church no longer sets the terms. The real question is not how to get the terms back. The real question is whether the church ever knew how to be the church without them.

This is the hard part to say to people who are grieving. Much of what we mourn as the loss of faith is the loss of advantage. We had a home-field edge for a long time, the assumption that decent and Christian were near synonyms, the social cost attached to leaving rather than to staying. Strip that away and church attendance falls, not because people stopped believing so much as because the people who never really believed stopped pretending. The decline is partly a subtraction of the nominal, the inherited, the convenient. It hurts, and it is also a kind of honesty arriving late.

The text I will carry is small and easy to misread as flattery. You are the salt of the earth, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored, it is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled (Matthew 5:13 ESV). We read the first clause as a compliment and skip the warning, which is the whole point. Salt works by being different from what it is added to. It does its work by concentration, by not dissolving entirely into the dish. The danger Jesus names is not that the world will overpower the salt. It is that the salt will lose the very quality that made it useful, that it will become indistinguishable from what surrounds it, and then be good for nothing. Christendom was the long temptation to dissolve. We added ourselves so thoroughly to the culture that no one could taste the difference anymore.

Steel-man the grief, because it is not foolish. The people who mourn the church's lost cultural power are often mourning real losses with real names. When the culture honored the faith, the unborn had more protection, the poor had more institutions tending them, marriage had more support around it, and a young person absorbed a moral grammar just by breathing the civic air. Those were goods, and a flippant Christianity that celebrates their loss as freedom is a Christianity that has stopped loving its neighbors. James Davison Hunter, no triumphalist, has documented how thoroughly the church has lost its place at the center of the culture and how poorly its strategies of political conquest have served it (Hunter 2010). When believers grieve, they are often grieving the visible erosion of things the gospel actually cares about. That grief is not weakness. It is love looking at a wound.

So answer the strong version. Yes, those were goods, and yes, their erosion is a real wound. But the question is whether the church protected them by being the church or by borrowing the state's machinery of compulsion, and the difference is everything. When the unborn were protected by a cultural consensus rather than by a converted people, the protection was always one election away from collapse, because it rested on power rather than on persuaded hearts. The church mistook a borrowed majority for its own strength. It learned to win by counting votes instead of making disciples, and a victory you win that way you cannot keep, because the moment the votes shift you have nothing left, no community formed deeply enough to live differently when the law no longer requires it. We were never as strong as the consensus made us look. We just could not tell, because the home-field edge hid the weakness.

Trace the root, briefly, because the pattern is old. The church learned to rely on cultural power in 312 and never fully unlearned it, and every later establishment, every state church and Christian nation and moral majority, repeated the same bargain. We traded the slow work of formation for the fast work of legislation. William Cavanaugh has argued that the modern church too often accepts the role the state assigns it, a private provider of values to prop up the public order, and in accepting that role it forgets that it is itself a public, a body politic with its own way of life (Cavanaugh 2002). We let the culture make us its chaplain and called it influence. Influence was the word we used while we were being domesticated.

The cross does the work here, and it does it by exposing what we actually trusted. A crucified Lord is the permanent refutation of the idea that the kingdom advances by holding the levers of power. Jesus held no levers. He had no majority, no favorable law, no cultural consensus, and the consensus he did encounter voted to kill him. If the gospel needed cultural power to be true and to spread, then the gospel died on a Friday afternoon outside a city wall with the entire establishment arrayed against it. It did not die. It rose, and it spread for three centuries with every cultural lever pulling the other way. The church that grieves its lost power is, without meaning to, confessing that it had started to trust the levers more than the cross.

Here is the reversal, and I include myself in it. We say we want the culture back so we can serve our neighbors better, protect the vulnerable, hold the moral line. Some of that is true. But some of it is that the loss of power has exposed how much of our religion was power, how little of our witness could survive without the wind at our back. The end of cultural Christianity is not only a loss. It is a test, and the test is whether anything is left when the advantage is gone.
