A church that can only be the church when the culture agrees with it was never depending on the Spirit. It was depending on the culture. Now it gets to find out the difference, and the finding out is mercy disguised as decline.

I have watched congregations respond to the loss in two ways, and the two ways reveal everything. Some grow frightened and angry, and they pour their energy into recapturing the levers, the school board and the legislature and the courts, convinced that if they can just get the power back the faith will be safe. Others, quieter, smaller, stop waiting for the culture to do their work and start doing it themselves, forming people, taking in the discarded, building communities so distinct that a watching neighbor has to ask what makes them that way. The first group is fighting to restore Christendom. The second group has accepted its death and gone looking for the church underneath it. I am not neutral about which one I want to hand my sons. The first has a louder voice and a worse record. The second looks like the people Pliny could not explain.

This is where the early church becomes the curriculum and not the museum piece. They never had the power we are mourning. They had no closed stores and no Christian calendar and no social reward for belonging, and they built a community so distinct that the empire could not understand it and so attractive that the empire could not stop it. They were salt because they had no choice but to be salt, no consensus to dissolve into. We are being handed the same conditions. The only question is whether we will read them as catastrophe or as a return to the ground where the faith has always grown best.

I have five sons who will pastor and parent and work in a country that no longer does the church's job for it. I will not lie to them that this is easy. But I would rather hand them a salt that remembers its taste than a comfort that forgot it. The trampling Jesus warned about does not come from the world's hostility. It comes from the salt forgetting what it was for.

The culture is done carrying us. Good. Now we find out if we believed any of it.

### Works Cited

Cavanaugh, William T. Theopolitical Imagination: Discovering the Liturgy as a Political Act in an Age of Global Consumerism. London: T and T Clark, 2002.

Hunter, James Davison. To Change the World: The Irony, Tragedy, and Possibility of Christianity in the Late Modern World. New York: Oxford University Press, 2010.

Newbigin, Lesslie. The Gospel in a Pluralist Society. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 1989.

Hauerwas, Stanley, and William H. Willimon. Resident Aliens: Life in the Christian Colony. Nashville: Abingdon Press, 1989.

chapters.title: The Church Held Captive to the Culture War
chapters.summary: We were promised the culture war would defend the faith, and instead it quietly rewrote the faith to fit the war.
chapters.body:
A man left my church a few years ago not over a doctrine but over a vote. He could not understand how I could shepherd people who voted the other way. He said it as a matter of faithfulness, and he meant it. What unsettled me was not that he was political. We are all political, and the gospel has public weight or it has none. What unsettled me was that he could no longer locate his deepest loyalty. When I asked him gently what he believed about the cross, he answered me with a position on a policy. The grammar had shifted underneath him, and he had not noticed, and I am not sure I would have noticed in his place.

The real question is not whether Christians should care about justice and law and the shape of the common life. We must. The question is what happens to a church when the framework through which it sees everything is no longer the kingdom of God but the war between two tribes, when the categories that organize the Christian mind are imported wholesale from a politics that was not built to carry the weight of the soul.

Here is the strongest defense of Christian engagement in the culture war, and it is not weak. The faith makes claims about reality. It says the unborn child is a person, that marriage has a given shape, that there is such a thing as truth, that the powerful will answer for the vulnerable. These are not private opinions to be kept behind the church door. They are public truths, and a church that retreats into a spiritual interior while the world burns has abandoned the prophets, who stood in the gates of the city and named the sins of the nation by name. The believer who fights for the weak in the public square is doing something the Bible commands. To call that captivity would be a slander. I hold these convictions. I have not softened them.

But here is what that defense cannot account for. There is a difference between the church speaking prophetically to the powers and the church being captured by one of the powers. The prophet stands outside the kingdoms and judges them all by a higher throne. The captive stands inside one kingdom and judges the other in its terms, and calls his captivity courage. The test is simple and brutal. When your political tribe does the very thing you condemned in the other tribe, do you say so. If the answer is no, if the sin becomes acceptable the moment your side commits it, then you are not a prophet. You are a chaplain to a faction, and the faction owns you.

Carry one text, the oldest temptation, told as a true story. The devil took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. And he said to him, All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me (Matthew 4:8 ESV). Read it slowly. The offer was the kingdoms. The offer was real power, real influence, the levers of the nations placed in the hand of the Son of God, and it would have skipped the cross entirely. The price was a single act of worship redirected. Not the abandonment of the kingdoms. The reordering of worship to obtain them. That is the precise shape of the church's captivity. We are not offered evil. We are offered influence, and asked only to bow slightly, to make the cause the thing and the cross the instrument, and we tell ourselves we are still worshiping God while we do it.

Trace the history, because this is older and more bipartisan than we admit. In the early 1980s a coalition formed that fused a wing of the American church to a political movement with a discipline neither had known before. It delivered real victories and a real cost, and the cost was that a generation of believers learned to read their Bibles through a partisan lens so total that the parties began to function as denominations. David Wells, watching the church across these decades, named the underlying disease before the politics ever crystallized. He argued that the evangelical church had already hollowed out its theology, had traded the weight of truth for the techniques of relevance and success, so that when the culture war came it found a church with no theological center strong enough to resist being annexed by something with a center of its own (Wells 1993). A church that had stopped being formed by its doctrine was available to be formed by its politics, and it was, and so was the church on the other side, the progressive congregation that discovered its entire moral vocabulary had quietly been issued by the latest social movement, with the cross retained as decoration.

Neil Postman saw the mechanism that made all of this possible and worse. He argued that the move of public life onto the screen does not merely change what we know, it changes the form of knowing itself, dissolving argument into image and conviction into entertainment, so that a culture organized around the television and now the feed comes to experience even its most serious commitments as a kind of show (Postman 1985). The culture war is not primarily a war of ideas. It is a war of feelings staged for an audience, and the church walked onto that stage carrying the gospel and started performing it for applause, and forgot it was holding something that was meant to be died for, not posted.

Now the reversal, and it cuts. We entered the culture war to defend the faith. The war did not destroy the faith from outside. It rewrote it from inside. It taught us to feel our deepest belonging with our tribe and only our nominal belonging with the brother across the aisle who shares our baptism. It made the enemy a category of people rather than the principalities and powers Paul actually names. We came to save the faith and we let the faith be conscripted, and the proof is that for many of us it now costs more to break with our political side than to break with our Lord. We would lose more friends. That sentence should stop us cold.

Law before grace, and I am inside the law. I have felt the warm pull of the applause line, the sermon that lands because it confirms what my people already wanted to hate. I have measured a brother by his vote before I measured him by his cross. I have been quieter about the sins of my own side because quiet was cheaper, and I have called that prudence when it was cowardice. The captivity does not happen to other pastors in other states. It happens at my desk, on the weeks I want my people to love me more than I want them to be free.

The grace runs straight through the temptation in the wilderness, because the one being offered the kingdoms refused them, and went and got them another way, by the cross, by dying, by rising, by a throne no election confers and no defeat removes. He owns the kingdoms now, all of them, the ones my tribe runs and the ones the other tribe runs, and he holds them so lightly and so surely that he can ask me to love my political enemy without fear, because the outcome was never riding on my faction. The kingdom does not need my captivity to advance. It only needs my allegiance, and allegiance has only ever had room for one throne.

The war promised to make us strong. It made us loud, and then it made us its own.

Not a prophet to the nation. A chaplain to a faction. We can still tell the difference, if we are willing to fail the tribe's test on purpose.

### Works Cited

Wells, David F. No Place for Truth: Or Whatever Happened to Evangelical Theology. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 1993.

Postman, Neil. Amusing Ourselves to Death: Public Discourse in the Age of Show Business. New York: Viking, 1985.

The Holy Bible. English Standard Version. Wheaton: Crossway, 2001.

chapters.title: The Death of Christendom
chapters.summary: For fifteen centuries, Christianity and Western civilization were so deeply fused that it was nearly impossible to distinguish where one ended and the other began. That era is over. The question is not whether Christendom is dying but whether its death might be the best thing that ever happened to the church.
chapters.body:
There is a cathedral in the center of Amsterdam that has been converted into a conference venue. You can rent it for corporate events, art exhibitions, and private parties. There is a church in London that is now a nightclub. Another in Dublin that houses a restaurant. Across Western Europe, the great physical monuments of Christendom are being repurposed, not because the buildings have failed but because the civilization they represented has moved on.

This is not a story about buildings. It is a story about the end of an arrangement that shaped Western civilization for a millennium and a half, an arrangement so pervasive that most people who lived within it could not see its edges. For fifteen centuries, to be European was to be Christian, to be Christian was to be civilized, and to be civilized was to belong to a world ordered by Christian assumptions about God, time, morality, law, art, sex, death, and meaning. That world, called Christendom, is dying. And the death, depending on where you stand, is either the greatest catastrophe in the history of the faith or its greatest opportunity.

What Christendom Was

Christendom is not a synonym for Christianity. Christianity is a faith, a set of convictions about who God is and what God has done. Christendom is a political and cultural arrangement in which that faith becomes the organizing principle of an entire civilization, fused with state power, embedded in law, assumed in education, and enforced, where necessary, by coercion.

The arrangement began with Constantine. In 313, the Edict of Milan granted Christianity legal toleration in the Roman Empire. By 380, under Theodosius I, Christianity became the official state religion. Pagan temples were closed or converted. Christian bishops assumed civic functions. Theological disputes became matters of imperial policy. The Nicene Creed was not merely a confession of faith. It was a product of an emperor's political need for religious unity. The church gained security, resources, and influence. It also gained entanglement with power that would prove extraordinarily difficult to disentangle.

For the next fifteen centuries, across the medieval and early modern periods, Christendom defined the shape of European civilization. The church baptized kings, legitimated wars, administered education, regulated marriage, kept time (the calendar itself was organized around Christian feasts), and provided the moral vocabulary with which Europeans understood their world. Even the Reformation, which shattered the institutional unity of Western Christianity, did not break the Christendom arrangement. Protestant nations simply created Protestant versions of it: the Church of England, the Lutheran state churches of Scandinavia, the Reformed churches of Switzerland and the Netherlands. The state still enforced religious conformity. The church still provided ideological support for the state. The fusion remained.

Charles Taylor and the Secular Age

The Canadian philosopher Charles Taylor, in his monumental 2007 work A Secular Age, provides what is arguably the most sophisticated account of how Christendom unraveled. Taylor's central question is not "Why do some people stop believing in God?" but rather "Why is it that in 1500, it was virtually impossible not to believe in God, and in 2000, it is entirely possible, even easy?" The question is not about individual belief but about the conditions of belief, the "background" against which belief or unbelief becomes thinkable.

Taylor traces a long, complex process that he calls the move from a "porous" self to a "buffered" self. In the medieval world, the self was porous, open to spiritual forces, vulnerable to demons and saints, embedded in a cosmos charged with divine meaning. Disenchantment was not an option because the world itself was experienced as enchanted. The modern self, by contrast, is buffered, self-contained, insulated from spiritual forces, capable of treating the world as a neutral object of scientific investigation. In this buffered condition, belief in God becomes one option among many rather than the default setting of consciousness.

This is not a story of simple secularization, the idea that modernity inevitably erodes religion. Taylor rejects that narrative. Instead, he describes a "nova effect" in which the range of available spiritual options has exploded. People in modern societies can be devout Catholics, committed atheists, spiritual-but-not-religious seekers, Buddhist-influenced meditators, or any number of other things. The key change is that faith is no longer the water everyone swims in. It is a choice, one option in a marketplace of meaning. And a faith that is chosen rather than assumed is a fundamentally different kind of faith, even if its content remains the same.

The European Collapse

The empirical evidence of Christendom's collapse in Europe is overwhelming. Church attendance in most of Western Europe has fallen below 10 percent. In the Netherlands, church membership dropped from 75 percent in 1960 to below 40 percent by 2020. In the United Kingdom, the Church of England, the established church, draws fewer than 700,000 people on a typical Sunday, less than 2 percent of the population. In Scandinavia, where Lutheran state churches remain technically established, Sunday attendance runs between 1 and 3 percent. France, "the eldest daughter of the Church," has fewer practicing Catholics than practicing Muslims. Ireland, once considered the most Catholic country in Europe, voted overwhelmingly to legalize both same-sex marriage (2015) and abortion (2018), completing a cultural revolution that would have been unthinkable a generation earlier.

Germany, the land of the Reformation, presents a particularly striking case. Both the Catholic Church and the Evangelical (Protestant) Church in Germany lose hundreds of thousands of members annually, a trend accelerated by the "church tax" system that makes formal membership financially costly. Empty churches dot the landscape. Theological faculties at state universities train fewer students each decade. The cultural infrastructure of German Christianity, its schools, hospitals, charitable organizations, remains vast, but it operates increasingly on institutional momentum rather than living faith.

These are not merely statistical declines. They represent the end of a civilizational paradigm. For centuries, European culture was Christian culture. Its art was Christian art, its architecture was Christian architecture, its moral vocabulary was Christian moral vocabulary. When Dante wrote the Divine Comedy, he assumed that every reader shared his cosmology. When Bach composed the Mass in B Minor, he assumed that every listener knew what a mass was. Those assumptions no longer hold. European civilization has not replaced Christianity with an alternative comprehensive worldview. It has simply moved into a condition that Taylor calls "exclusive humanism," a vision of human flourishing that makes no reference to anything beyond the immanent world.

The American Version

The United States never had a formal Christendom in the European sense. The First Amendment prohibited the establishment of religion at the federal level, and the last state establishments were dissolved by the 1830s. But America developed its own version: a civil religion in which Christianity, specifically Protestant Christianity, was woven into the national identity without being formally established. "In God We Trust" on the currency, "under God" in the Pledge of Allegiance, prayers at presidential inaugurations, the assumption that political leaders would be churchgoing Christians, these constituted an informal Christendom, softer than the European version but remarkably durable.

The "Christian nation" narrative, the belief that the United States was founded as an explicitly Christian country and that its laws and institutions are rooted in Christian principles, has been a powerful force in American public life. It is also, in its strongest form, historically indefensible. The Constitution does not mention God (except in the date formula, "in the Year of our Lord"). The founders included devout Christians, nominal Christians, Deists, and religious skeptics. Thomas Jefferson literally cut the miracles out of the Gospels with a razor. Benjamin Franklin attended church sporadically and expressed doubts about the divinity of Christ. The First Amendment was not a grudging concession to pluralism. It was a deliberate design choice by men who had seen the devastation that established religion caused in Europe.

But the "Christian nation" myth persists because it serves a powerful psychological function. It provides a sacred canopy, a sense that America is not merely a political arrangement but a divinely ordained project. When that canopy frays, the resulting anxiety is immense, which explains much of the intensity of the culture wars. What is experienced as a battle over "religious freedom" or "family values" is often, at a deeper level, a battle over whether the informal Christendom of American civil religion will survive.

The Rise of the Nones

The empirical evidence suggests it will not. The Pew Research Center documented a transformation in the American religious landscape that has accelerated rapidly since the 1990s. The proportion of Americans who identify as religiously unaffiliated, the so-called "nones," rose from approximately 6 percent in 1991 to over 28 percent by 2023. Among adults under thirty, the figure approaches 40 percent. This is the fastest demographic shift in American religious history.

The "nones" are not, for the most part, militant atheists. Only a small percentage identify as atheist or agnostic. The majority describe themselves as "nothing in particular," people who have simply drifted away from organized religion without replacing it with an alternative philosophical commitment. They are not hostile to religion. They are indifferent to it, which may be more devastating to institutional Christianity than hostility.

The causes are debated, but several factors are well-documented. The politicization of Christianity, particularly the identification of evangelical Christianity with the Republican Party, has driven away moderates and progressives who refuse to join an institution they perceive as a political operation. The clergy sexual abuse crisis, particularly in the Catholic Church, has destroyed institutional credibility. The increasing availability of alternative sources of community, meaning, and moral formation, from secular nonprofits to online communities to wellness culture, has reduced the social necessity of church membership. And the simple fact that religious non-affiliation is now socially acceptable, even normative in many contexts, has removed the stigma that once kept nominal believers in the pews.

What Christendom Provided

It is important to be honest about what is being lost. Christendom, for all its failures, provided things that are not easily replaced. It provided a shared moral framework, a common language of right and wrong rooted in a tradition deep enough to sustain centuries of ethical reflection. It provided institutional infrastructure: hospitals, universities, orphanages, poor relief, systems of care that the church built long before the modern welfare state existed. It provided cultural coherence, a sense that life has a shape, a story with a beginning, middle, and end, a drama of creation, fall, and redemption that gave meaning to suffering, beauty to art, and purpose to existence.

The loss of this framework is not merely an ecclesiastical problem. It is a civilizational one. The "deaths of despair" documented by economists Anne Case and Angus Deaton, rising rates of suicide, drug overdose, and alcoholism, particularly among middle-aged white Americans, correlate with the collapse of the institutions, churches prominent among them, that once provided meaning, community, and purpose. The loneliness epidemic, the decline of civic participation, the fragmentation of shared reality into competing information silos, all of these have roots in the dissolution of the communal structures that Christendom, for better and worse, sustained.

What Christendom Cost

But honesty also requires acknowledging what Christendom cost. The price was enormous, paid disproportionately by those without power.

Christendom cost coercion. When Christianity becomes the official religion of a civilization, dissent becomes not merely heresy but treason. The Inquisition, the wars of religion, the forced conversion of indigenous peoples, the persecution of Jews, the burning of heretics, these were not aberrations of Christendom. They were its logical expressions. A faith fused with state power will, inevitably, use that power to enforce conformity. The history of Christendom is, in significant part, a history of violence committed in the name of the Prince of Peace.

Christendom cost complicity. The church's fusion with political power meant that it consistently served the interests of the powerful rather than the powerless. It blessed wars of conquest. It sanctified slavery. It legitimated colonialism. It provided theological cover for the subjugation of women, the persecution of sexual minorities, and the dispossession of indigenous peoples. The prophetic tradition, the strand of Christianity that speaks truth to power on behalf of the marginalized, was never extinguished, but it was consistently marginalized by the dominant Christendom tradition that identified the church's interests with the interests of the ruling class.

Christendom cost the church its capacity for self-critique. When the church is the establishment, it cannot easily critique the establishment. When bishops are political figures, they cannot easily challenge political power. When theological dissent is punishable by death, the free inquiry that theology requires is stifled. Christendom produced magnificent cathedrals, profound theology, and extraordinary art. It also produced institutional arrogance, intellectual conformity, and a fatal inability to distinguish between the gospel and the culture that claimed to embody it.

Bonhoeffer's Religionless Christianity

Dietrich Bonhoeffer, writing from a Nazi prison in 1944, asked a question that has haunted theology ever since: "What is bothering me incessantly is the question what Christianity really is, or indeed who Christ really is, for us today." Bonhoeffer observed that the world had "come of age," that humanity no longer needed religion as a "working hypothesis" to explain the gaps in scientific knowledge or to manage the anxieties of existence. God was being pushed to the margins of life, invoked only in moments of crisis or weakness.

Bonhoeffer's response was not to mourn this development but to embrace it. He called for a "religionless Christianity," a faith that did not depend on the "religious premise," the assumption that people need religion and will therefore come to the church when they are desperate enough. Instead, Bonhoeffer envisioned a church that would exist not at the center of power but at the margins, not as the chaplain to the status quo but as a community of discipleship, solidarity, and sacrificial service.

Bonhoeffer was executed by the Nazis on April 9, 1945, two weeks before the liberation of the concentration camp where he was held. His fragmentary prison writings have been interpreted in many directions. But his core intuition, that the end of Christendom might be the beginning of authentic Christianity, has proven prophetic. A church that no longer has cultural power might rediscover what it means to follow a crucified Lord.

Hauerwas: The Church Should Be Glad

The American theologian Stanley Hauerwas has argued, with characteristic bluntness, that the church should celebrate the death of Christendom. Hauerwas contends that Christendom was always a corruption of authentic Christianity. By accepting Constantine's offer of power, the church traded its prophetic identity for institutional security. It became the chaplain of empire rather than the community of the cross. It produced nominal Christians by the millions, people who were Christian because everyone was Christian, but whose faith had no distinctive shape, no costly commitment, no capacity to resist the dominant culture when that culture was unjust.

Hauerwas's alternative is a church that knows itself to be "resident aliens," a community with its own distinctive practices, narratives, and virtues, existing within but not fully assimilated to the surrounding culture. This church does not seek to run the world. It seeks to be the church, a visible community of worship, mutual care, and prophetic witness that demonstrates what human life looks like when it is ordered by the story of Jesus rather than the story of the nation-state or the market.

The critique of Hauerwas, and it has force, is that his vision can become sectarian, a church so focused on its own internal life that it abandons responsibility for the common good. But his central claim stands: a church that exists to serve the interests of the state, the market, or the culture has ceased to be the church. And Christendom, whatever its other accomplishments, consistently produced exactly that kind of church.

What Post-Christendom Christianity Looks Like

If Christendom is dying, what emerges in its place? Several characteristics are already visible.

Voluntary rather than inherited. In a post-Christendom world, no one is born Christian. Faith is a choice, not a default. This means that Christian communities will be smaller but more intentional. The nominal Christianity of the Christendom era, in which membership was a social convention rather than a personal commitment, will disappear. What remains will be people who have chosen to be there, who have counted the cost and decided that following Jesus is worth it. This is, arguably, a return to the conditions of the early church, which grew not through state support but through the attractiveness of its communal life.

Prophetic rather than chaplaincy. A church that no longer serves the establishment is free to critique the establishment. Post-Christendom Christianity is liberated from the obligation to bless whatever the nation does. It can speak truth to power without fear of losing its privileged position, because it no longer has a privileged position to lose. The prophetic tradition, suppressed for centuries by the church's entanglement with power, can reemerge as the church's primary public posture.

Communal rather than individual. In a culture of atomized individualism, the church's distinctive gift is community: embodied, committed, intergenerational relationships formed around shared practices of worship, service, and mutual care. The early church was known not primarily for its doctrines but for its communal life. "See how they love one another," Tertullian reported the pagans saying. In a lonely, fragmented culture, that witness is more needed than ever.

Costly rather than convenient. Christendom made Christianity easy. You were born into it, confirmed into it, married in it, and buried by it. Post-Christendom faith will be costly. It will require intentional formation, countercultural commitment, and the willingness to be different in a culture that punishes difference. The theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer distinguished between "cheap grace," grace as a doctrine without discipleship, and "costly grace," grace that calls to follow Jesus on the way of the cross. Christendom was the institutional embodiment of cheap grace. Its death may be the precondition for costly grace to reemerge.

The Opportunity

There is a passage in the Gospel of Mark that is rarely quoted in this context but is strikingly relevant. Jesus says: "Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit" (John 12:24, actually). The principle of death and resurrection is not merely a doctrine about the afterlife. It is the pattern of God's work in history. Institutions die so that new life can emerge. Structures collapse so that what was buried beneath them can grow.

The death of Christendom is not the death of Christianity. It is the death of a particular arrangement, the fusion of faith with cultural power, that served certain purposes for certain centuries but also distorted the faith in ways that are only now becoming fully visible. A church that no longer rules the culture might rediscover the subversive, world-altering power of the gospel. A faith that can no longer be inherited might become, once again, a faith worth choosing. A tradition that has lost its institutional privilege might recover its prophetic voice.

This is not optimism. It is theology. The same God who raised Jesus from the dead is capable of raising the church from its institutional grave. But resurrection, in the Christian tradition, always requires death first. The grain of wheat must fall into the ground. The old wineskins must burst before new wine can be poured. The temple must be torn down before it can be rebuilt in three days.

The death of Christendom is painful, disorienting, and in many ways tragic. But it may also be precisely what the church needs. A church stripped of power, prestige, and cultural dominance might finally become what it was always meant to be: a community of people who follow a crucified Lord, who live by a different story than the one the culture tells, and who bear witness to a kingdom that is not of this world but is, nevertheless, the truest thing in it.

chapters.title: The Difference Between Loving and Worshiping Your Country
chapters.summary: Love can be corrected, and worship cannot, and that single difference is the whole line between honoring your country and serving it as a god.
chapters.body:
My oldest son asked me once, after a parade, why we put our hands over our hearts. I gave him the easy answer about respect and the people who died. Then I drove home turning the question over, because it was a better question than my answer. We put our hands over our hearts in two settings. One is in front of the flag. The other is when we pray. A child notices the rhyme that an adult has stopped hearing.

The question underneath my son's question is the oldest one a believer faces. What may I love, and how much, before love becomes worship. Because love and worship are not opposites. Worship is what love becomes when it stops admitting any limit. And a country is one of the easiest things in the world to love past its limit, because a country asks for that love openly, with music and graves and the names of the fallen, and to withhold it feels like betrayal of the dead.

I want to defend the love before I warn against the worship, because the warning is dishonest without the defense. A Christian may love his country, truly and without apology. The same Scripture that exiled Israel to Babylon told them to love Babylon, to seek its welfare, to pray for it, to plant gardens in it (Jeremiah 29:7 ESV). That is not grudging tolerance. That is a command to care for a place that was not even their own. How much more may a person care for the country that raised him, fed him, schooled his children, buried his father. The instinct that tightens a man's throat at a military funeral is not a sin. It is a love, and love is a good thing, and the people who sneer at it have usually never loved a place enough to be embarrassed by their own tears.

The strongest objection to everything I am about to say comes from the believer who hears warnings against nationalism as warnings against love itself. He says the warnings always cut one direction, that nobody scolds the cosmopolitan who feels nothing for any place, that the suspicion of patriotism is itself a kind of contempt for ordinary people and their ordinary loyalties. He is right that the contempt is real and common. He is right that a man who loves nowhere is not more holy than a man who loves somewhere. Rootlessness is not a virtue. So I am not arguing for the cold heart that the warnings sometimes smuggle in. I am arguing for the difference between a warm heart and an enthroned one.

Here is the line, and I will draw it as plainly as I can. Love can be corrected. Worship cannot. You can love your wife and still tell her she is wrong, still grieve when she sins, still refuse to follow her into something evil, and the love survives the correction, even deepens through it. But the thing you worship cannot be corrected, because correction assumes a standard above the thing, and worship has put the thing at the top where no standard reaches it. The test of whether you love your country or worship it is not how you feel at the parade. It is what you do when your country is wrong. The lover says my country, and grieves, and resists. The worshiper says my country, and defends it, because the alternative would mean his god has failed.

Reinhold Niebuhr named this near the end of his life, watching the United States sanctify its own power in the Cold War. Patriotism, he wrote, is a high form of devotion, but it becomes demonic when it claims an unconditioned loyalty, the loyalty that belongs to God alone (Niebuhr 1952). The word he chose was demonic, and he did not choose it for effect. He meant that a good thing loved past its limit does not stay good and shrink. It becomes a power that demands sacrifice, that silences conscience, that turns the love of a place into the willingness to do evil for it. That is the mechanism of every idol. The idol is rarely a bad thing. It is usually a good thing that has been asked to be God.

Augustine saw the same mechanism a millennium and a half earlier, and he gave it the cleanest definition we have. Sin, he taught, is disordered love, love poured out in the wrong proportion, the lesser good loved as though it were the greatest (Augustine 397). The drunk does not love wine too much in some simple sense. He loves it out of order, above his health, above his family, above God. The nationalist does not love his country too much. He loves it out of order, above the kingdom, above the stranger his country fears, above the Christ who told him the stranger bears the image of God. The problem was never the size of the love. It was the place the love was put.

Carry one text as the spine of this. When the people demanded a king so they could be like the nations around them, God told Samuel something that should unsettle every patriot who has ever wanted his country to be great. They have not rejected you, he said. They have rejected me from being king over them (1 Samuel 8:7 ESV). Israel wanted a nation that could stand tall among the nations, a king they could see, a strength they could point to. God read that desire correctly. It was not a political preference. It was a transfer of trust, away from the God they could not see and toward the nation they could. He gave them the king they asked for, and the king taxed them and conscripted their sons and led them into the very ruin they had been warned about. The desire to be like the nations is never merely political. It is always, underneath, a quiet abdication of the throne.

This is where I have to stop pointing and step into the indictment, because the line I have drawn runs through me. I have loved my country out of order. There have been seasons when I would have been more upset to hear my nation criticized than to hear my Lord ignored, and that ratio is the whole diagnosis. The thing you defend most fiercely is the thing you actually worship, whatever your mouth confesses on Sunday. I have watched myself grow hot at an insult to the flag and cool at an insult to the cross, and the temperature gauge does not lie. The law has to land here before any grace can. You cannot be forgiven for an idol you are still defending as devotion.

The cross does the actual work at exactly this point. Because the cross is what God does with disordered love. Christ does not come to scold us into reordering our affections by willpower. He comes to die, and in dying he exposes every false king for what it is, the nation that crucified him no less than the temple that handed him over. The empire put him on a Roman cross under a sign that named him a political threat, and he let it, and in letting it he broke the spell that says power saves. Caesar killed God and God rose anyway. After that morning no nation can credibly claim to be the thing that saves, because the strongest nation that ever lived already killed the one who saves and could not keep him dead. The resurrection is the permanent demotion of every empire.

So what do I tell my son now, when he asks again why we put our hands over our hearts. I tell him we love this place, and loving it is good, and he should love it too. Then I tell him that the same hand goes over the heart in two rooms, and the order of the two rooms is the whole of the Christian life. In one room we honor a country that can be wrong. In the other we worship a Lord who cannot. The day we forget which room is which, we will still be putting our hands over our hearts, and we will have no idea that the gesture has changed its god.

Love your country. Refuse to worship it. The difference is whether you can still tell it the truth.

### Works Cited

Augustine. Confessions. Circa 397.

Augustine. On Christian Doctrine. Circa 397.

Niebuhr, Reinhold. The Irony of American History. Scribner, 1952.

chapters.title: The Early Church Under Rome: Faith Without Power
chapters.summary: For three centuries the church grew with no army, no law, and no protection, and that is the period we should study hardest now.
chapters.body:
Pliny the Younger did not know what to do with them, so he wrote to the emperor. Around the year 112, governing a province in what is now Turkey, he sent Trajan a letter asking how to handle the Christians he kept having to execute. He had tried giving them three chances to curse Christ and worship the emperor's image. The stubborn ones he sent to die, not for any crime he could name, but for the obstinacy itself, the flat refusal to do the one small civic thing that would have saved them (Pliny, Letters 10.96). Read that letter and you meet the early church the way Rome met it, not as a comfortable majority but as a problem to be managed by a puzzled bureaucrat with the power to kill.

This is the church we forget. We picture the faith with cathedrals and councils and a bishop who could write to a king as an equal. But for almost three hundred years, from the cross to Constantine, the church had no army, no friendly law, no social standing worth defending, and no guarantee that confessing the name would not cost you your life. It was faith without power. And it grew. The hard question, the one I want to sit inside, is how, and the harder question is whether we have any idea how to do it again.

The text I will carry is a sentence written from inside the experience, not about it. We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed, perplexed, but not driven to despair, struck down, but not destroyed (2 Corinthians 4:8-9 ESV). Paul wrote that as a description of ordinary Christian life under Rome, not a slogan for a coffee mug. The grammar matters. Afflicted but. Perplexed but. Struck down but. The faith of the early church lived in that conjunction, in the gap between what the empire could do to the body and what it could not do to the hope. They were not winning. They were not crushed. Those are different claims, and we have spent a long time pretending the second requires the first.

Now steel-man the empire, because Rome was not a cartoon villain and the persecution was not always blind cruelty. Rome was, by the standards of the ancient world, tolerant of religion. It absorbed gods the way it absorbed provinces. What it could not absorb was a group that refused to absorb back, that would not add the emperor to its shelf of gods, that called the civic religion idolatry and then declined the small public sacrifice that signaled you were a safe member of society. From Rome's side this looked like sedition dressed as piety. Robert Louis Wilken makes the case fairly, that educated Romans like Celsus and later Porphyry saw Christians as a corrosive sect, antisocial, secretive, undermining the bonds that held a fragile civilization together (Wilken 1984). If you believed the gods kept the harvest coming and the borders firm, then a movement teaching people to insult the gods was not a private spiritual matter. It was a public danger. The persecutors, by their own lights, were defending the common good.

So answer that strong version. Yes, the refusal looked antisocial, and yes, the empire had reasons. But the thing Rome read as corrosion was the precise thing that made the church grow, and here the modern reader has to slow down. The Christians did not grow because they offered a better civic religion. They grew because they offered something the empire structurally could not, a community that treated a slave and a senator as the same kind of creature, that buried the poor with dignity, that took in the infants Rome exposed on the hillside to die, that nursed the sick during plagues when the healthy fled the cities. The sociologist Rodney Stark argued that the church grew through plagues precisely because Christians stayed and cared for the dying while pagan neighbors ran, and the simple math of who survived and who was loved did the rest (Stark 1996). The thing that looked antisocial to Rome was a different society, planted inside the old one, visible mostly in how it treated the people Rome threw away.

This is what faith without power can do that faith with power forgets. When you cannot compel, you can only attract. When you have no law to enforce your ethic, the ethic has to be lived in the open or it does not exist at all. Tertullian, writing around 197 to a hostile public, threw their own observation back at them. See how they love one another, he reported the pagans saying, and he meant it as the church's only argument, the visible care that the surrounding world could not produce and could not explain (Tertullian, Apology 39). The early church had no other apologetic that the empire could see. It had bodies that stayed when others fled, and tables where the wrong people ate together, and a refusal to expose its infants, and a stubborn insistence that the executed Galilean was Lord and the emperor was not.

Trace the cost honestly, with dates, because sentiment is cheap and martyrdom was not. The persecution under Nero after the fire of 64. The deaths under Marcus Aurelius, the philosopher-emperor, including the martyrs of Lyon in 177 whom Eusebius recorded in unbearable detail (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 5.1). The empire-wide persecution under Decius in 250, when every citizen had to produce a certificate proving they had sacrificed. The Great Persecution under Diocletian beginning in 303, the last and worst, scriptures burned and churches razed, a decade before everything reversed. For three centuries the church paid in blood to say four words it would not stop saying. The cross was not a symbol they wore. It was a sentence they expected.

Here is the reversal, and it cuts toward us. We assume the church needs power to do its work, that without a seat at the table and a friendly law and a place in the culture the faith will wither. The first three centuries say the opposite. The church did its clearest work, grew at its fastest rate, and produced its purest witness precisely when it had no power at all. The blood of the martyrs, Tertullian wrote, is the seed (Tertullian, Apology 50). It was the powerlessness that made the love legible. Once the church gained the empire, the love got harder to see, because now you could not tell who came for Christ and who came for Constantine.

There is a detail in the persecutions that we rush past, and it deserves a slow look. Rome rarely demanded that Christians stop believing. It demanded a gesture, a pinch of incense on the altar, a few words acknowledging the emperor, the certificate under Decius proving you had sacrificed. The empire did not care what you held in your heart. It cared whether you would perform the public act that signaled your final loyalty belonged to the state. The Christians died over the gesture, and to a Roman that looked insane, since the belief could be kept privately if only the body would bow publicly. But the early church understood what the empire was actually asking. It was asking for the one thing they had already given to Christ, the last word, the deepest allegiance, the place in the soul where only one Lord can sit. They would not perform the gesture because the gesture was the whole point. A faith that bows the body while reserving the heart has already lost the argument the martyrs refused to lose.

The cross is the whole logic of it, not a decoration on it. A movement founded on a man who refused to call down legions, who let the empire kill him and forgave it from the wood, cannot be surprised when it suffers, and cannot be saved by becoming the thing that killed its Lord. The early church understood that it was following a crucified King, so a cross of its own was not a failure of the plan. It was the plan. That is the piece we lost the moment the persecution stopped, and it is the piece we may be about to relearn whether we want to or not.

I think about my sons inheriting a country where the faith costs something again, where being a Christian is no longer the respectable default but a choice with a price. Part of me fears it. But the church I read about in those three centuries was not afraid in the way I am afraid. It had already lost the thing I am trying to protect, the safety, the standing, the law on its side, and it had found that the losing did not touch the only thing that mattered.

They had no power. They had a tomb that would not stay shut. It was enough to outlast Rome.

### Works Cited

Eusebius. The Ecclesiastical History. Translated by Kirsopp Lake. Loeb Classical Library. Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 1926.

Pliny the Younger. The Letters of the Younger Pliny. Translated by Betty Radice. London: Penguin, 1963.

Stark, Rodney. The Rise of Christianity: How the Obscure, Marginal Jesus Movement Became the Dominant Religious Force in the Western World. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1996.

Tertullian. Apology. In Ante-Nicene Fathers, Volume 3. Edited by Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson. Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing, 1885.

Wilken, Robert Louis. The Christians as the Romans Saw Them. New Haven: Yale University Press, 1984.

chapters.title: The Prosperity Gospel Is Not the Gospel
chapters.summary: The prosperity gospel is not a heresy because it promises too much. It is a heresy because it promises the wrong things, to the wrong people, for the wrong reasons, while calling the transaction 'faith.'
chapters.body:
The prosperity gospel did not emerge from nothing. It has a genealogy, and tracing it is essential for understanding why it persists, why it appeals, and why it is, at its theological core, a betrayal of the faith it claims to represent.

The roots reach into the New Thought movement of the nineteenth century — a metaphysical tradition that taught the power of mental states to shape physical reality. Phineas Quimby, Warren Felt Evans, and other New Thought practitioners developed a framework in which belief was understood as a causal force: what you think determines what you experience. This was not Christian theology. It was philosophical idealism dressed in spiritual language. But it would provide the conceptual scaffolding for everything that followed.

E.W. Kenyon, a Baptist minister and educator who operated in the early twentieth century, became the bridge between New Thought metaphysics and Pentecostal Christianity. Kenyon's writings — particularly "The Two Kinds of Knowledge" and "The Two Kinds of Faith" — introduced concepts that would become foundational to the prosperity gospel: the distinction between "sense knowledge" (empirical reality) and "revelation knowledge" (spiritual reality that supersedes the physical), the power of spoken words to create reality, and the idea that sickness and poverty were not merely unfortunate but were actively caused by deficient faith. Kenyon's intellectual debts to New Thought have been documented by scholars including D.R. McConnell, whose "A Different Gospel" traced the lineage with meticulous detail. Kenyon himself never fully acknowledged these debts. The movement that inherited his ideas has been even less forthcoming.

Kenneth Hagin Sr., widely regarded as the father of the Word of Faith movement, built on Kenyon's foundation — at times, scholars have noted, with passages that appear to be direct reproductions of Kenyon's prose. Hagin's Rhema Bible Training Center, founded in Tulsa, Oklahoma in 1974, became the institutional engine that mass-produced Word of Faith pastors and sent them into pulpits across the country. Hagin taught that God's will for every believer was health, wealth, and victory in every area of life, and that the mechanism for receiving these blessings was "positive confession" — the spoken declaration of what faith claims to be true, regardless of what circumstances appear to show.

The theology is internally consistent, which is part of its power. If words create reality, then speaking health produces health and speaking wealth produces wealth. If sickness and poverty are the result of inadequate faith, then the remedy is not medical treatment or economic analysis but more faith, better confession, deeper giving. The system is closed: every outcome confirms it. Prosperity proves the theology works. Suffering proves the sufferer needs more faith. There is no possible evidence that could falsify the framework from within.

The Major Figures

The prosperity gospel's institutional power has been built by a succession of charismatic figures whose personal wealth serves as the movement's primary evidence for its own validity.

Oral Roberts pioneered the "seed-faith" concept in the 1970s — the idea that a financial gift to a ministry functions as a seed that God will multiply back to the giver. Roberts was explicit about the transactional nature of this theology: give and you will receive, in direct proportion to your gift. His fundraising letters promised specific returns on spiritual investment and warned that failure to give would result in specific negative consequences. In 1987, Roberts told his television audience that God would "call him home" if he did not raise eight million dollars by a certain date. He raised the money. The theology was confirmed, at least to those already within the system.

Kenneth Copeland, perhaps the most visible of the second-generation prosperity teachers, expanded the framework into what can only be described as a theology of divine entitlement. Copeland teaches that believers are "little gods" with the same creative power as God himself, that Jesus was wealthy during his earthly ministry, and that financial prosperity is not merely available to the faithful but is their covenant right. Copeland's personal wealth — multiple private jets, a lakefront mansion in Newark, Texas, tax-exempt status for properties classified as parsonages — has been the subject of Senate inquiries and investigative journalism. His response to criticism has been consistent: the wealth is evidence that the theology works.

Creflo Dollar, whose very name seems calibrated for irony, built World Changers Church International in College Park, Georgia into a megachurch empire while teaching that financial blessing is the inevitable result of faithful giving. In 2015, Dollar solicited donations from his congregation to purchase a sixty-five-million-dollar Gulfstream G650 jet. The request was not presented as luxury. It was presented as ministry necessity and as an opportunity for congregants to participate in what God was doing. That the congregants were, by and large, less wealthy than the pastor soliciting their donations was a fact the theology was designed to obscure.

Joel Osteen occupies a more complex position. His Lakewood Church in Houston is the largest megachurch in America, and his books have sold tens of millions of copies. Osteen's prosperity theology is softer than Copeland's or Dollar's — less Word of Faith mechanics and more therapeutic optimism. He rarely discusses hell, sin, or suffering in any sustained way. His message is relentlessly positive: God wants you to live your best life. You are blessed. Good things are coming. The theological problem with Osteen is not that he is cruel. It is that he is incomplete. He preaches a gospel from which the cross has been functionally removed — a Christianity of aspiration without sacrifice, of blessing without cost, of resurrection without death. It is Christianity with the difficult parts redacted, and whatever remains after that redaction is not Christianity. It is something else.

T.D. Jakes requires more nuance. Jakes is a genuinely gifted preacher and a figure of enormous influence in the Black church. His theology contains prosperity elements, but it also contains a depth of pastoral engagement with suffering, a rootedness in the Black preaching tradition, and a theological seriousness that distinguishes him from the more nakedly transactional figures in the movement. Jakes is not Kenneth Copeland. But neither has he fully separated his theology from the prosperity framework, and his personal wealth — his mansion in Fort Worth, his media empire, his business ventures — raises questions that his genuine pastoral gifts do not fully answer. The most honest thing to say about Jakes is that he is a complicated figure in a movement that prefers simplicity, and that his best moments transcend the prosperity theology that his institutional success has been built on.

The Biblical Problems

The prosperity gospel's relationship with scripture is not exegesis. It is ventriloquism — putting words in the mouth of a text that says something fundamentally different from what the prosperity preachers claim.

The book of Job is the most comprehensive biblical refutation of prosperity theology in the canon, and it is remarkable how infrequently prosperity preachers engage with it. Job is a righteous man who suffers catastrophically — not because of sin, not because of insufficient faith, not because of inadequate giving, but because suffering in a fallen world does not operate on a moral calculus. The entire argument of Job's friends — that his suffering must be the result of hidden sin — is the argument of the prosperity gospel, and the book exists to demolish it. God's speech from the whirlwind in chapters 38-41 is not an explanation of Job's suffering. It is a refusal to provide one, on the grounds that the human demand for suffering to make sense is a demand that exceeds human capacity and misunderstands the nature of God's relationship to creation. The prosperity gospel is the theology of Job's friends, and the book of Job is God's response to it.

Paul's testimony is equally devastating to the prosperity framework. In 2 Corinthians 12, Paul describes his "thorn in the flesh" — a persistent affliction that he asked God three times to remove. God's response was not healing. It was "my grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness." This is the opposite of prosperity theology. God's power is not demonstrated through the removal of suffering but through its transformation. Paul's conclusion — "when I am weak, then I am strong" — is incomprehensible within the prosperity framework. If weakness is evidence of insufficient faith, then Paul was a man of insufficient faith. The absurdity of that conclusion reveals the absurdity of the framework.

Jesus himself is the most inconvenient figure for prosperity theology. He was born in a borrowed stable, lived an itinerant life without property, told his followers that foxes have holes and birds have nests but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head (Matthew 8:20), instructed a rich young ruler to sell everything and give it to the poor (Mark 10:21), and died naked on a Roman cross. The attempt to recast Jesus as wealthy — Copeland has argued that Jesus wore designer clothes and that the magi's gifts constituted significant wealth — requires a hermeneutical violence so extreme that it would be amusing if it were not so consequential. The Jesus of the Gospels is not the Jesus of the prosperity gospel. They are two different figures, and only one of them is in the Bible.

The early church's experience confirms the pattern. The apostles were imprisoned, beaten, shipwrecked, impoverished, and martyred. The book of Hebrews catalogs the suffering of the faithful in chapter 11 — people who were stoned, sawn in two, destitute, afflicted, wandering in deserts and caves — and calls them heroes of faith, not failures of faith. The suffering church in Smyrna, which Jesus addresses in Revelation 2:9, is told "I know your tribulation and your poverty" — and then, remarkably, "but you are rich." The richness Jesus identifies has nothing to do with their bank accounts. It has everything to do with their faithfulness under pressure.

Why It Works

The sociological appeal of the prosperity gospel is not mysterious, and dismissing it as mere gullibility is both inaccurate and condescending. The prosperity gospel thrives in communities experiencing economic deprivation, racial marginalization, and social instability — precisely the communities where the promise that God wants to bless you financially carries the most existential weight.

In the Black community, prosperity theology intersects with the legacy of economic exclusion — redlining, employment discrimination, the systematic destruction of Black wealth from Reconstruction through the twentieth century. When Creflo Dollar tells a congregation of Black working-class families that God wants them to be wealthy, he is speaking to people for whom wealth has been systematically denied by the same society that claims to be Christian. The appeal is not stupidity. It is hope operating in a context where other avenues of economic mobility have been blocked. This does not make the theology true. But it makes its appeal comprehensible and its exploitation unforgivable.

In the Global South, where the prosperity gospel has spread with extraordinary speed, the dynamic is similar. In Lagos, Sao Paulo, and Manila, prosperity churches draw millions of adherents from communities experiencing rapid urbanization, economic precarity, and the disorientation of traditional social structures. The prosperity gospel offers a framework that makes sense of their economic aspirations in spiritual terms and promises divine participation in their upward mobility. That the framework is theologically bankrupt does not diminish its psychological power. People believe it because they need it to be true, and the alternatives — a theology that takes suffering seriously, that does not promise escape from poverty, that locates God's faithfulness in presence rather than provision — are harder to preach and harder to hear.

The Damage

The prosperity gospel's damage is not theoretical. It is measured in dollars extracted from people who cannot afford to give them, in medical treatment refused because seeking a doctor was framed as a failure of faith, in the spiritual devastation of people who tithed faithfully, confessed positively, and remained poor — and concluded that the problem was their own insufficient belief.

The financial exploitation is systematic. Prosperity churches typically teach tithing as an absolute obligation — ten percent of gross income, given to the local church, as a minimum. On top of this, they solicit "seed-faith" offerings, building fund contributions, pastoral appreciation gifts, and special offerings tied to specific prophetic promises. The mechanism is consistent: give, and God will give back to you. The framing makes it nearly impossible for the giver to stop giving, because reducing their gift would be interpreted as reducing their faith, and reducing their faith would explain why the promised blessing has not arrived. The system is, in its economic structure, indistinguishable from a confidence scheme. The product being sold is hope. The currency is guilt. The profit accrues to the seller.

The spiritual abuse is no less real. When suffering is reframed as a faith problem, the sufferer is not merely in pain. They are guilty. The cancer patient who does not recover is told, implicitly or explicitly, that their faith was insufficient. The family that remains in poverty despite years of faithful giving is left to conclude that they are the problem. The theology that was supposed to liberate them from suffering has instead added a layer of spiritual shame to their material hardship. They are poor and it is their fault. They are sick and it is their fault. The God who was supposed to deliver them is instead, through the prosperity framework, indicting them.

This is not the gospel. This is the gospel's inversion. The actual gospel meets people in their suffering and says "I am with you." The prosperity gospel meets people in their suffering and says "what did you do wrong?"

The Distinction That Matters

The rejection of the prosperity gospel is not the rejection of generosity, material blessing, or the biblical principle that God provides. The Bible is full of texts that affirm God's provision, that celebrate material abundance, that connect generosity with flourishing. Malachi 3:10 — the prosperity gospel's favorite text — genuinely invites God's people to test divine faithfulness through giving. Proverbs associates wisdom with prosperity. The Psalms celebrate God as a provider. These texts are real and they matter.

The distinction is between a theology that acknowledges God's provision as a dimension of grace and a theology that demands God's provision as an obligation triggered by human behavior. The first is biblical. The second is magic dressed in Christian vocabulary. The first holds space for mystery — for the reality that God's faithful people sometimes suffer, sometimes lack, sometimes experience the silence of heaven in the face of desperate need. The second eliminates mystery entirely, replacing it with a formula: do this, get that. The first produces gratitude. The second produces entitlement.

Biblical generosity is given without expectation of return. Prosperity giving is investment, and the investor expects a dividend. The cheerful giver of 2 Corinthians 9:7 is not cheerful because they expect to get their money back multiplied. They are cheerful because giving is an act of trust in a God whose provision does not operate on a ledger.

The God of the Bible is not a vending machine. You do not insert faith and receive blessing. You receive grace — unmerited, unearned, often arriving in forms you did not request and would not have chosen — and you respond with gratitude and generosity, not because it will make you rich, but because it will make you free.

The prosperity gospel must be named for what it is: a theological system that exploits the vulnerable, distorts the scripture, contradicts the witness of Jesus, and reduces the God of the universe to a transaction partner. It is not the gospel. It is the gospel's replacement, and the replacement is not an upgrade. It is a diminishment so severe that what remains after the substitution is not Christianity at all, but a religion of acquisition that has borrowed Christian vocabulary to legitimize desires that Jesus explicitly warned against.

"You cannot serve both God and money," Jesus said in Matthew 6:24. He did not say it might be difficult. He said it was impossible. The prosperity gospel is the sustained institutional attempt to prove him wrong. Two thousand years of evidence suggest that it cannot.

The church's task is not merely to critique the prosperity gospel but to offer something better — a theology of God's faithfulness that does not flinch from suffering, that does not promise what God has not promised, that holds material provision and material lack within the same framework of grace, and that trusts the people in the pews with the full complexity of the biblical witness rather than offering them a simplification that will eventually, inevitably, fail them when they need it most.

That theology is harder to preach. It fills fewer arenas. It sells fewer books. It does not produce celebrity pastors with private jets. But it has the singular advantage of being true. And in the long run, truth is the only foundation that does not give way beneath the weight of real life, real suffering, and the real God who is present in both.

chapters.title: The Rise of the Nones
chapters.summary: They are the fastest-growing 'religious' group in America, and they are not what the church assumes. The 'nones' are not anti-God. They are anti-institution. Understanding the difference is the first step toward a faith that can speak to them.
chapters.body:
In 1972, when the General Social Survey first asked Americans about their religious affiliation, 5 percent chose "none." The category was so small that most researchers treated it as a rounding error, a residual population of eccentrics and contrarians who would always exist at the margins of an overwhelmingly religious nation. No serious social scientist predicted what would happen next.

By 1990, the figure had risen to 7 percent. By 2000, it was 14 percent. By 2012, Pew Research Center reported that 20 percent of American adults, and 34 percent of adults under thirty, claimed no religious affiliation. The 2023 data from the Public Religion Research Institute placed the overall figure at 27 percent. In raw numbers, that is approximately 70 million American adults, more than the membership of any single Christian denomination, more than the total number of evangelicals, more than the combined membership of every mainline Protestant body in the country.

The "nones," as they have come to be called, are now the largest single category in the American religious landscape, and they are reshaping the nation's politics, culture, and institutional life in ways that most religious leaders have yet to comprehend.

Who the Nones Are (And Who They Are Not)

The first and most important thing to understand about the nones is that the label describes what they are not, not what they are. "No religious affiliation" is a negative category. It tells you that a person does not identify with any organized religious tradition. It tells you almost nothing about what that person actually believes, practices, or values.

The category contains multitudes. It includes committed atheists who have concluded, on philosophical grounds, that no deity exists. It includes agnostics who regard the question of God's existence as unanswerable or unimportant. It includes people who believe in God but dislike organized religion. It includes people who consider themselves deeply spiritual but reject the label "religious." It includes people who were raised in religious households and left, and people who were raised in secular households and never joined. It includes people who attend religious services occasionally and people who have never set foot in a house of worship. Treating this population as a monolith is the analytical equivalent of treating "non-European" as a meaningful ethnic category.

The sociologist Ryan Burge, whose book The Nones (2021) provides the most comprehensive analysis of this population, breaks the category into three subgroups: atheists (approximately 4 percent of the total population), agnostics (approximately 5 percent), and "nothing in particular" (approximately 20 percent). This last group is by far the largest and the least understood. They are not philosophical materialists. They are not committed secularists. They are, in many cases, people who believe in something but have not found an institution that represents what they believe.

The Demographics

The nones are not evenly distributed across the American population. Their concentration varies dramatically by age, education, geography, and, to a lesser extent, race.

Age is the most powerful predictor. Among Americans over sixty-five, only about 15 percent are religiously unaffiliated. Among those between eighteen and twenty-nine, the figure exceeds 40 percent. This age gradient has led some observers to predict that disaffiliation is merely a phase, that young people will return to religion as they marry, have children, and face mortality. The data do not support this comforting hypothesis. Longitudinal studies tracking cohorts over time show that while some individuals do return to religious affiliation in middle age, the rate of return is far lower than in previous generations. The baby boomers who left the church in the 1960s and 1970s returned in significant numbers when they had children. Generation X returned at a lower rate. Millennials are showing almost no signs of returning. The pattern is not cyclical. It is directional.

Education correlates with disaffiliation, but not in the way popular stereotypes suggest. It is true that Americans with postgraduate degrees are more likely to be nones than those with only a high school education. But the fastest growth in disaffiliation is occurring among Americans without college degrees, a development that confounds the narrative of secularization as an elite phenomenon. The nones are not predominantly coastal intellectuals sipping lattes and reading Nietzsche. They are increasingly working-class Americans in the heartland who have simply stopped showing up.

Geographically, the nones are concentrated in the Pacific Northwest, the Northeast, and the Mountain West, but they are growing everywhere, including the South and the Midwest, regions historically considered the heartland of American religiosity. The "Bible Belt" is fraying at the edges, and the growth of disaffiliation in states like Texas, Georgia, and North Carolina is among the most significant demographic developments in contemporary American religion.

Racially, the nones remain disproportionately white, but this is changing rapidly. Disaffiliation among Hispanic Americans has accelerated sharply, with the percentage of Hispanic nones nearly doubling between 2010 and 2023. Black Americans remain the most religiously affiliated racial group in the United States, but even here, disaffiliation among young Black adults is rising. The Black church, long the most durable religious institution in American life, is not immune to the forces driving disaffiliation elsewhere.

What Nones Actually Believe

The assumption that nones are uniformly secular is flatly contradicted by the data. Pew Research Center's detailed surveys have found that among the "nothing in particular" subgroup, 72 percent believe in God or a higher power. Roughly half say they pray at least monthly. More than 30 percent say religion is at least "somewhat important" in their lives. A significant minority report having had mystical or spiritual experiences. These are not the profiles of committed materialists.

What the nones have rejected is not the sacred but the institutional mediation of the sacred. They have concluded that the organizations claiming to represent God do not, in fact, represent God, or at least do not represent God in a way they find credible. This is a judgment about institutions, not about transcendence. It is an ecclesiological crisis, not a theological one.

The distinction matters enormously. If the nones were atheists, the church's task would be apologetics: making the case for God's existence. But most nones do not need to be convinced that God exists. They need to be convinced that the church is a trustworthy community in which to explore what God's existence means. These are very different problems, and they require very different responses.

The sociologist Nancy Ammerman, in her landmark study Sacred Stories, Spiritual Tribes (2013), found that many religiously unaffiliated Americans maintain rich spiritual lives that include practices of gratitude, mindfulness, service to others, and engagement with nature. They have not abandoned the search for meaning. They have privatized it, concluding that spiritual life is best pursued individually or in small, informal communities rather than through the structures of organized religion.

Why "None" Means "None of the Above"

The label "none" is misleading because it sounds like "nothing," and many religious leaders have interpreted it precisely that way, as if 70 million Americans have simply opted for spiritual emptiness. This interpretation reveals more about the church's assumptions than about the nones' reality.

"None" does not mean "nothing." It means "none of the above." It is the response of a person who looks at the available options, Catholicism, mainline Protestantism, evangelicalism, Orthodoxy, and finds none of them adequate to describe their spiritual reality. It is a market failure, not a demand failure. The demand for meaning, community, and transcendence is as strong as ever. The supply, as currently constituted, is not meeting it.

This framing is important because it shifts the diagnostic question. The church has spent decades asking, "What is wrong with the nones?" The more productive question is, "What is wrong with the options?" When 27 percent of a population rejects every available religious brand, the problem is almost certainly with the brands, not with 70 million individuals who have all simultaneously become spiritually deficient.

The Sociological Factors

The rise of the nones is not a single-cause phenomenon. It is the product of multiple converging forces, each of which would be significant on its own and which together constitute a tidal shift in American religious life.

The first is institutional distrust. The nones are part of a broader pattern of declining confidence in institutions of all kinds: government, media, education, medicine, and religion. Gallup's annual confidence surveys show that trust in organized religion has fallen from 68 percent in 1975 to 32 percent in 2023, the lowest figure ever recorded. This decline tracks closely with the rise of the nones, and it suggests that disaffiliation is not primarily a theological phenomenon but a sociological one. People are not losing faith in God. They are losing faith in organizations.

The second is political polarization. As the previous article in this series discussed, the identification of Christianity, particularly white evangelicalism, with conservative Republican politics has driven millions of politically moderate and progressive Americans away from religious affiliation. The sociologists Michael Hout and Claude Fischer demonstrated in a groundbreaking 2002 paper that a significant portion of the growth in the "no religion" category was a direct reaction to the religious right. People who might otherwise have maintained a nominal religious affiliation actively rejected one because they did not want to be associated with the political positions the church had come to represent.

The third is individualism. American culture has always prized individual autonomy, but the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries have seen an intensification of individualism that makes institutional belonging of any kind feel constraining. Robert Putnam documented this in Bowling Alone (2000), showing that Americans were withdrawing from civic organizations of all types: unions, lodges, clubs, political parties, and churches. The decline of religious affiliation is part of a broader decline in associational life, driven by suburban sprawl, the internet, and a cultural ethic that privileges personal choice over communal obligation.

The fourth, and perhaps most underappreciated, factor is the failure of Christian public witness. James Davison Hunter, in his influential To Change the World (2010), argued that American Christianity had failed not because it was too engaged with the culture but because its engagement had taken the wrong form. Instead of embodying an alternative vision of human flourishing, the church had adopted the culture's own tools of power, politics, and coercion, and had thereby rendered itself indistinguishable from every other interest group competing for cultural dominance. Hunter's analysis is devastating because it comes from within the Christian tradition and because it identifies the church's own behavior, not secular hostility, as the primary driver of its declining influence.
