Hunter argued that the church's fixation on "changing the world" through political power and cultural warfare had obscured its actual vocation: faithful presence, the quiet, sustained work of being a community that embodies the values it proclaims. When the church spends more energy on political campaigns than on feeding the hungry, more resources on culture war than on community formation, more attention on winning arguments than on loving neighbors, it should not be surprised when thoughtful people conclude that it has nothing distinctive to offer.

What the Church Gets Wrong About Reaching Nones

The church's response to the rise of the nones has been, with some notable exceptions, a masterclass in misdiagnosis.

The most common strategy is attraction: make the church more appealing through better production values, more relevant programming, and a less "churchy" atmosphere. This approach assumes that the nones are essentially consumers who have been turned off by an unappealing product and can be won back with better packaging. The assumption is wrong. The nones are not looking for a better-produced church experience. Many of them have already had extensive church experience and found it wanting. Rebranding the same product does not address the underlying objections.

The second common strategy is apologetics: marshaling philosophical and scientific arguments for the existence of God, the reliability of the Bible, and the truth of Christian doctrine. This approach assumes that the nones are intellectually persuaded secularists who need to be argued back into faith. Again, the assumption is wrong. Most nones already believe in God or a higher power. Their objection is not to the existence of God but to the behavior of God's self-appointed representatives.

The third common strategy is guilt: lamenting the selfishness, shallowness, and spiritual laziness of a generation that has abandoned the faith. This approach assumes that the nones are morally deficient and need to be shamed into returning. This strategy is not only wrong but actively counterproductive. It confirms the nones' suspicion that the church is more interested in maintaining its institutional prerogatives than in genuinely caring for people.

What all three strategies share is a refusal to consider the possibility that the church itself bears significant responsibility for the exodus. They treat the nones as a problem to be solved rather than as a prophetic sign to be heeded. They assume that the institution is fundamentally sound and that the task is to convince people to return to it as it is. This assumption is precisely what the data contradict.

What Nones Actually Need

The research on what draws religiously unaffiliated people toward (or back toward) religious community reveals a set of needs that are deeply consonant with the church's historical vocation, if the church can find the honesty and courage to fulfill them.

The first is authenticity. The nones have finely tuned hypocrisy detectors, sharpened by the experience of institutions that said one thing and did another. They are not looking for perfection. They are looking for honesty: communities that acknowledge their failures, that do not pretend to have all the answers, that practice what they preach even when it is costly. The sociologist Brene Brown's research on vulnerability, though not specifically about religion, illuminates what the nones are seeking: communities where pretense is abandoned and genuine human connection is possible.

The second is intellectual honesty. The nones, particularly younger nones, have been shaped by an information environment that makes intellectual gatekeeping impossible. They have access to biblical scholarship, church history, and comparative religion that previous generations could only encounter in seminary. A church that insists on young-earth creationism, that pretends the Bible has no contradictions, that refuses to engage with legitimate historical and scientific questions, is a church that has disqualified itself in the eyes of anyone with an internet connection and a willingness to read. The nones do not need the church to abandon its convictions. They need the church to hold its convictions honestly, acknowledging complexity, engaging counterarguments, and trusting that truth does not need to be protected from scrutiny.

The third is justice. The nones are, as a group, strongly committed to racial justice, economic equality, LGBTQ inclusion, and environmental stewardship. They are not looking for a church that adopts progressive positions as a marketing strategy. They are looking for a community that takes the prophetic tradition seriously, that reads Amos and Isaiah and the Sermon on the Mount and actually does what they say. The Black church tradition, which has always understood faith and justice as inseparable, offers a model that the broader church has largely failed to learn from.

The fourth is space for doubt. The nones have been burned by communities that demanded certainty and punished questions. They are looking for a tradition robust enough to contain doubt, a faith that does not shatter when tested. The ancient practice of lament, the honest prayer of a person who does not understand what God is doing and refuses to pretend otherwise, is precisely the spiritual resource the nones need. But most churches have eliminated lament from their worship, replacing it with an unrelenting optimism that feels dishonest to anyone who has suffered.

The fifth, and perhaps most fundamental, is genuine community. Not the superficial friendliness of a church lobby, where strangers shake hands and exchange pleasantries before retreating to their separate lives. Not the programmatic community of small groups organized by demographic category and guided by packaged curricula. But the deep, costly, vulnerable community that the New Testament describes: a body in which every member is known and needed, in which burdens are shared and sorrows are borne together, in which the weak are not discarded and the strong are not idolized.

The rise of the nones is not, fundamentally, a story about the decline of faith. It is a story about the decline of institutions that have failed to embody what they claim to believe. The hunger for God, for meaning, for community, for justice, for transcendence has not diminished. What has diminished is the church's credibility as the place where those hungers can be fed.

This is not a counsel of despair. It is, if the church can hear it, a counsel of hope. The nones are not enemies of faith. They are, in many cases, seekers of faith who have been failed by the institutions that promised to nurture it. They have not stopped asking the deepest human questions: Why am I here? What is the meaning of suffering? How should I live? Is there something beyond this material existence that gives it all significance? They have merely stopped expecting the church to provide honest answers.

The path forward is not to develop better strategies for attracting the nones. It is to become the kind of community that does not need a strategy because its life together is its argument. A community that tells the truth. A community that does justice. A community that makes space for doubt and mystery. A community that worships a God who is not threatened by honest questions. A community that looks, in short, more like the one Jesus described and less like the ones we have built in his name.

The nones are watching. Some of them are waiting. Whether the church has the courage to become what it claims to be will determine whether they ever come through the door, not because they were marketed to, argued with, or guilted into returning, but because they saw something real and recognized it as the thing they had been looking for all along.

chapters.title: Two Kingdoms: How Christians Relate Faith and State
chapters.summary: The old teaching that there are two kingdoms has been used both to silence the church and to baptize the state, and it was meant to do neither.
chapters.body:
A man asked me once whether a Christian should care about politics, and behind his question were two opposite fears. He was afraid the church had become a wing of a political party, praying in the colors of a campaign. He was also afraid that if he answered no, he would be telling Christians to abandon the poor and the unborn and the prisoner to whatever the powerful decided. Both fears are right. That is what makes the question hard, and that is what the old language of two kingdoms was built to hold.

The phrase has a long history and a worse reputation than it deserves. Two kingdoms means roughly this, that God rules the world in two ways at once, through the church by the word and the cross, and through the civil order by law and the sword, and that these are not the same rule and must not be collapsed into each other. It is an old idea, and like every old idea it has been abused in both directions. Some have used it to tell the church to stay out of public life entirely, render your soul to God and everything else to Caesar. Others have used it to let the state do whatever it wants, since the sword is God's appointed instrument and who are we to judge it. Neither is what the teaching was for.

The text I will carry is the one everyone reaches for and few read whole. Let every person be subject to the governing authorities, for there is no authority except from God (Romans 13:1 ESV). That sentence has been used to bless tyrants for two thousand years. But Paul wrote it to a church in the capital of the empire that would, within a decade, light his own people on fire in Nero's gardens, and he wrote it not as a blank check but with a leash attached. The authority is a servant of God, Paul says, an instrument for good, a terror to bad conduct and not to good (Romans 13:3-4 ESV). The state is given a job. The text that commands submission is the same text that defines the job, and a job defined is a job that can be failed.

Steel-man the strongest version of the separation, because it is not cowardice, it is wisdom paid for in blood. The people who most want faith and state kept in distinct kingdoms are often the people who have read the most history. They know what happened when the church held the sword, the crusade and the inquisition and the religious wars that turned Europe into a charnel house in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. They know that a church with state power stops persuading and starts coercing, and that a gospel enforced at the point of a sword is no longer the gospel. They know that the state, when it claims divine sanction, becomes a god, and a god with an army is the most dangerous thing in the world. When such people insist on two kingdoms, they are guarding against the church's worst memory and the state's oldest temptation at the same time. They are not telling the church to be silent. They are telling it not to pick up the sword.

So answer that, and answer it from inside the tradition. Augustine wrote The City of God after Rome fell in 410, when pagans blamed the Christians for abandoning the gods who had kept the city safe. His answer was to describe two cities, one built on love of God and one on love of self, mingled together in history until the end, distinguishable not by their address but by their loves (Augustine, City of God 14:28). Augustine did not tell Christians to abandon the earthly city. He told them to use it, to seek its peace, to serve it, while never confusing it with home. That is the heart of a healthy two kingdoms. The Christian works for the good of the city without ever believing the city is the kingdom of God. You can love your country hard and still know it is not your King.

Here the cross does its work, and it works against both abuses at once. A church that grabs the state's sword forgets that its Lord refused the sword, that he told Peter to put it away, that he conquered by being conquered (Matthew 26:52 ESV). And a state that claims the church's authority forgets that the only throne the church recognizes is occupied by a man Rome executed. The cross is the line between the two kingdoms. It tells the church it does not rule by force, because its Lord did not. And it tells the state it does not rule by right of heaven, because heaven's chosen King is the one the state put to death. Stand at the cross and you cannot baptize the sword and you cannot silence the church. Both lies die there.

Trace the failure, because the doctrine has a graveyard. The worst chapter is German, and it is recent. In the 1930s a strand of Lutheran two kingdoms thinking had decayed into a tidy division of labor, the church handles the soul and the gospel, the state handles the body and the law, and the church has no business judging what the state does in its own sphere. That decayed doctrine helped a church stay quiet while a regime did what it did. Dietrich Bonhoeffer broke with it, and the Confessing Church declared at Barmen in 1934 that Jesus Christ, not the state, is the one Word of God we must obey, that there are no areas of life where we belong to another lord (Barth and the Barmen Declaration 1934). Two kingdoms had become two sealed rooms, and the sealing let evil rule one room unchallenged. That is what the doctrine becomes when you forget that both kingdoms answer to the same Lord.

Here is the reversal. People reach for two kingdoms to get the church out of politics, but the doctrine done right does the opposite. It does not free the state from judgment. It subjects the state to a higher court. If the governing authority is God's servant with a defined job, then the church is exactly the body that can say when the servant has betrayed the master. The separation of the kingdoms is not a wall that protects the state from the church's voice. It is the very thing that gives the church a place to stand outside the state, a vantage from which to tell Caesar he is not God. The church that has confused itself with the state has lost the ability to prophesy to it. Only the church that knows it is a different kingdom can speak the word the state needs most to hear and least wants to.

Consider how easily the misuse hides itself, because it always wears the costume of faithfulness. The church that captures the state believes it is serving God, since it is using power to do what it thinks God wants, and the church that goes silent before the state also believes it is serving God, since it is staying in its lane and rendering to Caesar what is his. Both errors quote scripture. Both feel like obedience from the inside. That is what makes the two kingdoms a discipline rather than a slogan, because it requires you to hold a tension that every instinct wants to release, the tension between honoring the office and judging the officeholder, between paying the tax and refusing the worship, between loving the city and never mistaking it for the kingdom. The moment you let the tension go in either direction, you have either a theocracy or a chaplaincy, and both have a long record of blessing things the cross condemns.

Which means the man who asked me whether a Christian should care about politics had the wrong shape in mind. The choice is not between a church that runs the state and a church that ignores it. It is between a church that serves the kingdom of God and therefore tells the truth to every earthly power, and a church that has sold its prophetic voice for a seat at the table, whichever table, whichever party. I have watched pastors trade the second kingdom for the first and call it courage. It was the opposite. They had so identified the gospel with a political program that they could no longer rebuke it, and a church that cannot rebuke the power it loves is a chaplain, not a prophet.

Serve the city. Pay the tax. Honor the office. And keep one foot planted in the other kingdom, the one with the crucified King, so that when the city asks you to bow to it as a god, you have somewhere to stand and the words to refuse.

Two kingdoms, one Lord. Forget the second clause and you have lost the point.

### Works Cited

Augustine. The City of God Against the Pagans. Translated by R.W. Dyson. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998.

The Barmen Declaration. 1934. In Karl Barth, The Church's Confession Under Hitler. Translated by Arthur C. Cochrane. Philadelphia: Westminster Press, 1962.

Bonhoeffer, Dietrich. Ethics. Edited by Clifford J. Green. Translated by Reinhard Krauss and others. Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2005.

O'Donovan, Oliver. The Desire of the Nations: Rediscovering the Roots of Political Theology. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1996.

chapters.title: What Christian Nationalism Is and What It Is Not
chapters.summary: The phrase has become a weapon thrown in both directions, and almost nobody using it has stopped to ask what it actually names.
chapters.body:
A man left my office last spring with his jaw set, certain I had insulted his grandfather. He had heard me use the phrase Christian nationalism in a sermon, and what he heard was an accusation against everyone who had ever stood for a flag with their hand over their heart, everyone who had wept at a military funeral, everyone who believed this country was given something by God worth keeping. His grandfather had landed at Normandy. He was not going to sit still while his pastor called that idolatry.

I did not call it idolatry. But I understood why he heard it that way, and the reason I understood is that the phrase has been ruined in both directions. To the man in my office it is a slur, a way for elites to sneer at ordinary patriotic faith. To the people who use it most loudly on the other side it is a catchall for everything they fear about conservative Christians, a word that means little more than people I disagree with who pray. Between those two distortions the actual thing the term was coined to describe has nearly disappeared. And the actual thing is real, and it is dangerous, and we cannot resist it until we can define it without slandering the man whose grandfather landed at Normandy.

So I want to do something slow. I want to say what Christian nationalism is not, at length and in good faith, before I say what it is. Because the first faith handed to me, after I came up out of atheism, was already fused with the flag. Nobody sat me down and taught me the fusion. It was in the air of the building, in the placement of the colors on the platform, in the assumption that to love Jesus and to love America were one undivided loyalty. I did not question it for years. I am not standing outside this. I am standing inside it, writing toward myself.

Let me make the strongest case for the man who fears the phrase, because that case has real weight. He says that loving your country is not a sin. He is right. Scripture does not command us to despise the place we were born or the people we live among. Jeremiah told the exiles to seek the welfare of the city where God had sent them, to build houses and plant gardens and pray for Babylon, because in its welfare they would find their own (Jeremiah 29:7 ESV). That is a kind of patriotism, a settled care for a particular place and its people. The man who fears the phrase says that gratitude for a country, its laws, its soldiers, its harvests, is a form of honoring the gifts of God, and he is right about that too. He says that the people who throw the phrase at him have often never set foot in his church, do not know that his congregation feeds the hungry and buries the poor and visits the prisoner, and use Christian nationalism as a way to dismiss faithful people without listening to them. He is frequently right about that, and the carelessness of his accusers is its own sin. I will not defend it.

Here is what he gets right that I most want to honor. He senses that the people warning about Christian nationalism are often selectively alarmed, that they fear religion in public only when it is the wrong religion, that a faith driven entirely out of public life is not neutrality but a different establishment wearing the mask of neutrality. Lesslie Newbigin spent forty years as a missionary in India and came home to a Western culture that imagined itself secular and neutral, and he saw through it (Newbigin 1989). There is no neutral public square. The question is never whether faith shapes public life but which faith and how. The man who fears the phrase has felt this in his bones, and he is not wrong to resent being told that only his convictions must be left at the door.

Now I will answer the strongest version of his case, not the weak one. Because everything he has said so far describes patriotism, and patriotism is not what the phrase names. The scholars who coined the term in its careful sociological sense were not describing love of country. Andrew Whitehead and Samuel Perry, in their 2020 study Taking America Back for God, drew on years of survey data to define Christian nationalism as a cultural framework, a set of beliefs that fuses American civic identity with a particular Christian identity, that holds the nation has a covenant with God, that its laws should privilege that faith, and that its decline is a story of fall from a Christian founding that must be reclaimed (Whitehead and Perry 2020). The key word is fuses. Patriotism loves a country. Christian nationalism marries the country to God and then refuses to let anyone file for divorce.

The distinction is not mine. Reinhold Niebuhr saw it, watching the Cold War sanctify American power. The love of country, he wrote, is a high form of natural devotion, but it becomes demonic the moment it claims the unconditioned loyalty that belongs to God alone (Niebuhr 1952). That is the line. Patriotism is a love with limits, a love that can be criticized, corrected, repented. Nationalism is a love that has become ultimate, that cannot be questioned, because to question the nation has become the same as questioning God. The grandfather who landed at Normandy was a patriot. The grandfather who came home and believed America could do no wrong because God was on its side had crossed over, and most of us cross over without noticing the line at our feet.

Robert Bellah gave us the older name for the milder version of this in 1967. He called it civil religion, the set of shared beliefs and rituals through which a nation understands itself in relation to the transcendent, the appeals to God in inaugural addresses, the sacred status of founding documents, the liturgy of national holidays (Bellah 1967). Bellah did not think civil religion was simply evil. He thought it could call a nation to judgment as easily as it could flatter it, that Lincoln at Gettysburg used it to indict the country he led. But civil religion is a loaded instrument. It can humble a nation before a God who stands above it, or it can hand the nation a God who exists to bless it. Christian nationalism is what civil religion becomes when the second wins.

So here is the distinction at its sharpest. Not the love of country. The worship of it. Patriotism can stand under judgment. Nationalism cannot, because it has made the nation the thing that judges. The test is not whether you sing the anthem or honor the dead or feel your throat tighten at the sight of the colors. I do all of that. The test is what happens when your country and your Christ command different things. The patriot grieves and obeys Christ. The nationalist has arranged his theology so the conflict can never arise, because he has quietly decided his country and his Christ want the same thing, always, by definition.

The history of how we got here is specific, and the specifics matter, because the man in my office is right that the phrase is often thrown without history. Mark Noll, the finest historian of American evangelicalism, has shown that the colonists did not arrive with a unified Christian nation in mind, that the founders were a theological mixture from devout Calvinists to skeptical deists, that the Constitution names no God and establishes no church on purpose (Noll 2002). The story of a Christian founding lost and needing reclaiming is itself a later construction, built in the nineteenth century and rebuilt in the twentieth. George Marsden has traced how fundamentalism in the 1920s came to see itself as the last defender of a Christian civilization under siege, how the loss at the Scopes trial in 1925 drove that conviction underground where it hardened (Marsden 2006). The sense of a stolen country is not ancient. It is roughly a hundred years old, and it was manufactured.

The figures matter because the dates do. The phrase one nation under God was not in the Pledge of Allegiance when the Pledge was written in 1892. Congress inserted it in 1954, at the height of the Cold War, to mark the difference between a godly America and a godless Soviet enemy. In God we trust became the official national motto in 1956, displacing the older and more modest e pluribus unum. These were not the recovery of a Christian founding. They were the manufacture of one, in living memory, under the pressure of a particular fear. The covenant so many believers now assume to be ancient was legislated within the lifetime of people still in my pews. A covenant you can date to an act of Congress is not a covenant with God. It is a national mood that learned to talk like one.

Kristin Kobes Du Mez carried the story forward in 2020, and she did it carefully, with the sources in front of her. She showed how across the twentieth century a particular vision of Christian manhood, rugged, militant, protective, took on the features of John Wayne, and how the defense of the nation and the defense of that manhood became a single project in much of white evangelicalism (Du Mez 2020). I know some readers will distrust her because of where her conclusions land. Read the footnotes anyway. The pattern she documents is not invented. It is the air I breathed in the first church that taught me to follow Jesus, and I did not know the air had a history until someone showed me.

The sociology of the present moment is more precise than either side's slogans. Whitehead and Perry did not simply assert that Christian nationalism exists. They measured it, sorting Americans along a spectrum from those who reject the fusion entirely to those who embrace it fully, and they found that where a person falls on that spectrum predicts a startling range of other things, attitudes toward immigrants, toward gun control, toward who counts as a real American, with more force than denomination or even church attendance (Whitehead and Perry 2020). That last finding is the one that should stop a believer cold. The strongest expressions of Christian nationalism are often found among people who do not attend church much at all. It is less a deep faith than an identity, a way of marking the boundary of the nation with the language of religion. Which means it can flourish in a heart that has very little of Christ in it, because it was never really about Christ. It was about the nation, dressed in his name.

Now carry the one text that should govern all of this. When Jesus stood before Pilate, the man who held Rome's power in that province, he said something that should have ended Christian nationalism before it was born. My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting (John 18:36 ESV). The kingdom Jesus announced does not arrive by capturing a nation. It does not advance by seizing the levers of the state. The moment a movement believes the gospel needs a country to enforce it, the moment it believes Christ requires Caesar's sword to finish his work, it has confessed that it does not believe what Jesus told Pilate. And that confession is the engine room of Christian nationalism. It does not trust the kingdom that is not of this world, so it builds a kingdom that is.

This is where the law does its work before grace can speak. The man who fears the phrase wanted me to absolve patriotic faith, and I can absolve patriotism. But I cannot absolve the deeper thing, because the deeper thing is in me. I have wanted my country to be the kingdom. I have wanted to win by the means Jesus refused. I have stood at the line Niebuhr drew and stepped across it, loving my nation with a loyalty that left no room for the nation to be wrong. That is not the grandfather's sin alone. It is mine, and naming it as sin is the only door to the grace that can heal it. You cannot repent of a thing you are still calling virtue.

Stanley Hauerwas spent a career insisting that the first task of the church is to be the church, not to run the country, that the church is itself a polity, a people gathered around a crucified Lord whose only weapon is the truth (Hauerwas 1991). When the church forgets this, it does not lose its faith all at once. It trades it slowly, a little theology for a little power, until the cross has become a flagpole and nobody remembers the exchange.

The deepest theological objection to Christian nationalism is not that it loves the wrong country. It is that it tells the wrong story about how God saves. The fusion always carries a quiet account of salvation along with it, an account in which the nation is the vehicle of God's purpose in history, its founding a kind of new covenant, its decline a fall, its restoration a redemption that faithful citizens are called to bring about by reclaiming what was lost. That is a complete account of sin and salvation, and Jesus is not at the center of it. The nation is. Mark Noll, surveying how American Christians have read their own history, warned against exactly this habit of reading providence directly off the events of national life, of assuming that we can know that God favored this army or blessed that founding, when Scripture is far more reticent about such certainties than we are (Noll 2002). The God who works through nations does not thereby endorse them. He used Assyria as a rod and then broke the rod. A nation can be an instrument in God's hand and still stand under his judgment, and the believer who cannot hold both has confused the instrument with the hand. Augustine saw the same trade sixteen centuries earlier, watching Rome fall and watching Christians panic as though the city of God could fall with it. Two cities, he said, built by two loves, the earthly city by the love of self reaching the contempt of God, the city of God by the love of God reaching the contempt of self (Augustine 426). Every generation is asked which city it serves. We answer not with our slogans but with what we will do for power.

There is a further danger that the man in my office did not see, and it cuts toward him rather than away from him. Christian nationalism does not finally serve the nation either. It corrupts both halves of what it fuses. It gives the believer a faith too small to judge his country and gives the country a god too tame to correct it, and the result is a Christianity that cannot speak prophetically to power because it has married power, and a patriotism that cannot be honest about its own history because honesty has become blasphemy. Newbigin saw that a gospel which simply blesses a culture has lost the very thing that makes it gospel, its capacity to call that culture to repentance (Newbigin 1989). A faith that can only affirm the nation has nothing left to say to it. It has become the chaplaincy of the status quo, and the status quo has never once been saved by its chaplains.

So what is Christian nationalism. It is not loving your country. It is not gratitude for a soldier's sacrifice or a settled care for the welfare of your city. It is the fusion of the nation and the faith into one loyalty that cannot be questioned, the belief that God has a covenant with this particular country that requires its laws to privilege this particular faith, and the conviction that the kingdom of Christ can be advanced by the capture of the state. It is patriotism that has stopped being able to repent.

The man left my office certain I had insulted his grandfather. I had not. I had described a fork in the road that his grandfather and mine both stood at, the same fork I stand at every time I am tempted to want the country more than the cross. The phrase is not a slur against patriotic faith. It is the name for what patriotic faith becomes the moment it forgets the kingdom is not of this world. Most of us forgot. I forgot. The question is whether we will remember before the flag finishes covering the cross.

### Works Cited
