Bellah, Robert N. Civil Religion in America. Daedalus, 1967.

Du Mez, Kristin Kobes. Jesus and John Wayne: How White Evangelicals Corrupted a Faith and Fractured a Nation. Liveright, 2020.

Hauerwas, Stanley. After Christendom. Abingdon Press, 1991.

Marsden, George M. Fundamentalism and American Culture. Oxford University Press, 2006.

Newbigin, Lesslie. The Gospel in a Pluralist Society. Eerdmans, 1989.

Niebuhr, Reinhold. The Irony of American History. Scribner, 1952.

Noll, Mark A. America's God: From Jonathan Edwards to Abraham Lincoln. Oxford University Press, 2002.

Whitehead, Andrew L., and Samuel L. Perry. Taking America Back for God: Christian Nationalism in the United States. Oxford University Press, 2020.

chapters.title: What Render Unto Caesar Actually Means
chapters.summary: The verse most often quoted to keep faith private was spoken to trap a man, and it does the opposite of what we have made it do.
chapters.body:
They brought him a coin because they wanted him dead. That is the first thing we lose when we quote the line. The Pharisees and the Herodians, two groups who agreed on almost nothing, agreed to set a trap, and the trap was a single question about a denarius (Mark 12:13-17 ESV). Pay tax to Caesar, or not. Say yes and lose the crowd that hated Rome. Say no and hand the governor a charge of sedition. There was no safe answer. That is the point of a trap.

We have turned the most dangerous sentence in the Gospels into a permission slip. Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's, and we hear two tidy drawers. One for politics, one for prayer. One for the public square, one for the private heart. We hear a man drawing a property line between religion and state, and we are relieved, because a property line is exactly what a comfortable faith wants. I have preached this line as if Jesus came to teach us how to keep our heads down. I was wrong, and the text knew it before I did.

Look at what he actually does. He asks for the coin. He does not carry one. He asks whose image is on it, and they say Caesar's, and the Greek word for image is eikon, the same word the Greek Old Testament uses in Genesis when the man is made in the image of God (Genesis 1:27 ESV). The coin bears Caesar's image, so give it back to him. Fine. But the question hanging in the air, the one the trappers do not see coming, is what bears the image of God. The answer is the person holding the coin. The answer is the person who asked the question. Render to God the things that are God's, and the thing that is God's is you.

Now the steel man, because the comfortable reading is not stupid. The two-drawer interpretation has carried real weight for centuries, and it has protected real things. It kept the church from becoming the state and the state from becoming the church. After the wars of religion in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, a continent soaked in blood over confession, the instinct to separate the spheres looked like mercy. William Cavanaugh has shown how the modern story of secular peace got told, the state presenting itself as the cool referee that ended religious violence (Cavanaugh 2009). There is something the two-drawer reading sees clearly. Caesar has a domain. Taxes are real. The coin goes back. Jesus does not lead a tax revolt, and a faith that treats every government as Pharaoh has misread its own scripture, which tells us to honor the emperor in the same breath that it tells us to fear God (1 Peter 2:17 ESV).

So answer the strong version, not the weak one. Yes, Caesar has a domain. The question is its size. The two-drawer reading assumes the two drawers are roughly equal, God over here with the soul and Caesar over there with the body and the budget and the army and the schools. But that is not what the sentence says when you weigh it. If everything that bears God's image belongs to God, and the human person bears God's image, then Caesar's drawer holds metal stamped with his face, and God's drawer holds every person who ever lived, including Caesar. The line does not divide reality in half. It puts a fence around a coin and gives everything else to God. Tertullian saw this plainly. Render the coin to Caesar and yourself to God, he wrote, for if all things are Caesar's, what will be left for God (Tertullian, On Idolatry 15). The trap was meant to make Jesus choose between Rome and the crowd. He chose neither. He relativized Caesar by naming the One whose image Caesar himself bears.

This is why they killed him anyway. The render line did not get Jesus off the hook. Read forward a few chapters and the charge at the cross is exactly the one the trap was designed to produce, that he forbade tribute to Caesar and made himself a king (Luke 23:2 ESV). Rome was not fooled by a clever answer. Rome understood, better than the modern reader does, that a man who tells you the emperor is made in the image of a higher King has not stayed out of politics. He has just refused to grant the emperor the one thing the emperor most demands, which is the last word. The cross is the receipt. It is what the world charges a man who renders to God the things that are God's when Caesar wanted them for himself.

N.T. Wright has argued for years that the confession Jesus is Lord was never a private devotional sentiment, because in the first century everyone knew the rest of the sentence, Caesar is not (Wright 2000). The early Christians were not killed for believing in life after death. The empire did not care what you thought happened to your soul. They were killed because they would not say the four words that kept the machine running, kurios kaisar, Caesar is lord, and they would not say them because they had already given that title to a crucified Galilean. The render line is the seed of that refusal, not the escape from it.

We inherited the comfortable reading for a reason. Robert Louis Wilken describes how the Romans saw the Christians, not as private mystics but as a stubborn, antisocial sect that withheld the small public gesture that held society together (Wilken 1984). The render line became a comfort to us only after we won, only after Christians sat in the seat of Caesar and needed a verse that let them keep both drawers. A church with no power reads the line as a sword. A church with power reads it as a truce. We have been reading it as a truce for sixteen centuries, and that is precisely the period in which we forgot what it cost.

Here is the reversal. We quote this line to keep faith out of public life, when Jesus spoke it to keep Caesar out of the human soul. The verse we use to make God small was spoken to make Caesar small. The boundary it draws does not run between the sacred and the secular, with God minding the chapel and Rome minding the world. It runs around the coin, and the coin is the only thing on the small side. Everything else, your money included once you remember whose image is on the one who spends it, sits on the side that belongs to God.

Consider how the trap was built, because the construction tells you what the answer had to undo. The Pharisees objected to the tax on religious grounds, since the denarius bore Caesar's image and an inscription naming him divine, the son of the divine Augustus, which to a faithful Jew was a small idol carried in the pocket. The Herodians collaborated with Rome and benefited from the arrangement. To put those two groups in the same delegation, sent with the same question, was to assemble every faction that wanted Jesus gone and let them think they had finally cornered him. He did not slip the corner with a clever evasion. He named the deeper thing the coin only pointed at, the image stamped on the human creature, and in naming it he turned the trap into a verdict on the people who set it. They marveled, the text says, and then they left, because there was nothing left to do with an answer like that except plot the next one.

There is a reason the early church did not read this line the way we do. They read it surrounded by the consequences of confessing a Lord above Caesar, and a sentence reads differently when you might die for what it implies. We read it surrounded by safety, and safety makes the dangerous sound domestic. The same words that sounded like a sword in 64 sound like a settlement in our hands, and the difference is not in the words. The difference is in who is reading them and what it costs the reader to mean them. We turned a subversion into a slogan because we no longer stand where the slogan would get us killed.

So the question the trap was meant to spring on Jesus springs instead on us. Not whether you will pay your taxes. You will, and you should, and the kingdom does not rise or fall on a denarius. The question is what you have quietly handed to Caesar that was never his. Your final allegiance. Your sense of who holds history. The part of you that votes its fear instead of its faith and calls it prudence. We sorted ourselves into Caesar's drawer and told ourselves we were being responsible.

Give the coin back. Keep nothing of yourself in his hand. The image you bear was never minted in Rome.

### Works Cited

Cavanaugh, William T. The Myth of Religious Violence: Secular Ideology and the Roots of Modern Conflict. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2009.

Tertullian. On Idolatry. In Ante-Nicene Fathers, Volume 3. Edited by Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson. Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing, 1885.

Wilken, Robert Louis. The Christians as the Romans Saw Them. New Haven: Yale University Press, 1984.

Wright, N.T. Paul's Gospel and Caesar's Empire. In Paul and Politics: Ekklesia, Israel, Imperium, Interpretation. Edited by Richard A. Horsley. Harrisburg: Trinity Press International, 2000. See also Wright, Paul and the Faithfulness of God. In Christian Origins and the Question of God, Volume 4. Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2013.

chapters.title: When Politics Replaced Theology
chapters.summary: The Religious Right did not emerge from a moral awakening. It was constructed — deliberately, strategically, and for reasons that had far more to do with racial segregation than with abortion. Understanding that origin story changes everything about how we evaluate the church's entanglement with partisan power.
chapters.body:
In 1965, Jerry Falwell preached a sermon titled "Ministers and Marches" in which he denounced clergy involvement in the civil rights movement. "Preachers are not called to be politicians but to be soul winners," he declared. The church's business was saving souls, not reforming society. Government was Caesar's domain. The pulpit had no business meddling in it.

Fourteen years later, the same Jerry Falwell founded the Moral Majority, one of the most consequential political organizations in modern American history. The man who had insisted that ministers should stay out of politics became the most politically visible minister in the country. This reversal was not hypocrisy in the simple sense. It was something more instructive: it was a theological capitulation so complete that the man who made it did not appear to notice he had made it. The question of when and why American evangelicalism abandoned its apolitical posture for partisan activism is not merely a question about politics. It is a question about what happens when a church trades its prophetic authority for political access — and discovers too late that the exchange is irreversible.

The Fundamentalist Withdrawal

To understand the Religious Right, one must first understand what preceded it: a half-century of deliberate disengagement. The fundamentalist-modernist controversy of the 1920s — dramatized most vividly in the 1925 Scopes trial — left conservative Protestantism humiliated and culturally marginalized. William Jennings Bryan won the legal battle in Dayton, Tennessee, but the cultural verdict was devastating. H.L. Mencken's savage reporting painted fundamentalists as ignorant rubes, and the image stuck. For the next four decades, the movement that would eventually become the Religious Right retreated from public life almost entirely.

This withdrawal was not merely strategic. It was theological. Dispensational premillennialism — the dominant eschatological framework among fundamentalists — taught that the world was in irreversible decline, hurtling toward the tribulation and the return of Christ. If the world was a sinking ship, there was no point rearranging the deck chairs. The task of the church was rescue, not renovation. Pull as many souls as possible from the wreckage before the end came. Political engagement was, at best, a distraction from this mission and, at worst, a sign that one had placed too much hope in human systems.

This theology produced a paradox. While mainline Protestants were marching at Selma and lobbying for the Civil Rights Act, fundamentalists and most evangelicals were conspicuously absent. Not because they supported segregation in every case — though many did — but because they had constructed a theological framework that rendered political engagement illegitimate. The irony is brutal: the same theological tradition that would later become the most politically mobilized religious movement in American history spent the mid-twentieth century insisting that politics was none of the church's business.

The Real Catalyst: Not Roe, but Race

The conventional story of the Religious Right's origin is simple and widely believed: the Supreme Court legalized abortion in Roe v. Wade (1973), conservative Christians were outraged, and they mobilized politically to fight back. This narrative is almost entirely false. It is a founding myth — retrospectively constructed, carefully maintained, and historically indefensible.

The historian Randall Balmer has documented this with meticulous care. In his research, including interviews with key figures like Paul Weyrich, the conservative activist who coined the term "Moral Majority," Balmer demonstrates that the actual catalyst for evangelical political mobilization was not abortion but racial segregation — specifically, the IRS's decision in 1971 to revoke the tax-exempt status of racially discriminatory private schools, and its application of that ruling to Bob Jones University in 1976.

Bob Jones University, in Greenville, South Carolina, had prohibited interracial dating and marriage among its students. When the IRS revoked its tax exemption on the grounds that racial discrimination disqualified an institution from charitable status, the evangelical world erupted — not in defense of segregation per se, but in defense of what they framed as religious liberty and institutional autonomy. The government, they argued, had no right to tell a Christian institution how to operate. The issue was not race. The issue was government overreach.

Paul Weyrich himself confirmed this sequence in multiple interviews. "I was trying to get those people interested in those issues and I utterly failed," Weyrich told Balmer, referring to his attempts to mobilize evangelicals around abortion, pornography, school prayer, and the Equal Rights Amendment in the mid-1970s. "What changed their mind was Jimmy Carter's intervention against the Christian schools, trying to deny them tax-exempt status on the basis of so-called de facto segregation." It was the tax-exemption issue, not Roe v. Wade, that provided the political energy for the movement.

Abortion was retrofitted as the movement's central cause only after the fact. It served as a more morally compelling rallying cry than the defense of racially segregated schools — for obvious reasons. But the timeline does not lie. The Southern Baptist Convention, the largest Protestant denomination in the country, passed a resolution in 1971 calling for legislation that would allow abortion in cases of rape, incest, fetal deformity, and "carefully ascertained evidence of the likelihood of damage to the emotional, mental, and physical health of the mother." W.A. Criswell, the pastor of First Baptist Dallas and one of the most prominent conservative Southern Baptist leaders, told reporters after Roe v. Wade, "I have always felt that it was only after a child was born and had a life separate from its mother that it became an individual person." These were not fringe voices. They were the establishment.

The rewriting of this history matters enormously. If the Religious Right was born from a righteous response to the murder of the unborn, then its political engagement has a moral foundation that transcends partisanship. If it was born from the defense of racial segregation and then retroactively re-narrated around abortion, then its moral authority rests on a fabrication. The historical evidence overwhelmingly supports the latter reading.

The Architects of the Movement

The Religious Right did not emerge spontaneously from the grassroots. It was constructed by a small group of political operatives and religious leaders who recognized the electoral potential of mobilizing white evangelicals as a voting bloc. The key figures are worth naming, because their strategic decisions shaped the movement's DNA.

Paul Weyrich was a Catholic conservative activist who had co-founded the Heritage Foundation in 1973. He understood, before most Republican strategists did, that white evangelicals represented an enormous untapped political resource — tens of millions of voters who had largely stayed home on Election Day. Weyrich provided the political infrastructure: the organizational models, the fundraising networks, the direct-mail strategies that would transform diffuse religious sentiment into coordinated political action.

Jerry Falwell provided the pastoral face. A Baptist minister from Lynchburg, Virginia, Falwell had built Thomas Road Baptist Church into a megachurch and launched a television ministry that reached millions. His founding of the Moral Majority in 1979 gave the movement institutional form. Falwell's genius was translating political positions into the language of moral absolutes. Opposition to abortion was not a policy preference; it was a stand against murder. Opposition to gay rights was not bigotry; it was faithfulness to Scripture. Support for a strong military was not geopolitics; it was obedience to Romans 13. Every political position was baptized in theological language, making disagreement feel like apostasy.

Pat Robertson extended the movement's reach through the 700 Club and his 1988 presidential campaign. Robertson's candidacy was ultimately unsuccessful, but it demonstrated that evangelical voters could be mobilized for electoral politics at the highest level. More significantly, Robertson's Christian Coalition, founded in 1989 under the direction of Ralph Reed, shifted strategy from national spectacle to local organizing. The Coalition trained activists to run for school boards, city councils, and state legislatures — building power from the bottom up with a sophistication that most observers did not recognize until it was too late.

James Dobson, through Focus on the Family, shaped the movement's domestic policy agenda. Dobson's influence was more cultural than directly political, but his radio program reached an estimated 220 million listeners worldwide, and his endorsement could make or break a Republican primary candidate. Dobson's framework was straightforward: the traditional nuclear family was under siege from feminism, homosexuality, and secular humanism, and the church's political task was to defend the family through legislation, judicial appointments, and cultural combat.

The Single-Issue Reduction

The most theologically damaging consequence of the Religious Right was not its political engagement per se. Christians have every right — and, arguably, every obligation — to participate in democratic governance. The damage was in the reduction of a complex, multi-dimensional ethical tradition to a handful of partisan litmus tests.

The Hebrew prophets spoke about economic justice, care for the stranger, the abuse of power, the corruption of courts, the exploitation of workers, the neglect of the poor. Jesus's teaching encompassed peacemaking, enemy love, radical generosity, the dangers of wealth, the inclusion of the marginalized, and the subversion of every human hierarchy. The Apostle Paul wrote about reconciliation across ethnic and social boundaries, the mutual submission of all believers, and the fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control. The Christian ethical tradition is extraordinarily broad.

The Religious Right compressed this tradition into a short list: abortion, homosexuality, school prayer, and support for Israel. A politician could endorse torture, slash programs for the poor, demonize immigrants, and promote economic policies that concentrated wealth among the already wealthy — and still be considered the "Christian" candidate, provided they opposed abortion and same-sex marriage. A politician who fed the hungry, welcomed the stranger, advocated for peace, and worked to reduce inequality was the "secular" candidate if they were pro-choice.

This was not merely a strategic narrowing. It was a theological distortion of the first order. It taught an entire generation of Christians that faithfulness could be measured by a voter guide. It reduced the prophetic tradition to a checklist. And it made the church's moral witness contingent on partisan outcomes — which meant that when the party failed morally, the church that had yoked itself to the party failed with it.

The Cost: Prophetic Voice Traded for Political Access

The transaction at the heart of the Religious Right was simple: the church gave the Republican Party its moral credibility, its voter mobilization infrastructure, and its cultural legitimacy. In return, the church received access — meetings with presidents, invitations to the White House, judicial nominations, and the rhetorical deference of politicians who needed evangelical votes. The question is whether the church got the better end of the deal.

The evidence suggests it did not. After four decades of political engagement, the Religious Right had achieved remarkably little of its stated agenda. Abortion remained legal until the Dobbs decision in 2022, and even that victory has proven more politically complicated than the movement anticipated. School prayer was not restored. The culture moved decisively in favor of LGBTQ rights. The divorce rate among evangelicals remained virtually identical to the national average. The pornography industry grew exponentially. By the movement's own metrics, it lost the culture war.

What it gained instead was power — but power of a specific and corrosive kind. Evangelical leaders gained proximity to political authority. They sat in the Oval Office. They advised presidents. They were consulted on judicial nominees. But this access came at a price that many did not recognize until it was too late: the church's ability to speak prophetically to power was compromised by its dependence on that power. A prophet who needs the king's favor is no prophet at all.

The Trump era exposed this dynamic with brutal clarity. When evangelical leaders embraced a thrice-married casino owner who bragged about sexual assault, paid hush money to a porn star, mocked prisoners of war, and separated children from their parents at the border, the theological emptiness of the movement's political theology was laid bare. The question was no longer whether the church could influence politics. The question was whether politics had consumed the church. For millions of Americans — particularly younger Americans, Black Americans, and those who had experienced the church's judgment firsthand — the answer was obvious.

The Theological Problem: Kingdom Ethics vs. Partisan Loyalty

The deepest problem with the Religious Right is not political but theological. The New Testament presents the kingdom of God as a reality that transcends and critiques every human political arrangement. Jesus refused the role of political messiah. He told Pilate that his kingdom was "not of this world" — not meaning it was irrelevant to this world, but that it operated by a fundamentally different logic. The kingdom advances through self-sacrifice, not coercion. Through persuasion, not legislation. Through the slow, patient work of communities living out an alternative vision of human flourishing.

When the church aligns itself with a political party, it inevitably subordinates kingdom ethics to partisan strategy. It must excuse the sins of its allies and exaggerate the sins of its opponents. It must treat electoral victory as evidence of divine favor and electoral defeat as evidence of spiritual warfare. It must, in short, adopt the logic of the political world — a logic of power, competition, and zero-sum calculation — and baptize it in the language of faith.

This is precisely what the prophets condemned. When Amos thundered against Israel, he was not addressing a secular state. He was addressing a religious society that had confused its own prosperity with God's approval. When Jeremiah wept over Jerusalem, he wept over a people who had placed their trust in political alliances and military power rather than in the justice and mercy of God. The prophetic tradition does not reject political engagement. It rejects the idolatry of political power — the belief that the right legislation, the right president, the right Supreme Court can accomplish what only the Spirit of God can accomplish.

"The church that marries the spirit of the age will find itself widowed in the next." This aphorism, often attributed to Dean Inge, describes precisely what has happened to American evangelicalism's political project. The movement married itself to the Republican Party, and as the party's character has changed, the church has found itself bound to positions and personalities that contradict its own stated values.

The Global Perspective

The American fusion of evangelical Christianity with right-wing politics is not universal. It is, in fact, an anomaly. In most of the world, politically engaged Christianity looks very different.

In Latin America, the most significant political theology of the twentieth century was liberation theology — a movement that read the Gospel through the lens of the poor and the oppressed and argued that God's preferential option was for those at the bottom of the social hierarchy. Whatever one thinks of liberation theology's Marxist analytical framework, its central claim — that the God of the Bible is not neutral in the face of injustice — is difficult to dismiss on scriptural grounds. Gustavo Gutierrez, Leonardo Boff, and Oscar Romero articulated a vision of political Christianity that was radical, justice-oriented, and rooted in the lived experience of the poor.

In South Africa, the church played a central role in the anti-apartheid movement. Desmond Tutu, Allan Boesak, and Beyers Naude drew on the prophetic tradition to challenge a system of racial oppression that was itself justified by a theological framework — the Dutch Reformed Church's theology of separate development. The Kairos Document of 1985, produced by South African theologians, distinguished between "state theology" (which legitimized the status quo), "church theology" (which offered vague appeals to reconciliation without addressing structural injustice), and "prophetic theology" (which named the sin and demanded concrete change). This taxonomy remains remarkably useful.

In South Korea, the minjung theology movement connected Christian faith with the struggles of workers, students, and democracy activists under authoritarian rule. In the Philippines, the church was instrumental in the People Power Revolution of 1986. In Poland, Catholic social teaching provided the intellectual framework for the Solidarity movement. In each case, political Christianity was oriented toward justice, liberation, and the empowerment of the oppressed — not toward the consolidation of power by those who already possessed it.

The American model, in which Christianity functions as the spiritual legitimation of an existing power structure, is the exception, not the rule. This should give American Christians pause.

How to Be Engaged Without Being Captured

None of this means Christians should withdraw from political life. The apolitical fundamentalism of the early twentieth century was its own form of failure — a refusal to love one's neighbor in the public square. The question is not whether Christians should be politically engaged but how they can be engaged without being captured by partisan loyalties that distort their witness.

Several principles emerge from the wreckage of the Religious Right. First, the church must maintain its prophetic independence from every party and every politician. This means the church must be willing to critique its allies as readily as its opponents. A church that speaks only against the sins of the other party is not prophetic. It is partisan with a stained-glass veneer.

Second, Christians must resist the reduction of their ethical tradition to a handful of issues selected for partisan convenience. The full range of biblical ethics — including economic justice, peacemaking, care for creation, hospitality to the stranger, and the dignity of every human being — must inform political engagement. A "whole-life" ethic, as articulated by figures like Ron Sider and the late Cardinal Joseph Bernardin, refuses to let any party claim a monopoly on Christian values.

Third, the church must recover the distinction between penultimate and ultimate loyalties. Political engagement is penultimate — important but not final. The kingdom of God is ultimate. When penultimate loyalties displace ultimate ones — when the party becomes the church, when the president becomes the pastor, when the platform becomes the creed — idolatry has occurred, regardless of how sincerely the participants believe otherwise.

Fourth, the church must learn from the global church. The American evangelical fusion of faith and right-wing politics is not the only model available. Christians in other contexts have demonstrated that it is possible to be politically engaged, passionately committed to justice, and theologically serious without becoming the chaplains of any political movement.

Finally, the church must recover its eschatological patience. The kingdom of God will not arrive through an election. It will not be established by a Supreme Court ruling. It will not be advanced by controlling school boards or winning culture wars. The kingdom comes as it has always come: through the slow, faithful, often invisible work of communities that embody an alternative way of being human. This does not mean politics is unimportant. It means politics is not ultimate. And when the church forgets that distinction, it loses not only its prophetic voice but its very identity.

The story of the Religious Right is a cautionary tale, not a model to be emulated. The church entered politics seeking to change the world and discovered that the world had changed the church. The path forward requires not less engagement but a fundamentally different kind — one rooted in the full breadth of the biblical tradition, accountable to the global church, and freed from the illusion that any political arrangement can substitute for the kingdom of God.

chapters.title: Whose Kingdom? Jesus and Political Power
chapters.summary: Jesus was offered every kingdom of the world by someone who actually had them to give, and what he did with the offer settles the question we keep reopening.
chapters.body:
Before Jesus preached a sermon or healed a single body, he was taken to a high place and shown every kingdom of the world. The one showing him had the authority to make the offer. All these I will give you, he said, if you will fall down and worship me (Matthew 4:9 ESV). It was not a hollow temptation. The kingdoms were really on the table. And the price was a single act of worship aimed in the wrong direction. Jesus refused, and the refusal is the founding decision of his entire ministry. He would not take the kingdoms of the world on the terms by which the kingdoms of the world are taken.

We reopen this question every election cycle as though Jesus never settled it. We ask how the church should hold political power, what it should do with influence, how it should bend the levers of the state toward righteousness. These are not foolish questions. But they are downstream of a prior question that the wilderness already answered, and we keep skipping the answer because we do not like it. The prior question is whether the kingdom of God advances by the means the world uses to advance its kingdoms. Jesus said no in the desert, said it again to Pilate, and said it most loudly on a cross. We have spent two thousand years pretending we did not hear.

The strongest objection to a hands-off reading deserves a full hearing, because it is not the objection of cowards. It comes from believers who say the church cannot retreat from public life and call the retreat holiness. They point out that the prophets confronted kings, that John the Baptist lost his head for telling Herod his marriage was unlawful, that William Wilberforce used political power to end the British slave trade, that Bonhoeffer joined a plot against Hitler. They say that to abandon the public square in the name of a kingdom not of this world is to leave the vulnerable at the mercy of whoever does not abandon it. That is a serious charge, and it is largely true. A church that washes its hands of power has often washed its hands of the people that power crushes.

I want to grant the whole of it, because the half-grant is a cheat. The prophets did confront kings. Christians did and should engage the machinery of justice. A faith that has nothing to say to Pharaoh is not the faith of the Exodus. The error I am warning against is not engagement. It is the belief that engagement means seizing the throne, that the kingdom of God is the kind of kingdom you install by winning, that Christ needs to govern through Caesar because he cannot govern any other way. Wilberforce did not try to make Britain the kingdom of God. He pressed a particular evil with the tools at hand and trusted a Lord who reigns whether or not the vote goes his way. The difference between that and Christian nationalism is the difference between salt and a coup.

So carry the governing text to its end. When Jesus stood before Pilate, the only man in the room with the power to kill him, Pilate asked if he was a king. Jesus answered with the sentence that should have ended the argument forever. My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting, that I might not be delivered over (John 18:36 ESV). Read what he is saying. He is not saying his kingdom has no bearing on this world. He is saying it does not come from this world's source and does not advance by this world's method. The proof he offers is the absence of fighting. A kingdom that fights to install its king is a kingdom of this world by definition. The kingdom of God is recognizable precisely by its refusal to take up the sword that every earthly kingdom requires.

This is the reversal that the nationalist reading cannot survive. The crowd on Palm Sunday wanted exactly the king the tempter offered, a king who would ride into Jerusalem and throw out Rome and restore the throne of David by force. They spread their cloaks and shouted hosanna, which means save us, and they meant save us from the empire. Jesus rode in on a donkey, the animal of peace, not a warhorse, and within the week the same crowd was screaming for his blood, because he would not be the king they wanted. They wanted power that conquers. He gave them power that dies. The triumphal entry is a deliberate refusal of the political kingship the people demanded, and we have turned it into a parade, missing that it was a protest against everything we use it to celebrate.

Augustine watched a Christian empire convince itself it was the kingdom of God, and he wrote the book that should have inoculated us. There are two cities, he said, built by two loves, and they are mixed together in this age so that no earthly city is the city of God and none is wholly outside it (Augustine 426). Rome was not the kingdom of God when it was pagan and did not become the kingdom of God when it was Christian. The two cities run through every nation and every heart, and the fatal mistake of every age is to identify one earthly kingdom as the city of God and then to defend that kingdom as though defending God. America is not the city of God. No nation is. The believer holds dual citizenship and knows which passport is eternal.

Stanley Hauerwas pressed this into the bone for our own time. The church does not have a social strategy, he wrote with William Willimon. The church is a social strategy (Hauerwas and Willimon 1989). The way the church holds power is by being a different kind of power, a community that tells the truth, welcomes the stranger, forgives the enemy, and refuses to win by the means that require it to stop being the church. The moment the church decides it must capture the state to accomplish its mission, it has confessed that it no longer believes its own gospel can accomplish anything, that it needs Caesar's sword because the cross was not enough. That confession is the heart of the thing, and it is a confession of unbelief dressed up as zeal.

I have to indict myself here, because I have wanted the shortcut. I have stood in election seasons and felt the pull to believe that if my side simply won, the kingdom would advance, that righteousness was one majority away. That is the wilderness temptation in a voting booth. It offers the kingdoms of the world for a single act of misdirected worship, the worship that says power saves. I have bowed toward it more than once, not with my words but with my anxieties, with where my hope went when the returns came in. The gauge of my hope on election night has told me the truth about which kingdom I was actually serving, and the truth has not always flattered me.

The cross does the decisive work. Because on the cross Jesus took the throne by the one means no empire understands. He did not seize power. He absorbed it. He let the combined authority of temple and empire do its worst, and he forgave them from inside the execution, and on the third day God overturned their verdict. That is how the kingdom comes. Not by climbing the high place and accepting the kingdoms on the tempter's terms, but by going down to the lowest place and being raised by a power no kingdom can kill. The church that grasps for political power has not understood the cross. It is trying to win a war that was already won by losing.

Whose kingdom. Not ours, and not our country's. His. And his does not need our majorities to arrive. It needs our faithfulness while we wait. The shortcut was offered once to a better man than any of us, in a high place, by someone who had the kingdoms to give. He said no, and his no is the pattern. We say yes, again and again, and call our yes obedience.

The kingdom is not of this world. He told us plainly. We keep voting otherwise.

### Works Cited

Augustine. The City of God. Circa 426.

Hauerwas, Stanley, and William H. Willimon. Resident Aliens: Life in the Christian Colony. Abingdon Press, 1989.

chapters.title: Why People Are Leaving the Church
chapters.summary: The exodus from organized Christianity is the defining religious story of our era. The reasons people leave are not the reasons most pastors assume, and what the departed still hunger for should unsettle every congregation that thinks the problem is better marketing.
chapters.body:
The numbers are no longer debatable. They have not been debatable for at least a decade, though the institutional church has spent much of that decade debating them anyway, as if the appropriate response to a hemorrhaging wound is a prolonged discussion about whether the patient is actually bleeding.

In 2006, Gallup found that 73 percent of Americans identified as Christian. By 2022, that number had fallen to 68 percent. Pew Research Center's 2021 data showed a steeper picture: only 63 percent of American adults identified as Christian, down from 78 percent in 2007. The Public Religion Research Institute placed the figure even lower, at 61 percent, in its 2023 American Values Atlas. These are not marginal fluctuations within the noise of survey methodology. These represent the most rapid secularization of any major Western nation in the modern era, compressed into roughly fifteen years.

But the headline numbers, as dramatic as they are, obscure what is actually happening. Christianity is not declining uniformly. Evangelical Protestantism has held relatively steady in raw numbers, though its share of the population is shrinking. Black Protestantism has remained stable. It is mainline Protestantism and, increasingly, Roman Catholicism that are experiencing catastrophic losses. The Catholic Church in the United States has lost roughly one-third of its cradle Catholics, a departure that would constitute a demographic emergency in any other institution. Former Catholics now represent the second-largest "denomination" in the country, outnumbered only by current Catholics.

The question that matters, of course, is not merely what the numbers say but why the numbers say it. And here the church has largely failed, not because it has not asked the question, but because it has consistently preferred comforting answers to honest ones.

The Reasons Pastors Assume (And Why They Are Mostly Wrong)

Ask a typical pastor why people are leaving the church, and you will hear a predictable set of explanations. People are too busy. The culture has become too secular. Young people are distracted by technology. Sunday sports leagues compete with worship services. People are selfish, individualistic, consumerist. They want comfort, not commitment. They have been led astray by a hostile media.

These explanations share a common feature: they locate the problem entirely outside the church. The institution is fine. The product is excellent. The customers are defective. This is, to borrow a phrase from the business world, a catastrophically bad diagnosis, the kind that precedes bankruptcy.

The data tell a different story. When researchers actually ask people why they left, the answers are remarkably consistent across multiple studies, and they point the finger squarely at the institution itself.

Josh Packard and Ashleigh Hope's research, published in Church Refugees (2015), found that the people leaving churches were not the nominally committed or the spiritually indifferent. They were, disproportionately, the most involved members: Sunday school teachers, worship leaders, committee chairs, small group facilitators. These were not people who drifted away out of apathy. They were people who had given years, sometimes decades, of committed service and finally concluded that the institution was no longer worthy of their investment.

The Barna Group's extensive research, spanning two decades, has identified five primary drivers of church departure: hypocrisy (perceived disconnect between what the church preaches and how it behaves), political entanglement (the sense that the church has become an arm of a political party), intellectual dishonesty (the refusal to engage honestly with science, history, or difficult questions), exclusion (the treatment of women, LGBTQ individuals, racial minorities, or doubters as second-class members), and clergy abuse and cover-ups (the institutional protection of predators at the expense of victims).

Notice what is absent from this list. Nobody is leaving because worship services need better lighting. Nobody is leaving because the church lacks a coffee bar in the lobby. Nobody is leaving because the sermons are not entertaining enough. The fixation on stylistic upgrades that has consumed American church culture for the past three decades, the millions spent on fog machines and branded sermon series and Instagram-worthy lobbies, has been an elaborate exercise in treating a symptom that does not exist while ignoring the disease that does.

Hypocrisy: The Original Sin of Institutional Religion

When leavers cite hypocrisy, they are not merely observing that Christians sometimes fail to live up to their ideals. Everyone understands that human beings are imperfect. What they are identifying is something more specific and more damaging: the systematic gap between the church's public moral pronouncements and its institutional behavior.

A church that preaches radical generosity while its senior pastor lives in a mansion funded by tithes from working-class families. A denomination that thunders against sexual immorality while quietly reassigning priests credibly accused of molesting children. A congregation that proclaims the equality of all people before God while maintaining an all-white, all-male leadership structure in a diverse community. These are not instances of individual moral failure. They are patterns of institutional dishonesty, and the people who leave can see them with a clarity that those inside the institution often cannot.

The sociologist Robert Wuthnow documented this dynamic extensively in his research on American religion. He found that institutional trust, once lost, is almost impossible to recover, and that the perception of hypocrisy is the single most corrosive force in religious disaffiliation. People can forgive failure. They cannot forgive pretense.

The Political Captivity of the Church

The entanglement of American Christianity with partisan politics, particularly the near-total identification of white evangelicalism with the Republican Party, has driven more people from the church than any theological dispute in modern memory. This is not a partisan observation. It is a demographic fact.

Ryan Burge, a political scientist at Eastern Illinois University and a Baptist pastor, has documented this extensively. His data show that political identity now predicts religious affiliation more reliably than religious affiliation predicts political identity. In other words, people are not joining the Republican Party because they are evangelical. They are leaving evangelicalism because they are not Republican. The causal arrow has reversed.

For younger Americans especially, the association between Christianity and conservative politics has become so tight that many cannot imagine one without the other. A 2022 survey by the Survey Center on American Life found that among Americans under thirty who left their childhood religion, 60 percent cited the church's stance on social and political issues as a significant factor. When a twenty-five-year-old says, "I am not a Christian," she may not be making a theological statement about the divinity of Jesus. She may be making a sociological statement: "I do not belong to the political tribe that has claimed Christianity as its brand."

The tragedy of this is difficult to overstate. A faith tradition that began with an itinerant rabbi executed by the state has become, in the public imagination, a chaplaincy for state power. The cross, which was Rome's instrument of political terror, now appears on the podiums of political rallies. Whether or not individual churches endorse specific candidates, the brand contamination is real, and it is driving a generation away.

What "Leaving" Actually Looks Like

The popular assumption, shared by both anxious churchgoers and triumphant secularists, is that people who leave the church become atheists. They do not. The data on this are unambiguous.

According to Pew Research Center's 2021 study, the fastest-growing religious category in America is not atheism or agnosticism but "nothing in particular," a category that now represents 20 percent of the adult population, up from 12 percent in 2007. This group is distinct from atheists and agnostics in important ways. Many of them believe in God or a higher power. Many pray, at least occasionally. Many describe themselves as spiritual. What they have rejected is not the sacred but the institution. They have not abandoned transcendence. They have abandoned organized religion.

The term that has emerged to describe this population is "spiritual but not religious," or SBNR. It is a clumsy phrase, and it frustrates theologians on both sides: traditional believers think it is shallow, and committed atheists think it is incoherent. But it describes something real. There are tens of millions of Americans who believe that the universe has a spiritual dimension, who seek meaning and connection beyond the material, who may even consider themselves followers of Jesus in some sense, but who have concluded that the institutional church is not the place where these needs can be met. They are not rejecting God. They are rejecting the church's claim to be God's authorized representative.

This distinction, between leaving God and leaving the institution, is one that the church has been catastrophically slow to understand. When a pastor says, "Young people are turning away from God," he is usually wrong. What young people are turning away from is the pastor's institution. The conflation of the two is itself part of the problem. An organization that cannot distinguish between itself and the divine has already lost the capacity for self-criticism that might save it.

What the Leavers Say

In qualitative research, the voices of those who have left are remarkably consistent, and remarkably painful to hear.

"I didn't leave because I stopped believing. I left because I couldn't keep pretending that what was happening in that building on Sunday morning had anything to do with Jesus." This sentiment, expressed with minor variations by hundreds of respondents in Packard and Hope's research, represents the dominant narrative of church departure.

David Kinnaman's research for the Barna Group, published in You Lost Me (2011) and UnChristian (2007), found that young adults who left the church described it as "overprotective" (stifling honest inquiry and engagement with the broader culture), "shallow" (failing to offer intellectually serious engagement with faith and doubt), "anti-science" (requiring rejection of established scientific consensus as a condition of belonging), "repressive" (particularly regarding sexuality, in ways perceived as harmful rather than holy), "exclusive" (unwelcoming to those who do not conform to narrow cultural norms), and "doubtless" (demanding certainty and punishing questions).

The theologian Sarah Bessey, who has written extensively about her own experience of church departure and return, describes what many leavers feel: "The church broke my heart long before the world ever could." This is not the language of indifference. It is the language of betrayal. People do not grieve institutions they never loved.

What makes these testimonies so devastating for the church is that they come disproportionately from people who were deeply invested. These are not outsiders lobbing criticism from a comfortable distance. These are people who sang in the choir, served on the building committee, led vacation Bible school, tithed faithfully, and wept during worship. They left not because they did not care enough but because they cared too much to keep participating in something they had come to see as dishonest.

What the Leavers Still Hunger For

Here is the part of the story that should keep every pastor, every denominational leader, every seminary professor awake at night: the people who left the church did not stop being hungry.

Casper ter Kuile's research at Harvard Divinity School, published in The Power of Ritual (2020), documented the ways in which people who have left organized religion are building alternative communities of meaning, purpose, and connection. CrossFit gyms function as covenant communities with shared suffering, mutual accountability, and communal identity. SoulCycle classes use candles, music, and inspirational language that is indistinguishable from a worship service. The Sunday Assembly movement explicitly offers "church for people who don't do God," complete with singing, readings, moments of reflection, and community meals.

These substitutes are revealing. They demonstrate that the needs the church exists to meet, the hunger for community, meaning, transcendence, moral formation, and encounters with something larger than the self, are not going away simply because the church is failing to meet them. Human beings are, as the sociologist Christian Smith has argued, "moral, believing animals." The question is not whether people will seek meaning and belonging. The question is where.

The research consistently identifies four persistent hungers among those who have left the church. The first is community: not the superficial friendliness of a church lobby but genuine, vulnerable, accountable relationships in which people are known and loved in their complexity. The second is meaning: a coherent narrative that makes sense of suffering, injustice, and death, something more robust than "everything happens for a reason" and more honest than "God has a plan." The third is transcendence: encounter with mystery, beauty, and awe, the sense that the universe is not merely material but shot through with significance. The fourth is justice: the conviction that faith should make the world more humane, not less, and that a God worth worshipping is a God who cares about the poor, the marginalized, and the oppressed.

Notice that every one of these hungers is something the church, at its best, is uniquely positioned to address. The church has two millennia of communal practice. It has a story vast enough to encompass every human experience. It has a liturgical tradition designed to cultivate encounters with the sacred. It has a prophetic tradition that has consistently demanded justice for the vulnerable. The raw materials are all there. The failure is not one of resources but of will, honesty, and imagination.

What the Church Must Hear

The people who have left the church are not its enemies. They are, in many cases, its most honest critics, the ones who loved it enough to be wounded by its failures and clear-eyed enough to name what went wrong. If the church cannot hear their voices without becoming defensive, it will continue to decline, not because the world is hostile to faith but because the institution has become hostile to honesty.

The sociologist Robert Bellah, in Habits of the Heart (1985), warned that American individualism was eroding the institutional structures that made community life possible. He was right. But the solution to individualism is not to demand that people return to institutions that have not earned their trust. The solution is to build institutions worthy of trust, communities that tell the truth about their own failures, that welcome questions instead of punishing them, that practice the justice they preach, and that offer not certainty but faithfulness.

The German theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer, writing from a Nazi prison in 1944, anticipated much of what we are witnessing. "We are moving toward a completely religionless time," he wrote. "People as they are now simply cannot be religious anymore." Bonhoeffer did not see this as a catastrophe. He saw it as an invitation, an opportunity for the church to strip away the institutional scaffolding and cultural prestige that had accumulated over centuries and rediscover what was essential: Jesus Christ, present in the midst of human suffering, calling his followers not to power but to service.

Bonhoeffer was executed by the Nazis in April 1945. He never had the chance to develop his vision of a "religionless Christianity." But his intuition was prophetically precise. The institutional trappings that the church clings to most fiercely, the buildings, the budgets, the cultural influence, the political access, are precisely the things that are driving people away. And the thing the church has always claimed to be about, encounter with a God who enters the world's suffering and transforms it from within, is precisely the thing people are still looking for.

The exodus from the church is not a crisis of faith. It is a crisis of integrity. People are not leaving because they have too little hunger for God. They are leaving because the church has too little hunger for honesty. And until the institution can hear that distinction, the bleeding will not stop.

The question before the church is not how to get people back. That framing already reveals the problem, treating human beings as a resource to be acquired rather than a community to be formed. The question is whether the church is willing to become the kind of community that people would not want to leave: truthful, just, humble, intellectually serious, spiritually alive, and genuinely committed to the way of Jesus rather than the preservation of its own institutional life.

That is a harder question. And the answer, so far, is not encouraging.

chapters.title: Why Young Adults Aren't Coming Back
chapters.summary: The exodus of 18-to-35-year-olds from American churches is not a mystery, and it is not about worship style. It is about credibility — and the church is losing on every front that matters to this generation.
chapters.body:
The numbers are no longer debatable. According to the Pew Research Center's 2021 survey, only 36 percent of Millennials and 31 percent of Generation Z identify as Protestant or Catholic, compared to 67 percent of the Silent Generation. The American Enterprise Institute's 2023 study found that fewer than one in four adults under 30 attends a religious service monthly. Gallup's longitudinal data shows that church membership among Americans aged 18-29 dropped from 51 percent in 1999 to 36 percent in 2020 — and that was before the pandemic accelerated the decline. The Survey Center on American Life at AEI reports that roughly 40 percent of Generation Z identifies as religiously unaffiliated, the highest percentage for any generation in American history.

These are not fluctuations. They are not a phase. They represent a structural shift in the relationship between American young adults and organized religion — a shift that shows no signs of reversing. And the church's dominant responses to this crisis reveal, with painful clarity, that most congregations do not understand what is happening to them or why.

The temptation is to frame this as a problem of marketing — as though the church were a product that simply needs better packaging. This instinct is catastrophically wrong, and acting on it has only accelerated the exodus. The young adults who are leaving (or who never arrived) are not looking for a more appealing consumer experience. They are asking whether the church is telling the truth. And too often, they are concluding that it is not.

What the Church Thinks the Problem Is

Walk into any denominational meeting, any pastoral conference, any megachurch leadership summit where the question of reaching young adults is on the agenda, and you will hear a remarkably consistent set of proposed solutions. Better coffee in the lobby. A more contemporary worship band. Fog machines and LED screens. A "young adult pastor" with skinny jeans and a curated Instagram presence. A sermon series on "relevant" topics — dating, anxiety, career discernment — delivered with self-deprecating humor and pop culture references. A rebrand that removes the word "church" from the name in favor of something that sounds like a boutique coworking space.

These efforts are not merely insufficient. They are actively counterproductive. Every young adult can see exactly what is happening: an institution attempting to disguise itself as something it is not. The effect is not attraction but repulsion. It communicates that the church has so little confidence in its own message that it must borrow credibility from consumer culture. A twenty-five-year-old who grew up marinated in advertising — who has been sold to since before she could read — can detect inauthenticity with the precision of a trained sommelier detecting cork taint. The church's attempts at cultural relevance do not read as relevant. They read as desperate.

The sociological data confirms this. The Barna Group's extensive research on young adult disengagement, published in their 2011 study You Lost Me and updated in subsequent surveys, identifies six primary reasons young adults leave the church. Not one of them is "the music was not contemporary enough." Not one is "the coffee was inadequate." The reasons are: the church feels overprotective, shallow, anti-science, repressive, exclusive, and unfriendly to doubt. These are not aesthetic complaints. They are credibility complaints. They concern the substance of what the church teaches and practices, not the style in which it is delivered.

What Young Adults Actually Want: Authenticity

The word "authenticity" has been so overused in church growth literature that it has nearly lost its meaning. But the concept it points to is real and specific. Young adults are not looking for perfection. They are looking for honesty — including, and especially, honesty about imperfection.

A church that presents itself as having all the answers alienates young adults who live daily with ambiguity, complexity, and uncertainty. A pastor who never admits doubt, never acknowledges the difficulty of a biblical text, never confesses that some questions do not have easy answers — that pastor is not perceived as strong. He is perceived as dishonest. Young adults have watched too many leaders who projected certainty in public and were exposed as frauds in private. The crisis of pastoral credibility — from Ted Haggard to Jerry Falwell Jr. to Ravi Zacharias — has made this generation deeply allergic to performative confidence.

What authenticity looks like in practice is painfully simple and painfully rare. It looks like a pastor saying "I do not know" when confronted with a question that has no clear answer. It looks like a church that acknowledges its own history of complicity in injustice rather than whitewashing its past. It looks like worship that makes space for lament, not just celebration — that takes seriously the reality of suffering rather than papering over it with triumphalist choruses. It looks like a community where vulnerability is modeled from the pulpit, not just expected from the pews.

The churches that are actually reaching young adults understand this intuitively. They tend to be smaller, less polished, and more willing to sit with discomfort. They do not have all the answers, and they are not embarrassed by this. They have traded the performance of certainty for the practice of honest wrestling — and young adults, starved for institutions that do not pretend, find this irresistible.

The Justice Factor

If authenticity is the doorway, justice is the hallway. For adults under thirty-five, a church's credibility is inseparable from its engagement with systemic injustice — and on this front, the American church has been failing catastrophically for decades.

The data here is unambiguous. The Public Religion Research Institute's 2022 survey found that 70 percent of adults aged 18-29 believe that racism remains a significant problem in American society. Yet when these same young adults look at the church, what do they see? In the aftermath of George Floyd's murder in 2020, the majority of white evangelical churches either said nothing, offered vaguely spiritual platitudes about "unity," or actively opposed the language of systemic racism as a secular ideology incompatible with the gospel. The Southern Baptist Convention passed a resolution acknowledging the reality of racism in 2019, only to see prominent leaders spend the next two years arguing that Critical Race Theory was a greater threat to the church than racism itself. For young adults who watched Black men and women die on their phone screens, the church's response was not just inadequate. It was morally disqualifying.

Climate is another front on which the church has surrendered credibility with an entire generation. A 2023 Pew survey found that 76 percent of adults under 30 say climate change is a major threat. Among white evangelicals of all ages, that number drops to 23 percent. Young adults who take seriously the scientific consensus on climate change — which is to say, the overwhelming majority of young adults — encounter a church that either ignores the issue entirely or actively dismisses it as a distraction from "the real gospel." The theological resources for environmental engagement are rich: the creation mandate, the prophetic tradition of caring for the land, the eschatological vision of a renewed earth. That the church has largely refused to deploy these resources in the face of a crisis that defines this generation's future is, for many young adults, evidence that the church cares more about political alignment than about the world God made.

Poverty presents a similar pattern. Young adults facing student debt, stagnant wages, and a housing market that has locked them out of homeownership look to churches and see institutions that preach individual responsibility while ignoring systemic economic structures. The biblical prophets — Amos, Micah, Isaiah — thundered against economic injustice with a specificity that would make most modern pastors profoundly uncomfortable. Yet the average evangelical sermon on poverty amounts to "be generous with your tithe" without engaging the structural questions of why, in the wealthiest nation in history, millions of people cannot afford medical care. For young adults who live these economic realities daily, the church's silence on systemic injustice is not neutral. It is a loud statement about whose interests the church serves.

The Inclusion Factor

No single issue has driven more young adults from the church than its posture toward LGBTQ+ people. The data on this point is overwhelming and has been consistent for over a decade.

Barna's research has found that the most common perception of the church among non-churchgoing young adults is that it is "anti-homosexual" — more common than "judgmental," "hypocritical," or "too political," all of which also rank high. PRRI's 2023 data shows that 79 percent of Americans aged 18-29 support same-sex marriage, including 51 percent of young white evangelicals. The gap between the church's official teaching and the moral convictions of an entire generation is not a gap. It is a chasm.

This is not the place to adjudicate the theological question of same-sex relationships. Faithful Christians hold a range of positions, and the exegetical and hermeneutical arguments are complex. But what must be said — what the church cannot avoid saying if it wants to understand why young adults are leaving — is that the way the church has engaged this issue has been, for millions of young adults, the single most powerful evidence that the church is not a safe or credible institution.

Young adults have watched churches use LGBTQ+ people as rhetorical targets while ignoring divorce, materialism, and gossip. They have watched pastors devote sermon after sermon to sexual ethics while remaining silent on racial injustice. They have watched denominations invest millions of dollars in political campaigns against same-sex marriage while cutting budgets for homeless ministries. They have watched families expel their own children in the name of biblical fidelity. The message received — regardless of the message intended — is that the church's moral passion is selective, and that its selectivity correlates suspiciously with the populations it finds most culturally threatening.

For a generation that counts LGBTQ+ people among their closest friends, family members, and colleagues — and that sees no contradiction between this reality and genuine faith — the church's posture is not merely a disagreement. It is a moral emergency. And increasingly, it is a dealbreaker.

The Hypocrisy Factor

Beneath the specific issues of justice and inclusion lies a deeper problem: the perception — grounded in abundant evidence — that the church does not practice what it preaches.

Young adults watched eighty-one percent of white evangelicals vote for a thrice-married casino owner who bragged about sexual assault, and then heard those same evangelicals lecture them about sexual morality. They watched church leaders who preached "family values" endorse policies that separated migrant children from their parents at the border. They watched pastors who thundered against "the world" accumulate personal wealth that would have scandalized the apostle Paul. They watched denominations that preached the authority of scripture ignore the parts of scripture that addressed their own sins while weaponizing the parts that addressed other people's.

The philosopher Charles Taylor, in his landmark A Secular Age, argued that the modern "malaise of immanence" — the sense of spiritual flatness that characterizes secular societies — is not primarily the result of intellectual arguments against God but of the failure of religious institutions to embody a compelling alternative to consumer capitalism. Young adults are not, by and large, philosophical materialists. Surveys consistently show that the majority describe themselves as "spiritual" even when they reject organized religion. They have not lost interest in transcendence. They have lost confidence that the church has access to it.

This is the hypocrisy factor at its deepest level. It is not merely that individual Christians are imperfect — every young adult understands that, and most would be drawn to a community that honestly acknowledged its imperfection. The problem is that the church as an institution systematically behaves in ways that contradict its own stated values, and then deploys theological language to justify the contradiction. When a pastor preaches humility from a stage designed to center his own celebrity, the medium contradicts the message. When a church preaches generosity while building a $130 million worship center, the budget contradicts the sermon. When a denomination preaches the authority of scripture while ignoring the 2,000 verses about poverty, the selectivity reveals the real authority: not the text, but the culture that determines which parts of the text to emphasize.

Young adults see this with devastating clarity, and they do not have the institutional loyalty to overlook it.

The Digital Factor

The pandemic accelerated a trend that was already well underway: the migration of spiritual life from embodied community to digital consumption. By 2021, the Barna Group found that one in three practicing Christians had stopped attending church entirely, with many replacing in-person participation with online content — podcasts, livestreams, YouTube sermons, and the curated social media presence of celebrity pastors.

For young adults, this shift has a particular valence. They have grown up in an ecosystem of parasocial relationships — one-directional connections with media figures who feel intimate but are not. A young adult who listens to a popular pastor's podcast three times a week, follows that pastor on Instagram, and watches their sermon livestream on Sunday may feel genuinely connected to that pastor and that community. But the connection is illusory. There is no mutual knowledge, no shared obligation, no friction, no cost. It is community without covenant — all the emotional resonance of belonging with none of the demands.

This is, in one sense, the ultimate consumer religion: a spiritual experience optimized for individual preference, available on demand, and requiring no sacrifice. It is also profoundly insufficient. The New Testament knows nothing of disembodied faith. The church, in Paul's theology, is a body — not a metaphor for a body, but an actual community of people who bear one another's burdens, confront one another's sins, share one another's meals, and are physically present to one another in suffering. You cannot weep with those who weep through a screen. You cannot bear a burden you do not know about because your only connection to the community is a weekly livestream. You cannot be formed into the image of Christ by a parasocial relationship with a charismatic communicator.

The digital factor is thus both a symptom and a cause of the exodus. It is a symptom because it reveals what young adults find missing in actual churches — they would not seek digital substitutes if the embodied reality were compelling. And it is a cause because the more spiritual life is consumed digitally, the less capacity people develop for the difficult, friction-filled, deeply transformative experience of actual community. The church's competitor is not other churches. It is the entire architecture of digital life, which offers an endless supply of content that feels like connection without any of the cost.

What Churches That Are Reaching Young Adults Do Differently

Despite the bleak data, there are churches that are reaching young adults — not by chasing cultural trends but by recovering something ancient. These churches share several characteristics that are worth examining closely because they point toward a way forward that does not require the church to abandon its identity.

They practice radical honesty. These churches do not pretend to have all the answers. They create space for questions, doubt, and intellectual struggle. They engage seriously with science, philosophy, and the genuine difficulties of biblical interpretation. They do not treat doubt as a spiritual disease to be cured but as a necessary companion to mature faith. The model here is not the certainty of the lecture hall but the honesty of the seminar room — a community of learners wrestling together with texts and traditions that are genuinely difficult.

They engage justice concretely, not abstractly. These churches do not merely preach about justice; they practice it. They run legal clinics for undocumented immigrants. They organize tenant unions. They show up at school board meetings. They partner with community organizations that address systemic issues. Their justice engagement is not a program staffed by volunteers; it is embedded in the church's identity and budget. Young adults can tell the difference between a church that talks about justice and a church that spends money on it.

They demand something. This may be the most counterintuitive finding: the churches that attract young adults are not the ones that ask the least of them but the ones that ask the most. Dietrich Bonhoeffer's distinction between cheap grace and costly grace is acutely relevant here. A faith that costs nothing is worth nothing, and young adults know it. The churches that are growing among this demographic tend to have rigorous membership processes, high expectations for community participation, and a clear sense of shared mission that requires actual sacrifice. Young adults are not looking for a low-commitment social club. They are looking for something worth giving their lives to.

They practice genuine community. Not community as a buzzword in a mission statement, but community as a daily reality — shared meals, mutual aid, physical proximity, honest conflict and honest reconciliation. These churches tend to be smaller, often meeting in homes or shared spaces rather than purpose-built campuses. They emphasize small groups not as a program but as the primary expression of church life. They create structures in which people actually know one another — not as fellow audience members at a weekly performance, but as members of an actual body with actual obligations to one another.

They separate the faith from partisan politics. Young adults have watched the church become so entangled with one political party that the gospel itself has become a partisan artifact. Churches that reach young adults tend to be politically engaged but not politically captured. They speak prophetically to both parties. They refuse to let the gospel be reduced to a voter guide. They recover the biblical tradition of prophetic critique that stands outside all human power structures rather than baptizing any one of them.

"The church that is married to the spirit of this age will be widowed in the next." — William Ralph Inge

The path forward for the American church is not more fog machines. It is not better branding. It is not a hipper pastor or a sleeker app. The path forward is the painful, exhilarating work of becoming what the church claims to be: a community that tells the truth, practices justice, welcomes the stranger, sits with suffering, demands sacrifice, and points beyond itself to a reality that consumer culture cannot provide. Young adults are not leaving the church because they have outgrown the need for transcendence. They are leaving because the church has failed to provide it.

The good news — and it is genuinely good news — is that the solution is not innovation but recovery. Everything the church needs to reach this generation, it already possesses. The prophetic tradition. The practice of radical hospitality. The theology of a God who enters suffering rather than explaining it away. The vision of a community that crosses every boundary the world erects. The church does not need to become something new. It needs to become what it always claimed to be. And if it does — if it trades performance for honesty, comfort for justice, and cultural power for prophetic faithfulness — it will find that the generation it thought it had lost was waiting for it all along.
